10569-skilled-assistance-ship-s-company-:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the ninth part of Ship's Company, opening with the night-watchman growling about a woman who asks after the ship Silvia. She has come four or five times in a week, sweet when she wants help, sharp when she does not, and she calls him the Sleeping Beauty of Wapping. Jacobs writes in comic, riverside speech.

Talk of women who start kind and soapy, then fly into temper, leads to Captain Pinner, who traded to Hull on the schooner Snipe. Skilled assistance, promised and botched, fills the tale. Readers get a short, funny Jacobs story of sailors, women, and well-meant help gone wrong.
10789-the-head-of-the-family-sailor-s-kn:
W. W. Jacobs's "The Head of the Family," the ninth tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, follows Mr. Letts, a ship's cook turned adrift. His crew musters to see him off from the schooner Curlew with relief, and unkind words follow him along the quay at Dunchurch. Undaunted, Letts lodges his sea-chest and sits by the sea, planning his future.

The comedy turns on Letts's schemes to become master of a household, with Jacobs's usual mix of sailors, lodging-houses, and sharp talk. The story stands alone, funny in its own right. Readers get another Thames-side yarn, told with the author's easy command of working men's speech.
11189-the-madness-of-mr-lister-captains-:
Old Jem Lister of the Susannah suffers, in the watchman's phrase, from two devils: love of strong drink and miserliness, united only in getting a drink without paying. His shipmates grow tired of watching him hover at public-house doors cadging drinks, and Bill Henshaw delivers a blistering rebuke. Lister's revenge, when it comes, is petty, funny, and entirely in character.

Jacobs uses Lister to mock a familiar waterfront type, the man who wants pleasure at others' expense. The story's comedy is verbal, carried by dialect and the watchman's asides. It reads quickly and stands as one of the sharper character sketches in the Captains All series.
11479-the-substitute-deep-waters-part-9:
The night-watchman returns to his office fire after answering the wharf bell. Boys have rung it three times that week, he complains. He remembers an office boy from an earlier time. The boy was undersized, with a face like bad pie-crust.

White cuffs, a stand-up collar, and a little bowler hat complete the picture. The tale that follows is the watchman's revenge comedy. A woman with a big bag arrives at the gate, smiling. The watchman trusts no smiles and keeps his guard up. Jacobs tells it in the old man's own voice.
12129-a-mixed-proposal-the-lady-of-the-b:
Part 9 of Jacobs's Lady of the Barge stories, A Mixed Proposal, opens with Major Brill, late of the Fenshire Volunteers. He stands before the small piece of glass in the hatstand and gives his new silk hat a slight tilt over the right eye. With cane and new gloves, and a military but squeaky tread, he passes out into the road on a glorious day.

The proposal that follows is mixed in more ways than one, as Brill's soldierly confidence meets the realities of courtship, money, and village opinion. Jacobs plays the major's vanity against his vulnerability, in a comedy where a tilted hat and a squeaky tread announce what kind of man is proposing.
12159-easy-money-night-watches-part-9:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short story for Night Watches, his 1911 collection of comic Thames-side tales told by a night watchman. The narrator frames the action with a sour moral about marriage, then lets Sam Small, Ginger Dick, and Peter Russet prove it.

Sam nephew, a young sailor new to London, falls hard for a girl his aunt distrusts, and the three sailors take it on themselves to test her. Ginger plays the suitor on a day out, complete with omnibus ride and flattery, to see how she responds. The scheme exposes more about the testers than the girl. Jacobs comedy rests on working men who pose as moral judges while enjoying the very flirtation they condemn.
12209-the-persecution-of-bob-pretty-odd-:
An old man on his bench outside the Cauliflower pub tells the tale in The Persecution of Bob Pretty, a comic story from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. Two young walkers, resting at noon with beer and a churchwarden pipe, listen politely to his memories of poaching.

Bob Pretty, a poacher of local fame, torments keepers and farmers with tricks, snares, and narrow escapes. Bill Chambers warns him he is foolhardy, and the next night Farmer Hall field proves it. Jacobs builds the comedy from village talk: boasts, warnings, and the slow revenge of gamekeepers. The story is a fond portrait of a rogue who lives by wits, and of neighbors who enjoy his exploits while scolding them.
12398-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of:
Samuel Richardson Clarissa reaches its end in this ninth and final volume, told in letters. Belford writes to Lovelace of Clarissa silent devotion, strong symptoms of approaching dissolution, and her comfort to cousin and seducer alike.

Clarissa wishes for her parents last blessing, but says God would not let her depend for comfort on any but Himself. She begs the Colonel not to avenge her wrongs and Belford to heal all breaches. Later letters follow Lovelace remorse, family grief, and the settlement of her affairs. The volume closes one of the longest novels in English with death, forgiveness, and moral reckoning. Richardson ending made Clarissa a landmark of the sentimental novel.
21898-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
St. Nicholas, the great American children's magazine, speaks in this July 1878 number, the ninth of its fifth volume. The lead tale, Charles H. Woodman's The Girl Who Saved the General, opens on St. John Island off the Carolina coast. Robert Gibbes keeps open hall in a brick mansion under live oaks. His house is full at all seasons, with eight children and seven orphan cousins at play.

The Revolutionary War presses on that peaceful house, as the frontispiece of a girl riding through shot and shell promises. St. Nicholas, edited for Scribner, set the standard for children's magazines of its age. Stories, poems, and pictures were made to a high polish. A single issue preserves the taste of a whole era of American childhood.
27717-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-october-:
Joseph R. Buchanan edited this October 1887 issue of his Journal of Man, a monthly devoted to anthropology, psychology, and reform. The issue mixes an essay on the Oriental view of humanity with a long miscellany of short news items and commentary.

Its pages touch religion and science, land reform, women's rights, education in France, electricity, and the telegraph, alongside a chapter correcting the organology of Gall and Spurzheim. The journal shows how one nineteenth-century editor linked mind science, medicine, and social reform into a single program. Buchanan's own chapter on cerebral science argues for correcting the organology of Gall and Spurzheim.
31194-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Volume nine of Stories by American Authors, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1896, collects six stories of the old South, the sea, and small-town life. Thomas Nelson Page opens with Marse Chan, a tale of old Virginia first printed in Century Magazine in April 1884. In it, a rider on an eastern Virginia ridge road meets a Black man calling for his dog by a worm fence.

Charles S. Gage follows with Mr. Bixby's Christmas Visitor, C. H. White with Eli, Milicent Washburn Shinn with Young Strong of The Clarion, Captain Roland T. Coffin with How Old Wiggins Wore Ship, and Leonard Kip with Mas Has Come. The volume samples American magazine fiction at its most regional and warm-hearted.
34043-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-9:
H. Bolingbroke Mudie edited this issue of The Esperantist, number nine for July 1904, published by the London Esperanto Club at Outer Temple. Single copies cost fourpence, and a yearly subscription cost three shillings. Contents run from editor's notes through the end of Act One of The Tempest, translated by A. Motteau, and meditations of Marcus Aurelius, translated by K. Eucharis.

Adventures of Count Fathom, Esperanto in Japan, poems, Boulogne, the language of flowers, and a certificate of merit fill the issue, with a night in Calabre and correspondence to close. The magazine shows Esperanto's early world in full. It serves readers curious about the planned language's first years.
7162-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-9:
Part nine of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter thirty two, Coronation Day, stepping back a few hours to Westminster Abbey at four o'clock in the morning. Though still night, torch lit galleries already fill with people. They are content to sit seven or eight hours for a sight they may not hope to see twice in their lives: the coronation of a king. London and Westminster have stirred since warning guns boomed at three o'clock.

Crowds of untitled rich folk who bought the privilege of seeking sitting room in the galleries flock in at entrances reserved for their sort. Hours drag tediously, all stir has ceased, and every gallery long ago packed tight. Readers may sit now, look, and think at leisure, catching glimpses here and there of a ceremony about to crown a boy king.
7250-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Nine opens under the interdict. Yet the Yankee's mind is snatched at once to a sick child, watched day and night by two parents who will let no one else help. Sandy, his wife, shows a right heart, simple, genuine, and good, flawless as wife and mother in his praise. Yet he married her for no better reason than chivalric custom: she was his property until some knight should win her in the field.

She hunted Britain over for him and found him at a hanging, a loyalty the Yankee now honours with grief and love. Twain pairs the church's great ban with a small sickroom, letting private tenderness outweigh public doom. This part holds the child, the watch, and Sandy's faithful heart.
8479-life-on-the-mississippi-part-9:
Part 9 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 41, The Metropolis of the South, as Twain's boat approaches New Orleans. He compares the approach to flying through London on a raised railway. There, one inspects miles of upper bedrooms through open windows while the lower halves of houses stay out of sight. High-river stage, he notes, hides New Orleans in a similar way.

This section gives the city at river level, familiar yet changed, with its commerce, its people, and its carnival past. Readers get Twain's New Orleans, seen by a river man returning after years. It is travel writing with a pilot's eye, where the city appears as a river town first, and a metropolis second.
8709-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-9:
This ninth and final volume of Gustave Dore's Bible gallery begins at the tomb. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, begs Pilate for the body of Jesus, wraps it in clean linen. Lays it in his own new rock tomb, rolling a great stone to the door, while Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite the sepulchre. The angel at the sepulchre, the journey to Emmaus, and the Ascension follow.

The Acts scenes complete the story: the martyrdom of Stephen, Saul's conversion, the deliverance of Peter, Paul at Ephesus, Paul menaced. Paul's shipwreck, closing with death on the pale horse from Revelation. The volume moves from grief to mission, ending the gallery where the Church begins. Readers get the New Testament's climax and sequel in Dore's chosen scenes, told in Scripture's own words.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
The final part opens in domestic quiet, with Hank and Sandy nursing their sick child, Hello-Central, before the Church's interdict falls. Worship stops, services end, and his trained people scatter without a blow struck. Hank fortifies Merlin's cave at the sand belt with Clarence and fifty-two loyal boys, behind wire fences and mines of his own planting.

War follows, and the Battle of the Sand Belt destroys an army of knights by electric wire, explosives. Gatling guns — a victory so complete it traps the victors among the unburied dead. Clarence's postscript closes the frame: Hank, wounded, sleeps thirteen centuries under Merlin's spell and wakes in his own time to die. Twain's satire ends as tragedy and warning at once.
a-mixed-proposal-the-lady-of-the-barge-a: William Wymark Jacobs tells a comic short story in which Major Brill, a retired volunteer officer, dresses with great care for a morning call and steels himself for a proposal. The humour comes from the gap between the major's military bearing and his nervous, squeaky tread. He walks a quiet English road in early autumn. The tale treats courtship as a small campaign, where vanity about a silk hat matters nearly as much as courage.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-9:
Newly found texts crowd volume nine of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, added after the main set was done. The Gospel of Peter and Tatian's Diatessaron lead a shelf of apocrypha: the Apocalypse of Peter, the Vision of Paul, the Testament of Abraham, and more. Roberts and Donaldson edited the volume in 1885.

The Diatessaron weaves the four Gospels into one story, as Syriac churches read it for centuries. The Vision of Paul tours heaven and hell, a trip that fed medieval visions including Dante's. The Acts of Xanthippe and Polyxena add a Christian romance of Spain. The volume ends with the Apology of Aristides, a lost defense of the faith recovered from a monastery. It is the set's treasure chest.
arabian-nights-payne-1884-vol-9:
Payne's ninth and last volume of the Thousand Nights and One Night closed the set in 1884. Shahrazad's thousand and one nights end at last, her life won by the stories themselves. John Payne's version, drawn from the Calcutta Arabic edition, stood complete: the first full English rendering of the cycle, unexpurgated throughout.

Burton's more famous version followed Payne's and owed it much, though the two men feuded in print. Readers who finish all nine volumes own the Nights as the nineteenth century first fully knew them. Volume IX brings down the curtain on a translator's marathon and a storyteller's triumph.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-9:
Volume nine of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud holds Aboth with the two Derech Eretz tractates, the Greater and the Lesser. Aboth, the Sayings of the Fathers, is the Talmud's beloved book of ethics. It stands out for teaching wisdom instead of law.

Aboth strings the maxims of the great rabbis in short chains: be slow to anger, judge every man fairly, and love peace. The Derech Eretz tractates then teach manners: how to eat, greet, travel, and treat servants and guests. Rodkinson's volume is the most quotable of his twenty. It shows the moral heart that the legal volumes assume.
bancroft-history-us-vol-9:
Washington's presidency anchors the ninth volume of Bancroft's History, from 1861. The early Constitution takes shape in practice, office by office and law by law. A federal government rises where lately there was only a league of states.

Bancroft published as the Union he loved began to fracture. His account of the republic's birth thus reads as both hope and elegy. Parties form, debts are funded, and precedents are set for all time. The volume shows the founding generation turning paper promises into a working state, while its author pleads, in effect, for that work to be preserved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100050008-9:
Letter from Drew S. Days III to Mr. Carl Stanberg, Assistant Director of the Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations in Washington, encloses a draft set of guidelines. Over the past several months, the letter states, officials from four agencies and their staffs had worked on the draft together. Named partners include Commissioner Norton of the FCC and Commissioner Sugarman of the Civil Service Commission.

The draft, dated October 13, 1977 and revised October 25, sets proposed uniform guidelines on employee selection procedures. Its aims were standards matching those of the psychological profession, adoption by all the agencies for uniformity, and guidance to employers and job agencies. It also sought adequate protection for blacks, Hispanics, other minorities, and women, the letter states. State and local officials had been consulted during drafting, it adds. The guidelines text warns that a procedure with a large adverse impact will face close review.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100090004-9:
Magazine interview titled by its editors as a search for weaknesses with psychological tests questions Dr. Arthur A. Witkin. He was chief psychologist for the Personnel Sciences Center of New York, and an associate professor at Queens College. Jim Bruno, managing editor of Administrative Management, conducted the interview.

Interest in employee testing was rising sharply after years of a hands-off stance, the piece opens. Witkin gives rising hiring costs as a prime cause: one firm put training at eight thousand dollars per worker, he says. Losses from faulty hiring choices were beyond counting, he adds. More minorities and women without experience were also entering the workforce, he notes, which made selection harder. His firm had helped pick some fifty thousand employees over twenty years, the introduction states. Later answers explain why a test that turns up nothing negative should worry an employer. Something has probably been missed, he argues.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100110001-9:
Policy statement titled Principles for the Validation and Use of Personnel Selection Procedures, second edition, was published in Berkeley in 1980. It is an official statement of the Division of Industrial-Organizational Psychology of the American Psychological Association. A notice adds that it does not necessarily represent the policy of the Association itself.

Copies were sold by the Division's Secretary-Treasurer, with prices falling for bulk orders, the front matter states. The foreword explains that in August 1978, division president C. Paul Sparks was told to appoint editors and an advisory panel. Their task was to revise and update the earlier edition. The body sets standards for building and checking selection tests. A passage on work samples warns that the closer a test domain comes to the whole job, the harder it is to run and score fairly. Cleaning tasks for mechanics are given as a case to cut.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130009-9:
Summary of major findings and recommendations accompanies the evaluation of PATB. It restates the consultants' brief: weigh the evidence for the battery's validity and reliability, judge its use in choosing professional staff, and assess its fairness for all applicants. Improvements to the tests and their use were also in scope.

The first findings concern use. Battery scores entered a hiring choice only after a unit showed interest in an applicant on a Skills Bank listing, the summary states. If no unit bit within ten days, no score report was made at all. Only about a quarter of supervisors gave the scores significant weight, it reports. About two thirds of recent hires said they had taken the battery, and a third said they had not. No consistent policy governed who had to take it, the summary finds. On fairness, no adverse impact studies had been done.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00m00244r000500030004-9:
Letter OLC 76-0273/a from George Bush to Representative Bella S. Abzug, who chaired a House subcommittee on government information and individual rights, answers her letter of 29 January 1976. She had sent him House Report 94-795, on federal use of the polygraph and similar devices. She had also asked for comments on the agency's continued use of the polygraph.

Banning the polygraph across government, as page 46 of that report urged, would seriously impair his statutory duty, Bush writes. The National Security Act of 1947 makes the Director guard intelligence sources and methods, he notes. The polygraph was an integral part of security processing for staff and operations alike, he argues. From 1963 to mid-1974, over 60 percent of applicants rejected on security grounds fell on information developed mainly in polygraph interviews, he states. Safeguards follow: notice to applicants up front, and advance written consent.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100020056-9:
Packet of February 1981 gathers a Director's letter and the staff work behind it, all on OSS materials. William J. Casey wrote to Professor Arthur L. Funk of the University of Florida on 8 February. The CIA had indeed re-established a historian's office, he confirms, and was weighing whether its work should stay in-house or reach the public.

Casey hoped in time to look more closely at the OSS materials himself, he writes. Their lengthy declassification for public access was moving forward, he understands. A staff memorandum of 3 February from Roberta Knapp sets out the History Staff's mandate: from 1947, the agency's founding, to the present. Wartime work entered only where wartime units carried on, it states, naming the Foreign Broadcast Information Service among them. A two-volume classified study, Donovan and the CIA, was about to be published, it adds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-01773r000400620004-9:
Final report of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence is the subject of a memorandum dated 26 April 1976, sent to the Director of Central Intelligence. The Chief of the Review Staff writes for the Director's information and for use in talks with other officials. Public release of the report was set for six that evening.

The report would appear in two main parts, foreign and domestic. Each part holds findings and recommendations, backed by long supporting papers. The memo warns that some members and staff may use the release to take parting shots at the Agency. It urges that spokesmen for the executive branch hold back in comment, so the release stays a smaller news event.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100070001-9:
National Security Decision Directive 52, on the future political status of Palau, is transmitted in a White House memorandum dated 20 August 1982. The note goes to the Vice President and the heads of State, Defense, Justice, Interior, and Energy, among others. A stamp on the file records that the directive was later rescinded or superseded.

The directive itself lets the chief status negotiator raise funding for Palau under the Compact of Free Association by up to 60 million dollars. In return he must win Palauan agreement to extend the compact to fifty years. The text also covers land-use rights under a military use agreement and a mutual security arrangement, including an American right of strategic denial.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100100007-9:
A meeting of the Systems Security Steering Group is reported to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence in a memorandum dated 20 December 1985. The Director of the Intelligence Community Staff had sat in for him. John Poindexter chaired, with Secretary Weinberger and senior aides from Justice and the Treasury among those present.

Don Latham reviewed the state of telecommunications and computer systems security and judged current systems extremely poor. Bill Odom covered programs to fix them, noting some 140,000 secure STU-3 telephones being bought across agencies. The group also heard of moves to protect sensitive information overseas, and of funding trouble when Congress reviewed the Agency quick-fix programs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02-06298r000900030003-9:
Factory guidance for industrial air compressors fills an operator's manual issued by Ingersoll-Rand, Form AP-0136, dated October 1980 and replacing a November 1974 edition. The copy held in Agency files opens with storage precautions and safety rules. Units ship with anti-corrosive treatment good for six months, and cylinders carry vapor phase inhibitor crystals.

Nine sections follow, covering installation, general operation, the frame and running gear, and lubrication of frame and cylinder. Later sections treat channel valves, regulation, and belt drive. Safety notes stress an aftercooler where oil appears in the discharge air, and a full review of the plant air system before a new unit is fitted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00184r000400030001-9:
Volume III of the same internal history carries the Project HTAUTOMAT story through 1956 to 1958. The volume is marked NPIC 3 and dated December 1974, with copies held by the CIA History Staff and the science directorate. A contents list reaches back across all three volumes, from the first looks behind the Iron Curtain onward.

Anatomy of the project office is laid out in that contents list: the chief's office, a special projects branch, industrial and geographic branches, a technical intelligence branch, and a support staff. Pages deep in the volume look ahead to a time when all photo interpreters might need to gather in one division. Missile, nuclear, and chemical target work drives that thinking.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100300001-9:
What would follow a cutoff of American aid to the Nicaraguan insurgents is estimated in a secret memorandum dated 17 April 1984. The Director of Central Intelligence requested the paper, and analysts from Central America, European, and Soviet offices contributed. National intelligence officers coordinated the work.

The paper judges that a cutoff would be a major win for the Sandinista regime, strengthening it at home and raising regional fears. It estimates the main insurgent group's military threat would fade within four to six weeks, while two smaller groups fought on at lower levels. Effects on Honduras, uneasy after the removal of its armed forces commander, and on the coming Salvadoran runoff are also weighed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100490001-9:
Foreign investment in Thailand is the subject of a secret intelligence assessment dated February 1984, EA 84-10016. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared the paper, which rests on information available as of 20 January 1984. Its title states the theme: outside money plays a growing role in Thai growth.

Key judgments say a slowdown in investment financing is forcing Bangkok to recruit private foreign investment actively for the first time, sending senior missions abroad. If Prime Minister Prem keeps easing the rules and carries out the current five-year plan, the paper projects net foreign investment could double or triple within four to five years. A figure on American investment across Southeast Asia is included.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100310001-9:
The Mozambique National Resistance, known as RENAMO, is profiled in a memorandum dated 4 March 1985. Analysts in the Africa Division wrote the paper, coordinated with the operations directorate and the Office of Central Reference. It carries the number ALA M 85-10023C.

RENAMO is described as a rural-based insurgent group with 12,000 or more armed guerrillas. Formed in 1976 from small groups opposed to the ruling FRELIMO party, it drew direction and support first from Rhodesia and, by 1980, from South Africa. It now works in all ten provinces, the paper reports. Its gains are tied to captured food handouts and hostility to farm collectivization. Active South African supply since the Nkomati Accord is doubted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100590001-9:
Taiwan's defense industries program is sized up in a secret research paper dated February 1985, EA 85-10033. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 1 February 1985. The title calls the program modest, and the summary bears that out.

Since the United States recognized China in 1979, Taiwan has tried to cut its reliance on American arms by building its own defense industry and widening its buying sources, the paper reports. Local media trumpet success beyond the facts, it suggests. The island's defense plants depend almost wholly on imported raw materials. Foreign sales also carry political risk: Dutch submarine work stopped in 1983 under Chinese pressure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000200760001-9:
A looming crisis on the Philippine island of Negros is the subject of a secret intelligence assessment dated May 1985, EA 85-10095. Islands Branch analysts in the East Asian office prepared the paper, using information available as of 29 April 1985. The communist insurgency is the thread.

Key judgments say the Communist Party and its armed wing, the New People's Army, are moving fast to use growing anger among workers on Negros. The government reply is hampered by split command: the island's two provinces sit in different regional commands, and rivalry inside and between them hurts operations. General Ramos has plans to unify the command, the paper reports, but President Marcos has not let him act.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000200850001-9:
Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party is profiled in a confidential research paper dated July 1985, EA 85-10127. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it. A production routing leaf at the front, coded for the East Asia division at headquarters, is part of the released copy.

The party and close ties between Washington and Tokyo have been linked for three decades, the paper opens. Its theme is adjustment: the party reshapes itself to meet new challenges while holding power. A chart of the party policymaking structure shows policy arms for cabinet affairs, local administration, defense, foreign affairs, finance, and many other fields, each with its own weight in the system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201570001-9:
China's recent economic reforms are summed up in a memorandum dated 19 April 1985. The summary says the reform program has gained speed since April of the year before. Reformers backed by Deng Xiaoping have pushed through major rulings on farming and industry.

The new policies are not capitalist, the paper stresses, but they break plainly with older Marxist practice and so stir dispute. A crackdown on price gouging, speculation, black market deals, and cadre abuse is meant to clear the way for wage and price reforms later in the year. In industry, an October 1984 plenum backed steps tested since 1979. Key goods stay under set state quotas, while most goods move to flexible guidance plans.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301920001-9:
Premier Zhao Ziyang's June visit to Western Europe is reported in a memorandum dated 23 July 1985, EA M 85-10136. Research for the paper closed on 8 July. Trade promotion was the visit's main purpose, the summary says.

Zhao signed several economic cooperation deals, including one with Britain on peaceful use of nuclear energy. A firm deal with West Germany's Kraftwerk Union for two reactors still waits, despite a cooperation memorandum. Zhao also played European countries, Japan, and the United States against each other for sales to China, the paper reports. On strategy, he urged Western Europe to press the superpowers to slow the arms race, above all in space.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302190001-9:
China might strike back at American protectionist law, in a memorandum dated 2 October 1985, EAM 85-10186. The Development Issues Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day. Proposed law in Washington forms the threat.

The paper judges that the proposed law would cut China's textile exports by as much as 40 percent. That would cost Beijing up to 520 million dollars at current trade levels. Beijing would feel forced to reply with sharp cuts in American imports, matched to the value lost. Timber is the most likely target. China's exports to the United States earn at least a tenth of its foreign exchange, and nearly three-quarters of their value sits in a few groups led by textiles and oil.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302280001-9:
Tourism in China takes on new weight in a memorandum dated 18 November 1985, EA M 85-10205. The Development Issues Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day. Premier Zhao has named tourism a target for national growth, the summary reports.

Beijing hopes to draw 4 million tourists a year by the end of the century, not counting overseas Chinese. That flow could yield 5 to 6 billion dollars, the paper estimates. Building for visitors in scenic areas is already lifting local economies and services. Reaching the goal will take steady investment, home and foreign, in lodging and transport. Travel, finance, and communications services for visitors also need work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302370001-9:
Cambodia in the rainy season is updated in a memorandum dated 1 July 1985. Southeast Asia analysts prepared the paper, using information available that day. The season is moving into its third month, and Vietnamese forces are on the move.

Vietnamese troops push hard against the non-communist resistance groups, the summary reports. Those groups are the Khmer People's National Liberation Front and Prince Sihanouk's national army, both trying to widen guerrilla work inland. Hanoi's stress on sealing the Thai border has left the communist Democratic Kampuchea forces under Pol Pot room to keep an active campaign in the provinces. Early analysis sees this pattern holding through the season, with Vietnam's military lead unchanged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100040004-9:
Vernon Walters seeks the Director's reaction to his draft Bar Association answers in a letter dated 27 March 1984. Walters, Ambassador at Large at the State Department, writes to William Casey. He encloses the Bar letter, its questionnaire, and his proposed answers.

Walters notes that he has been away from the Agency a long time and that circumstances may have changed without his knowing. He does not want to say anything that could harm the Director's mission, so he asks for comment before returning the papers to the working group. The Bar's own letter explains the study: its task force on intelligence is reviewing oversight and accountability in the intelligence community.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200370001-9:
A New York and Yale trip for the Director, set for 7 and 8 December 1977, is planned in a memorandum dated 6 December 1977. A folder sheet notes sensitive material removed to the declassification center. The official party lists the Director, Herb Hetu, and security staff.

The New York day runs from a Morgan Stanley luncheon address to a black tie Economic Club dinner at the Hilton, where Ambassador Peter Jay would speak first. The next morning brings breakfast at the Harvard Club and a meeting with Congressman Wolff. The file then swells far beyond the trip: long lists of names with class years follow, the raw bulk of a large trip folder.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200460001-9:
A one-day New York trip for the Director on 18 January 1978 is planned in a memorandum dated 17 January 1978. A folder sheet notes sensitive material removed. The party is the Director, Herb Hetu, and security, and the day is packed from a 10:25 departure from headquarters.

Lunch is with the publishers of the New York Times. The afternoon brings the Calvin Bullock Forum on Wall Street, with an address and a reception. Evening moves to the Waldorf Astoria for cocktails, dinner, and a further reception for head table guests. The party is due back at Washington National by 23:00. Guest lists and letters of praise for the Director's talk fill out the folder.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200490017-9:
A fellowship competition is announced in a Council on Foreign Relations letter dated 1 August 1979. Alton Frye, director of the International Affairs Fellowships, writes to Vince Davis at the Harold Pratt House address in New York. The competition is for the 1980-81 year.

The program aims to nourish the bond between scholarship and stewardship in international affairs. It gives analysts active policy work and gives practitioners time for reflective analysis. Grants go to outstanding candidates aged twenty-seven to thirty-five, drawn from government, academic life, business, and the professions. Davis is asked for nominees, with a name, age, address, and a brief account of background and the reasons for the recommendation. Full application papers come later.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300730037-9:
Stansfield Turner writes to a university president about a faculty proposal on CIA contacts. His letter is dated 12 July 1978. Robben Flemming's Academic Senate is weighing a new rule. Any member's clear prior consent would be needed first. Only then could another member pass his name to the Agency. The name could be passed as a possible employee, consultant, or agent.

Turner notes that agent is not a term the Agency uses for academic associates. Its own word, asset, may please no one better, but it is accurate. The senate report also urges care not to compromise foreign students. Turner argues that employers often seek such tips in confidence. The Agency acts no differently, he says. He states that the Agency has no objection to the proposed rule on inquiries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401040004-9:
DCI Schedules, October 1977 opens with a topic index of the Director's actions. The headings are Africa, Asia, the FBI, and Panama. Paramilitary matters, SALT, and the State Department appear too. So does reorganization. The entries cite records of talks on Yemen and the Horn of Africa. Talks on Korea and Panama are cited as well. One entry is a study of peacetime paramilitary needs. It was prepared for the Special Coordination Committee. A meeting with Secretary Vance also appears.

The daily pages log cabinet meetings. They also log a briefing on estimate NIE 11-3/8. Breakfasts with members of Congress appear. So does an Agency family day. At that event, the Director addressed employees' families. A round-table talk on the Agency's use of journalists also appears. It is listed among the month's appointments.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401150002-9:
Trip New York and Atlanta, 5-6 October 1977 papers center on the Atlanta leg. The file is the second of three files. Briefing notes describe the Atlanta City Forum's first meeting. It was a sellout of more than two hundred people. The notes list the head table, including the Reverend P. C. Ennis and attorney Bob Wildau. It included J. D. Humphries, who would introduce the Director. The notes give the Forum's advisory board.

A 5 October letter went to Turner's aide at the Peachtree Plaza Hotel. It lays out the next morning minute by minute. The plan starts with the 7:40 meeting in the lobby. It ends with the walk to the Equitable Building. A history of the Forum's past speakers is included. They ran from Admiral Byrd and Huey Long to Hubert Humphrey. Ralph Nader appears on the list too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401160001-9:
Trip to Pascagoula, 29 October 1977 is a large file built around one Navy event. The event was the christening of the destroyer John Hancock (DD-981). It took place at Ingalls Shipbuilding in Pascagoula, Mississippi. Director of Central Intelligence Stansfield Turner took a leading part. He was part of the ship's sponsor's party. The papers list the platform party and the official party in detail. They name Turner and his parents. They name Navy shipbuilding officials from NAVSEA. Officials from the Pascagoula supervisor's office appear too. Fleet officers of the Spruance class program are listed. So are Ingalls executives, led by president Leonard Erb.

Seating plans follow the lists. An order of ceremony and a printed program follow too. The program shows paintings and Navy photos. Credits go to the Bruce Gallery, General Dynamics, and Ingalls Shipbuilding.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501240001-9:
May and June 1978 press clippings fill a thick CIA file. The agency kept news on itself and on world affairs. Early pages carry book news. One item tells of John Marks and his study of CIA drug tests. The tests used unwitting subjects. A second item notes a book of essays called Uncloaking the CIA.

Later pages turn to hard news. Reports cover Cuba and Angola. Others cover talks in Washington. Claims about Soviet arms and spy work get much space. Read as a whole, the file shows what print said about the agency then. Past abuse, cold war rivalry and the case for spy work lead the themes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501330001-9:
Clippings saved across 1979 fill a wide Central Intelligence Agency file. News and comment from the whole year sit in it. A Washington Star piece is dated 8 December 1979. Cord Meyer wrote it. He looks at Soviet radio and at world communist parties. Most such parties still owe Moscow their loyalty, he argues. Most are funded by Moscow too.

Other pages carry talk on terror risk at home. A speaker warns of a grave attack one day. A city such as New York could face it, he says. Year-end pages thus mix cold war themes. Soviet reach, arms and faith in the West all get space.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601360016-9:
Brigadier General Pietro Pozzi wrote to the spy chief on 5 April 1977. He wrote from the allied headquarters in Naples, Italy. His short cover letter sends on an Italian paper. The paper is Il Giornale. He points to a page three piece. Its title casts the Kremlin ahead of the Pentagon.

The enclosed piece appears in English dress. It weighs growing Soviet military strength. It weighs the shift in United States plans toward Moscow. It cites the new Director of Central Intelligence's first public words on the theme. The file pairs a brief note of courtesy with a long press study. The study shows how the arms balance looked from Europe that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601400002-9:
Hearings held on 22 and 23 February 1977 fill this bound volume. The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence ran them. The subject was the choice of Admiral Stansfield Turner. He was picked as Director of Central Intelligence. The volume lists the panel's members. It prints two days of sworn talk on the pick.

Senators probe Turner's views and plans. Papers at the back deal with his private wealth. A letter sets out a trust deal there. The deal put his stake in a family trust past his reach. Rules from the President's counsel shaped it. The file is the full public record of the vetting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460042-9:
Captains of Achievement for 1978 fill a glossy Academy of Achievement program. The American Academy presents its Golden Plate recipients here. It calls them stand-ins for the many who excel in the great walks of life. Each guest gets a warm sketch of a life and a career.

An oil chief from Los Angeles leads the pages in this copy. Press praise styles him a jet-age man of many parts. Later sketches cover a minerals builder and a brave Pan Am stewardess. She won the top transport award for valor in a crash. The program, kept in Central Intelligence Agency files, is the banquet book for the June 1978 awards at Owensboro.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601560050-9:
Cathryn Zambetti wrote for the Young Presidents' Organization about a San Francisco school. The event was the 28th annual University for Presidents. It ran from February 5 to 11, 1978. Her letter encloses a standard tape release form. The tapes were for members' use only, not for general sale.

No press is invited to any event, she notes. A signed copy could go back by post or be handed over on site. The file explains the group's tape library at headquarters. Planners study past tapes to pick speakers for future events. Taped matter is never released beyond the membership, she stresses, in a letter kept in Central Intelligence Agency files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601580012-9:
John S Belew wrote on January 14, 1981 from Baylor University in Waco, Texas. Belew was vice president for academic affairs there. He had spoken that morning with Turner's assistant. Word came that Turner may visit Baylor. Belew encloses a list of past Koeppler Institute lecturers.

The list would show the quality of the program, he writes. The school is delighted at the prospect of a visit. The letter is short and formal, written after Turner had left the agency. Its address is a Navy Yard room in Washington. The file holds the invite and its enclosure list, a late paper in the director's speaking file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100040001-9:
Address to CIA employees by the Director of Central Intelligence fills this file. The date is 9 August 1977. Turner opens by saying he asked this group to gather as one of several such groups. They would help pass the word through the agency. He wishes he could talk to everyone at once, he says.

The talk then turns to the business that brought him out. Staff cuts and change in the house stood behind the meeting, in that season of strain. The file is a transcript of a director speaking to his own people face to face. It catches his plain style: frank, brief and aimed at morale in a hard year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100110012-9:
Presidential documents fill this file with the text of Executive Order 12036. President Carter issued it on January 24, 1978. Its subject is United States intelligence activities. The print carries the Federal Register page marks and the order's own contents list.

Section one treats direction, duties and responsibilities for the national intelligence effort. Later parts treat the bodies of the spy world and the rules that bind them. The order replaced the Ford order of 1976. It tightened curbs on acts at home and set fresh watch rules. The file holds the full text as published, a base rule book for the agency in Turner's years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100200003-9:
Herbert E Hetu's note to the Director of Central Intelligence opens this long file. Stan is the greeting used. Attached is a proposal for setting up an information institution of some sort. An ADP specialist drafted this first cut, his biography included. The draft lacks some human warmth, the note grants.

The idea, as the writer sees it, puts people back in control. Humans would organize and steer the automated information systems that seemed set to rule daily life. More examples of people problems were being worked in. The file holds a period piece: an early plea, inside the spy world, for human command of the coming data age.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100220001-9:
Thinkfile notes on the intelligence community fill this outline, marked secret. Broad purposes lead the page: security for the United States, lower tensions and less risk of war, prosperity at home, and world economic order. Human rights close the list of five.

The concept sketched is bold. The United States must shape a new international system, much as in 1945. Atlantic ties and containment ruled then, the notes say. Global engagement rules now, reaching beyond the rich lands. Closer work with Western Europe and Japan comes first among the goals. The file is a thinker's one-page map of aims, kept in the Director of Central Intelligence's papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200430034-9:
Central Intelligence Agency publications released to the public get a listing for 1972 through 1977. The National Foreign Assessment Center issued it in July 1978. Its mark is NFAC 78-0002 in the print. The list runs through the Library of Congress DOCEX project. That project expedited documents to users.

The front matter explains who may get the works. They are made for United States government officials first. Others may subscribe through the Library of Congress. Single copies may be bought as reproductions. The file is a catalog of what the analytic arm let the public read in those years: titles, order facts and the terms of release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650012-9:
Secretarial-clerical concerns move through this routing slip package of March 1978. An official routing slip from the administration arm heads the file. It is dated 9 March 1978. Remarks on the slip treat new drafts in tabs B, C and E. The drafts reflect changes the Director of Central Intelligence had requested.

The package had passed through two registries already, the note says. The covering memo was not redone for that reason. It could go back through the system as it stood, the sender presumes. The file shows a staff concerns paper in its late drafts, shaped by the top and routed for final action in the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660020-9:
Themes on women fills a memo dated 27 May 1977. The Federal Women's Program Board writes to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence. The board thanks him for his interest at their meeting of 10 May. It is pleased he will raise the problems of women with agency managers.

Attached notes answer his request for themes to use in those talks. Each theme gets its own draft paragraph. That form serves a speaker better than one long text, the board suggests. The memo shows the board arming a deputy with words: short, ready passages on pay, promotion and fair treatment of women in the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200730004-9:
Intelligence analysis quality is the subject of this top secret memo of 23 April 1979. An earlier memo had urged better management of analysis. Defining good analysis is a needed first step, that memo held. An attached essay takes a first cut at the definition. The writer calls it rambling and claims no pride in it.

It will satisfy no one, the writer grants. Those who have analyzed well will see their instincts in it, he hopes. It is abstract, he warns. Readers must supply their own examples for a time. The file is a Central Intelligence Agency insider's honest try at a hard question: what makes a judgment good, before one can manage for it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000300890006-9:
FIA 1978 winter meeting fills this program for Palm Springs, California. The Forging Industry Association met from November 12 to 16, 1978. The Canyon Hotel hosted the week. A president's message leads the book. Members get the most from the meeting by taking an active part, Andrew B Sides Jr writes.

Talking shop and renewing friendships fill the week, he promises. The business program is called no-nonsense in his note. It would instruct and challenge, with a payback for each firm. This was the association's first trip to Palm Springs. The program, kept in Central Intelligence Agency files, is the meeting book for a trade group in a resort week.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090021-9:
Pace University candidates for degrees fill this commencement list for 1980. The Pleasantville and Briarcliff campus issued it. Graduate school names lead the sampled pages. The Master of Business Administration roll opens with Louis G Alba. Martin Altman and Marcia Ogden Andreoli follow in alphabet order.

Hundreds of names fill the lists by degree and school. Each name is a graduate of that spring. The list is dry by design: a roll, not a story. It came to the Director of Central Intelligence as part of the commencement pack for the ceremony he addressed. As a record, it fixes the class of 1980 name by name.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301100010-9:
Trip book for Denver, Grand Teton and San Francisco covers 31 July to 12 August 1980. Tabs from A to Q sort the pack. Schedule and points of contact lead. A copy of remarks to the Tenth Circuit Court and the San Francisco Press Club follows. Background on the court comes next.

Copies of intelligence legislation sit at one tab. Luncheon participants, photos and correspondence fill others. Contact lists for Denver and San Francisco each get a tab. A proposed message for Signal Magazine is drafted in the pack. The book is a full working brief for the Central Intelligence Agency director on a long western swing, built to be carried and used day by day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401140024-9:
A scheduling item for the Director of Central Intelligence scheduling item 80-5 logs a federal conference on equal employment for 16 January 1980. A letter from Eleanor Holmes Norton brought the item, received on 7 January. A suspense date of 9 January is marked. The conference would run from 0830 to 1230 that Wednesday. James McIntyre was the keynote speaker named.

A point of contact is given on the form, with a phone number. The file is the staff sheet for an EEO conference invitation. Norton then led the field of equal employment in the capital. Her conference drew the heads of agencies into one room on a standing theme of the era: fair chances at work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150005-9: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item 80-120 logs an appointment ask from Kevin Lynch in this form. It was received on 25 April 1980, with a suspense date of 1 May. The event was left open between the beginning of May and the first week of June. A routing slip rides with the form. The file is a thin staff sheet for a spring speaking ask, with the day yet to be fixed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150032-9: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 80-100 logs a college dinner for Friday 27 June 1980. An invitation card brought it, received on 8 April. The hosts were the Rector and Fellows of Exeter College. Dinner would start at 1945 hours. Exeter College is the place named. Attire was black tie. An RSVP card was attached to the papers, the form notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401150069-9:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) scheduling item logs a meeting ask from J Paul Austin for 9 April 1980. The item was received on 14 March 1980. A suspense date of 19 March is marked. Board members and officers would gather that Wednesday. The Madison Hotel in Washington is the place named. A contact, Mrs Lee Meyer, is given with a phone number.

Austin was a chief of industry with wide civic ties. His asks carried weight in the capital. The form is brief: a source, a date, a hotel and a list of the kind of men who would sit in the room. The file is the staff sheet by which the director's office judged one more spring meeting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401320006-9:
Agency fitness report system gets a memorandum from the Director to his deputy. Turner writes under his policy of direct communication with the Director. A staff member had lately sent him a memorandum under that policy. It carried comments on the agency's fitness report system. Turner passes the matter up in form.

Fitness reports are the yearly grades by which officers rise or stall. A system that staff distrust can warp a whole service. The memo shows the top of the house treating a single officer's complaint as a window on the system. The file is short, but it marks a standing theme of the Turner years: personnel machinery under review.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501350002-9:
Press clippings in this file center on charters for the spy services. The Nation of 12 February 1980 leads the sampled pages. Its headline charges that the agency's bill unleashes the CIA. The piece recalls that the CIA has spied on its own people. It recalls FBI wrongs in the same breath.

Other pages weigh the same bills from other sides. A charter would set the agency's rules in law for the first time. Friends called it protection; foes called it a license. The file holds the print fight of that season in one bundle: magazines and papers arguing over how tightly a free state should bind its secret arm.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501360001-9:
Press clippings in this file open under a charters head, from late February 1980. U.S. News and World Report of 25 February 1980 leads the sampled pages. It prints a pro and con interview with Senator Walter D Huddleston of Kentucky. He favors easing the rules on spy work. Deal with the world as it is, he urges.

The interview form lets the senator make the case in his own words. Questions press him on why limits should loosen. The file around it holds the same debate in other papers. The bundle is the charter argument again, this time with a lawmaker's voice at its center, kept by the agency that the argument concerned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501450001-9:
Press clippings on the 1980 change of power in Washington form an Agency file from late that year. A Christian Science Monitor report dated 4 December 1980 opens the set. It portrays the team forming around Ronald Reagan as tough and practical rather than fixed on doctrine.

Names weighed for top posts run through the coverage at length. Alexander Haig, Caspar Weinberger, William French Smith, and William Casey all appear as likely picks. Later pages shift to Poland, Soviet warnings, and troop readiness near its borders. The file holds both the cabinet guessing game and the tense foreign news of that winter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601600003-9:
Talks on where key technologies are heading fill the first volume of a colloquium report from spring 1978. Sessions ran from 29 March to 1 April 1978 at the Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland. The volume is the rapporteur's account, dated June 1978, and sorts the talks by theme.

Speakers were asked where major fields are moving and where military weight lies. The report stresses that the same advances could serve either side in a contest. Pages on nuclear spread weigh which states might seek bombs and why. Named risks include India, Pakistan, Iran, Korea, Taiwan, and Israel, among others.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601730027-9:
Aims for personnel management are listed in a short Agency paper dated November 1978. Numbered aims run across three pages in terse note form. Early aims call for career planning by chiefs who can shape careers, not by counselors alone.

Other aims seek fair promotion steps that staff grasp and trust. Panels alone would judge each grade, with minimum marks made public in advance. Further aims cover a staff handbook, training for leaders, set specialist corps, and a 25 percent cut in staffing. Rotation outside a home service is required for those seeking top grades, the notes state.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601730063-9:
Fitness reports, the Agency form for rating staff work, are debated in a set of memos from late 1978. A 22 November 1978 memo from the Deputy Director shares a draft new form. Views were sought from all deputy directors by 4 December 1978.

John N. McMahon replies on 4 December 1978 for the operations side. Chiefs he sampled judge that the draft change would not help fair rating of staff. Later pages trace past form changes and a 1977 task force on rating. Points raised include double rating of the same skill and the risk that traits crowd out job facts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100020001-9:
How to present numbers well is taught in a research aid dated March 1955. The aid, ORR Project 11.3, came from the Office of Research and Reports. A foreword states it grew from faults seen most often in draft reports sent for printing.

Chapters treat proofing, key digits, ranges, rounding, totals, and index numbers. Worked cases show how to shift an index base and how to find a rate of rise or fall. Later chapters set rules for tables, from headings and units to source notes. A final part covers charts, bar graphs, and curves drawn on plain and log scales.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100110001-9:
Economic tables for 1965 fill a handbook issued by the Directorate of Intelligence. The Office of Research and Reports compiled the volume as an intelligence research aid. Its stated aim is sound, current figures on Communist and NATO economies, made fit to compare.

Data run across chosen years from 1955 to 1964, with plan figures added. Footnotes spell out terms, odd cases, and methods used in each table. A table of conversion factors sits after the contents, and an index closes the book. One table tracks fish catch from 1958 to 1964, with China shown well above the Soviet bloc total.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-02247r000200190010-9:
Press coverage of great Soviet building works is measured in a report dated September 1953. The report, CD No. BS-190, draws on four Soviet newspapers in Russian. Papers checked are Pravda, Pravda Ukrainy, Turkmenskaya Iskra, and Leninskoye Znamya.

Column space on the works was counted for set spans in 1952 and 1953. Works tracked include the Kakhovka power centre and the Main Turkmen Canal. The report weighs why coverage fell, from dull routine to lack of men and goods. It judges that work on the Main Turkmen Canal had most likely slowed or halted for a time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-02247r000200200027-9:
Subjugating the Desert, by chief engineer Semyonov, sets out the Main Turkmen Canal scheme in full. A Soviet government ruling of 12 September 1950 launched the canal, the article states. It would run from the Amu Darya to Krasnovodsk across the Kara Kum.

The canal is planned at 1,100 kilometres long with a flow like the Dnieper at Kiev. Aims join watering of land, water supply, power, and boat traffic in one scheme. Its flow is put at 360 to 400 cubic metres of water a second. Three power plants on the route would yield 100,000 kilowatts in total.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-00105r000201950001-9:
Fighting low flying targets is the theme of a Soviet article by General-Mayor of Artillery S. Prosvirkin. The piece comes from Military Thought and runs nine pages in translation. Prosvirkin calls low height attack the hardest task for field air defence.

Missile systems in service work best at mid and high heights, he argues. Jets also fail below 1,000 metres and can do little below 300 metres. Radar sets in the field cannot see well below 300 to 500 metres, he states. He urges a new cheap, mobile gun system built around the Shilka mount on a wheeled base.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100100001-9:
N.I.A. Directive No. 2, copy number 103, constitutes the Central Intelligence Group on 6 February 1946. The directive is marked tentative and cites the President's letter of 22 January 1946. State, War, and Navy must assign staff to the Group under set authorizations.

Initial staff is the least needed to organize, survey hard problems, and meet first demands, the text states. The Director will seek more staff as soon as that can be done. Offices listed include an Administrative Section and a Central Reports Staff. The Reports Staff helps weigh and spread intelligence tied to national security. The Director answers for all Group work and assigns all staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100470004-9:
London office affairs fill a huge file catalogued for mission, staff, and European war work. Other heads listed name psychological warfare, ties to organized labor abroad, and joint committee work. Inner stamps in the copy held here name a twin record number, and hosted text governs.

A memo dated 27 July 1943 from Captain Robert H. Alvord treats British currency for secret funds. Alvord warns against buying British currency below the legal rate for the London office. Special funds accounts in his name face British Treasury checks, he states. Notes above five pounds do not pass freely in Britain, he adds. Disposal of 100 pound notes had proved hard and risky for the work there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100030007-9:
Project OXCART roles are laid out in a short paper on organization and duties. Joint direction sits with the Director of Central Intelligence and the Chief of Staff, USAF, the text states. A project headquarters comes first among the parts listed.

An Air Force officer serves as Deputy Project Director under that setup. An operating unit abroad is to be manned by Agency and Air Force staff in set shares. Command in the field runs between the Project Director and the Air Force Project Officer. The Project Director holds first duty for security of activities tied to the United States government. The scan is rough, but the command lines can be read.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100030052-9:
General John D. Ryan is profiled in an Air Force biography held in Agency files. Ryan was born in Cherokee, Iowa, on 10 December 1915, the biography states. He took his degree at West Point in 1938 and earned his pilot wings in Texas.

War service took him to Italy, where he flew 58 combat missions in the B-17. Hours in combat are put at 340 in the profile. Later posts run from the 509th Bombardment Wing to the Sixteenth Air Force in Spain. He rose to Chief of Staff of the United States Air Force. Further officer profiles follow in the file, among them a radar and research chief born in Wilkes-Barre.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100080020-9:
Project AQUATONE planning data fill a Top Secret volume marked TS 142636, copy 3 of 8. Opening text states the same core gap as the plan's case for flight. The United States lacks firm knowledge of Soviet war capacity, it argues, and aerial photography is the strongest tool to gain it.

Joint direction sits with the Director and the Chief of Staff, USAF. A project director heads the headquarters, with an Air Force officer as deputy. SAC must supply and align Air Force support, with a sub-headquarters set for that task. Field chiefs get limited power to plan and launch flights on their own. Delivery tables then run twenty aircraft from July 1955 to November 1956.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200350074-9:
United States aerial spying is attacked in a Soviet Aviation article dated 5 December 1957. B. Aleksandrov writes under the head Provocative equipment and blackmail, in English rendering. Two F-84 type planes over a socialist state open the charge sheet.

Flights over Syria and Egypt are named as part of the same pattern. Air spying is placed at the heart of atomic war plans, the article argues. United States doctrine is quoted as calling air spying a prime source of war data. Infra-red photography and airborne television are tracked as fresh tools in that work. Tactical and strategic air spying arms are then set out in turn.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050002-9:
Host and tenant duties at an Okinawa base are split in an attachment marked For Official Use Only. PACAF and Kadena Air Base file marks head the pages held here. Rows pair each base service with who must provide or fund it.

The host gives accounting and finance help under Air Force rules, the table states. Base rules on security, safety, and dress go out to the tenant unit. The tenant runs its own civilian and military personnel affairs. Courts martial power stays with Headquarters USAF, not the host. Field upkeep beyond tenant skill falls to the host, the table states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050048-9:
Draft paper on CIA and the National Reconnaissance Program argues that recent problems show a breakdown in understanding of the Agency's place in the program. Its introduction states the case plainly: a central coordinating body is sound, but CIA should hold a managing role, not the secondary membership it now has. Changes to the standing agreements are urged so the Agency gains a senior partnership.

A draft history follows, tracing the Office from the 6 September 1961 memorandum by Deputy Secretary Gilpatric to Director Allen Dulles. That paper set the program on a covert footing, under the joint direction of the Under Secretary of the Air Force and the CIA Deputy Director for Plans. Later sections narrate incidents from the Office's young life and build the case for the changes proposed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400060010-9:
Agreement dated 11 September 1963 between the Director of the National Reconnaissance Office and the Joint Chiefs of Staff, acting through the Joint Reconnaissance Center, formalises NRO use of Defense resources. Covered assets include peripheral and special mission aircraft, aircraft flying assigned overflight missions, drones, and advanced manned aircraft in development. Ground and logistic support for other missions also falls under the terms.

In war or in periods of tension, airborne reconnaissance becomes a Joint Chiefs responsibility. Tension is as defined by the Secretary of Defense with the Director of Central Intelligence. Control then passes over as needed. To keep that transfer smooth, the Chief of the Joint Reconnaissance Center takes on staff duties for the NRO Director. The Joint Chiefs are to stay fully informed on mission planning and status at all times.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400300004-9:
Memorandum dated 1970, numbered 6414-70 and sent to the Director of Central Intelligence, comments on the report of the IDEALIST Task Force before final decisions are taken. The writer finds the report's facts in general agreement with his own understanding, yet faults it in two major areas. It dwells far too much on mainland China coverage, and it treats the alternatives for a follow-on capability in an unrealistic way.

Limited use of the U-2 against China in the past two years, the memo argues, cannot justify the program alone. The case for keeping it rests on contingency: a sudden need to watch China or trouble spots across Asia, the Mid East, Africa, or South America. The writer also questions whether any operation since the Gary Powers shoot down of 1960 has truly been covert.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120003-9:
Memorandum COMIREX-D-33.4/1, dated 1 August and sent to the Committee on Imagery Requirements and Exploitation, carries a summary of non-conventional film systems. It follows an 18 July briefing by OSA/DDS&T, after which the committee chairman asked the EXRAND chairman for a short report on dry and other unusual processing systems known to his group. The attachment compares new film materials at mixed stages of development.

The covering note is careful about scope: the survey presents materials that may now compete for a given need, but it is by no means complete. Only major developments under watch are summarised, with more to follow in the same format as data arrives. An attachment explains the Kodak BIMAT transfer process, in which a soaked transfer film is pressed to the exposed negative so the negative develops while a positive forms on the transfer film.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500320010-9:
Technical report on experiments to cut Ka band radar echoes from an aircraft model opens with work begun in April 1957. The scan is rough in places, but the aim reads clearly: find the main echo directions from a target and locate the parts of the model that produce each echo. A scale model, twelve to one, was tested over a full circle of azimuth.

Early results suffered from clutter near the target, so the test range was shortened to six hundred feet. The team then reports six main echo directions, linked to the nose, fuselage sides, and tail surfaces. Later pages look ahead to a longer, cleaner range with faster data capture for future model tests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500390095-9:
Memorandum for the record GUS-0116, dated 27 February 1959, records a meeting held the day before on support for Project GUSTO. Staff from operations, contracts, materiel, personnel, security, and finance met to plan contract and logistics backing for the Convair GUSTO vehicle, called the Super Hustler in the discussion of flight articles.

Those present agreed that at least seven flight articles should be bought, with two or three for flight test and four for operations. Other questions cover contractor employee maintenance, drawn from Project CHALICE practice, and agency support for the B-58 carrier aircraft. No schedule was set, and a follow-up meeting in early May was proposed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500410001-9:
National Reconnaissance Office directive sets out who handles film and photo gear for the National Reconnaissance Program. It covers budgeting, buying, storing, asking for, and issuing aerial film and processing supplies for aircraft flights. Support for the SR-71 is included where contracting through CIA still fits. Satellite work is left out of its scope.

Part two deals with a reserve of key processing gear, held for use in an emergency. That gear could open an extra processing site or back up a site already in use. Forms and notes at the end track film received, film exposed on missions, shipments to other units, gear written off, and likely use over the next ninety days.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040010-9:
Departure and recovery routes for mission aircraft are fixed in Detachment H SOP H-50-16, dated 3 April 1969. The home base name is blacked out in the scan. Pilots climb on a heading of 320 degrees after takeoff. They hold 1,500 feet or the height for visual flight, whichever is higher. After fifteen nautical miles they turn back, at or above flight level 240.

Return to base is by a TACAN approach from the high altitude book, followed by radar guidance on final approach. Backup steps cover loss of radar contact, using the tower and ADF or TACAN aids instead. An older 1966 SOP, H-50-15, bound with it covers a pogo release fault, with holding steps and fuel burn-off.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040038-9:
Recalling staff to base on days off is the subject of Detachment H SOP H-20-4, dated 21 June 1968. The Staff Duty Officer runs the recall, most often after a mission alert arrives from project headquarters. The same steps can also serve the evacuation plan or the severe weather plan when either is put into effect.

Each directorate names staff who stay within reach on days off, with a main and a backup contact sent in by noon on the last work day. Materiel staff on recall help get a mission ready. Later steps cover phone alerts through the officers' club and off-base homes, and first moves under the evacuation or weather plans.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040119-9:
Fuel handling at Detachment H is covered by SOP H-45-39, dated 10 August 1970, replacing a November 1969 version. The Logistics Officer enforces the rules, and the Director of Materiel watches all fuel work. It applies to those two officers, the Logistics Supervisor, and the Fuel Specialist. Fuel policy itself comes from a Project Headquarters directive of September 1968.

Daily stock and issue forms, kept by the Fuel Supervisor, track use and supply over one week spans. Checks on mobile refueling units fill much of the text: gauge calibration every six months, daily hose, nozzle, and screen checks, and water drain checks. Filter change rules and a daily stock form close the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600050037-9:
Cargo movement by air for the 1130th group is set out in ATTG Reg 67-7, dated 16 October 1969. It puts Project Directive 45-3 into local effect. All cargo on project aircraft is classed as mission product or as general cargo, with training take treated as general cargo unless higher authority directs otherwise for a given flight.

The Director of Materiel holds overall charge. Operations runs control of sensitive material, and Unit Supply gathers, stores, loads, and off-loads all other cargo. Security handles material needing special care, marking and manifesting it and sending a courier with it. Attached forms list mission numbers, film footage, can weights, security markings, and gear types for each shipment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070008-9:
Standing operating procedure 50-3105-1, dated 18 November 1965, fixes when weather counts as severe at a desert test area whose name is redacted. Severe weather means winds over twenty-five knots, any rain or snow, thunderstorms nearby, strong cross winds, or blowing dust with visibility under one mile. A lesser advisory covers ceilings below 2,000 feet and runway visibility under three miles.

The Base Weather Officer must warn Base Operations at least two hours ahead of a forecast event. Operations then alerts the Command Post, control tower, test and hangar groups, rescue, security, and other named offices. Each office must pass word to its own sections. The file also holds the earlier 21 May 1965 version of the same procedure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020001-9:
Memorandum 9311-68, dated 22 October 1968, from Brigadier General Donald H. Ross, Director of Special Activities, sends program progress reports to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs. The attached reports cover OXCART and IDEALIST for 1 July to 30 September 1968, in five copies each. Tab A reports that OXCART development wound down after the SCOPE COTTON decision to phase the program out on 30 June 1968.

IDEALIST sections report U-2R work, including escape training for carrier operations in which the life support gear gave good protection in submerged tests. A refit effort for the S-1010 pressure suit followed comfort and safety points raised at Detachment G. A delivery table closes the report, listing rollout, first flight, and acceptance dates for aircraft 3 through 9.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250006-9:
Progress packet 8949-68, signed by Brigadier General Paul N. Bacalis, sends OXCART and IDEALIST reports for 1 January to 31 March 1968 to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs. Tab A opens the OXCART development summary with airframe work and an A-12 flight handbook item. Flight data tables for the quarter follow, with sorties and hours set out by aircraft in the attached pages.

Propulsion trouble holds the IDEALIST section. The U-2R flight test program was slowed by its ejector exhaust nozzle, which caused uneven thrust on takeoff and high noise in ground running. Flow separation in the nozzle's widening part is named as the likely cause. A life support review by the Air Force Surgeon General's staff at Detachment G is also recorded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250015-9:
Monthly OXCART summary 2746-67, dated 13 November 1967, covers 1 to 31 October 1967 for the Deputy for Operations, OSA. Contingency planning under SKYLARK shows no change. The overflight section, PINWHEEL, reports seven A-12 operational missions flown in October. All launched from Kadena Air Base, Okinawa, and all recovered there, one after a diversion noted in the text.

Mission details name targets in North Vietnam. One flight of 4 hours 9 minutes covered 144 SAM sites, eighteen of them occupied, and one new site was identified. Six of nine first priority SSM targets were covered. Tanker support on one mission worked from Clark Air Base after a typhoon move. A final section lists A-12 aircraft at the project detachment and at Kadena.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800290002-9:
Letter dated 11 July 1969, from Robert F. Froehlke, Assistant Secretary of Defense, to Carl Duckett, Deputy Director for Science and Technology at CIA, sends his interim report on defense intelligence to two senior officials named in the letter. Froehlke hopes the report covers the major issues in a way Duckett can accept. If there is no word by 21 July, he will take that as agreement, he writes.

The attached report concludes that the defense intelligence community's main need is a special assistant for intelligence reporting to the Secretary of Defense. He would run a full review and decision process for intelligence management. Staffing options are weighed, one reaching about 150 to 200 professionals for a central staff. A council to advise the Secretary is proposed at the end.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800290011-9:
Memorandum recommending an agency funded research and development program for OSA for fiscal year 1969 carries a signature block for approval by the Director of Central Intelligence. It recalls that OSA once ran a large independent program on overhead reconnaissance, which produced the IDEALIST U-2 and OXCART A-12. Funding moved to the NRO when that office was set up, the memo states.

Since then OSA research has centered on further work for those two programs, with small studies of other systems. One, ISINGLASS, was funded in its early studies by the McDonnell Aircraft Company alone. The memo quotes Central Intelligence Directive language on research needs, and argues OSA must keep an independent capacity to develop new collection methods.
cia-crest-cia-rdp51-00036a000100040009-9:
Set of CIA organization charts dated 15 October 1947 replaces all earlier charts and amendments, as the heading on the file states. A national security council block sits at the top, with the President and service secretaries above the agency.
