The Executive Director is described as the principal staff officer for the Director, controlling and coordinating agency activities and handling liaison with the council and outside agencies.

Function statements follow for each major office. The Interdepartmental Coordinating and Planning Staff develops overall plans for interagency intelligence work. Collection and Dissemination runs coordinated collection policy. Reports and Estimates, Special Operations, and Operations each carry their own function statements. An executive for inspection and security closes the set, with security policy and audits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000100130073-9:
Operations report dated 6 December 1951, from the chief of the Building Maintenance and Utilities Division, covers November 1951. Service demand is counted at the top: 268 written requests in the month, 2,350 telephone calls, and 287 orders still incomplete for services at month's end. Orders to the General Services Administration are split between those charged to a quarterly fund and those sent outside it.

Money figures follow. The November share of the quarterly fund for alterations and installations is 18,200 dollars. Special orders outside that fund total 74,779 dollars, mostly renovations at 70,674 dollars. Space moves in the month covered 530 people and 22 equipment moves. A telephone branch report bound after the main report gives September 1951 phone bills totaling 26,789.72 dollars.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030028-9:
Table of contents for a Manual of Administrative Issuances maps the whole of the agency's housekeeping rules. Fiscal sections come first: budget development and administration, accounting, payroll and leave, travel, transportation billing, purchases, collections, disbursements, audits, and field matters. Communications sections follow, covering official repositories, the inter-office chain envelope, messenger and courier service, and logging and routing of documents by classification level.

Later lists reach filing systems and office records, research service, and archival action. A security chapter names physical, document, and personnel security, top secret control procedures, and dissemination policy. Travel and transportation contents close the set, from domestic travel and overseas points to local motor transport. The file is a contents map only; the manual text itself is not included.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030073-9:
Office of General Services regulation OGS 10-1, dated 1 September 1952, sets security rules for that office, replacing the Administrative Service Office security regulations of 8 June 1951. The rules add to, and do not replace, the overall CIA security regulations. Exceptions need written approval in advance from the Chief, General Services, sought through the Office Security Officer.

A yearly reading of the current CIA and office security regulations is required of every employee, each July. A signed certification that the reading is done is due by 31 July. A security officer is appointed from a roster of staff at GS-9 level and above. Division chiefs name staff security check teams each month, pairing a senior member at GS-7 or above with a junior one. Penalties for violations close the regulation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050107-9:
Executive Order 10100 sets rules for allowances granted by the Director of Central Intelligence under section 5(b) of the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949. Allowances must match those the Secretary of State grants under the Foreign Service Act of 1946 and Executive Order 10011, for places where those rules apply. Elsewhere, the Director's allowances must follow the same general standards and rates as far as practical, and the Director may issue further rules as needed.

Medical provisions in the bound text cover staff posted abroad. The agency can pay travel for an ill employee to the nearest place with a suitable hospital, and for his return when recovered. Attendant travel can be paid if the patient cannot travel alone. First aid stations with a nurse can be set up at large posts. The CIA Act of 1949 itself is bound after the order.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100002-9:
Monthly report of operations for the period ending 30 September 1953, from the Chief, Records Management and Distribution Branch. Leave of three days or more touched seventeen Mail Control staff, eight at the Records Center, and four in Records Management. Pending separations are listed: none in Records Management, five at the Records Center, and thirteen in Mail Control. One staff member serves as a full time courier with the Transportation Division, as in other months in this run.

Work improvement Project 4-53, the mail room handbook for courier and messenger staff, is estimated ninety percent complete. The Correspondence Manual was in preparation for distribution. Filming results close the report: images filmed in the month run above ninety-five thousand, almost all on the flatbed camera. Reel counts are given in process, to be reviewed, and reviewed, with fiscal year totals carried since July 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100011-9:
January 1953 report of the Records Management and Distribution Branch is dated 3 February 1953. Five staff serve on special detail for the full month. Four men are in the Far East for microphotographic work, and one man serves as full time courier in Transportation. Thirteen Mail Control staff await transfer or reassignment. Two new applicants were interviewed, both recruited by the branch itself, none by Personnel.

New project reports fill much of the file. Project 3-53 will build a retention and disposal schedule for records of the overt fiscal work, for the Comptroller and the Budget and Fiscal Divisions. Completion is expected about 1 March 1953, after an inventory of the records and disposal authority from the general schedules. The revised control card project is also set out: new cards arrived in January, arranged by office of origin and type of report, with completion expected in April.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00195a000100020110-9:
TRD Library accession list for July 1951 gathers new books under area headings, Russia and Communism first. Titles named include The Russian Purge and the Extraction of Confession by F. Bock and W. Godin, Judgment on Deltchev, and Total Empire. Leon Trotsky appears several times as author, with James Cannon, C. Haldane, Edward Crankshaw, Eric Ambler, Edmund Walsh, and Freda Utley also listed. A Department of State title on propaganda and control in the Soviet system is included.

Europe and Asia sections follow. The Asia list names works on China and the Far East, including Double Ten by Carl Glick and a revised 1951 title by Victor Purcell. A Pacific Islands heading begins at the foot of the page. The list is a holdings record only: title, year, and author for each item.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020022-9:
Summary dated 23 July 1952, sent by Director of Training Matthew Baird to all assistant directors, sets out the courses and programs of the Office of Training (General), TR(G). A covering memorandum explains the summary follows a talk to the DD/I and his staff. A fuller TR(G) Training Bulletin is in preparation and will replace it. Copies are enclosed for distribution inside each office.

Course entries give purpose, description, length, and quota. An indoctrination course for all incoming staff leads. A Soviet studies course runs eighteen months from September, taught in Russian. It mixes lectures and seminars on the military, economic, and political structure of the USSR and its satellites. Advanced language work and field trips are included. Closing pages record a new duty: after a survey found office briefings wanting, the Office of Training now runs agency briefings of outgoing service attaches.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020040-9:
Course outline for Section VI, The Intelligence Structure of the Government, plans seven lectures and four field trips. Students are to learn the government's intelligence structure from the inside. The course studies the organizations, missions, and relationships of its intelligence departments. The Central Intelligence Agency gets detailed treatment. Five areas are named: lines of command and working contact among the agencies, and the Intelligence Advisory Committee. The CIA itself comes third. Intelligence arms of State, the Joint Chiefs, and the three services follow, then intelligence work in other departments.

Lectures are assigned agency by agency. State, Army, and Navy intelligence each receive a session on mission, organization, functions, and ties to CIA. The Navy lecture is by Felix Johnson. A final lecture surveys intelligence activity in non-IAC bodies such as Treasury, Commerce, Interior, and Justice with the FBI.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100140011-9:
Memorandum dated 15 January 1952, from the Chief, Plans and Policy Staff, to the Director of Training, surveys training run by CIA offices outside O/TR. The Office of Research and Reports leads. Its opening lectures run about ten hours, monthly, for some twenty students. Eleven instructors are drawn from four offices. Film training shows analysts movies on the plants their division studies, for an hour and a half a week. The Office of Scientific Intelligence reports no formal courses.

Two proposed Far East courses close the legible body. One would set a standard way to treat Chinese names in Far East reports. The other would teach the structure of Chinese characters. The survey ends with advice. A list of outside courses should be compiled and sent to all offices from time to time. The need for language courses for special clerical staff should also be studied.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00011a000100020130-9:
Weekly report dated 2 October 1952, from the Chief, Orientation and Briefing Division, covers 25 September to 1 October 1952. Newcomers attended the opening program on Monday 29 September. All such courses stand complete, the report notes. Orientation planning took work. Sessions with OCD staff who had screened reports sought realistic material for a panel discussion, and found it wanting. A program built with the division was laid before the DD/TR(G). The Office of Operations moved its senior field staff meeting to meet the Orientation Program of 13 to 21 November.

Presentations drew good numbers, though the level of those attending caused some worry at first. A briefing on 26 September is recorded as well treated. Security cleared the named staff for a special program for the Foreign Service Institute. State officers Nordbeck and Esman visited to discuss the program built for institute staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000100030050-9:
Weekly Activity Report number 45, dated 10 November 1952, reports the work of the Assessment and Evaluation staff. The acting chief's office met with Col. Baird on scheduling of assessments and spreading of results. A memorandum on assessment is being drafted for possible issue to the DD/P. IBM cards for test scores were punched and verified in the Research and Validation Branch, for use in statistical study of the scores.

Counts for the week are given: eleven assessment cases scheduled, eleven performed, seven written. Tests were given to four prospective professional trainees and one language trainee, and all were scored and recorded. A study of the mental qualities wanted in an intelligence officer goes on, with seven training staff members interviewed so far. Work also continues on scoring of the Work Attitudes Inventory and on item study of test questions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00037a000200030022-9:
Lesson plan for Methods of Instruction: Problem Solving sets out a panel session on live problems and practical exercises. The panel chairman puts set questions to a named member, with a time limit for each answer, from two to five minutes. Early questions ask whether the live problem is a good teaching method for TSS techniques, and when such methods suit the teaching of photography. A fourth question asks how advanced and specialized courses could gain from the two methods.

A second panel round follows a ten minute break. Questions turn to set courses: the Communist Party Operations Course, investigative techniques, and logistics teaching for TSS and other staff. Each speaker is asked where a live problem would help, which techniques it could teach, and what parts of his own course it would most benefit. The plan is a script for the session, with answers left blank.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100030003-9:
Opening remarks by the Director of Training at the Tenth Agency Orientation Course frame the program for its house. The Office of Training runs it, with help from officers inside and outside the Agency. Its goal, like that of all training, is to make each person more effective in his present or next assignment.

General Smith's part in the Agency's growth is praised at length. His stress on selectivity in hiring is called one of his greatest contributions. The fast growth of 1951 was a mixed blessing, the speaker states. The personnel ceiling Smith set was an effort to hold standards. About forty percent of the house had been in CIA less than six months. The remarks close by introducing Lt. General Cabell, Deputy Director, as the first IAC speaker, on General Smith's instant choice: Get Cabell.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100050029-9:
Memorandum dated 20 July 1953 presents comments and advice on student evaluation in BIC (CS). The paper grew out of meetings of the course's teaching staff. They disliked how evaluations are presented on the present form. The aim: tests and problems that let instructors judge the working knowledge a student gained. Four fixed points governed the talks, the memo states.

Evaluation is vital to a student's future in the Agency. It must be presented so the reader grasps it at once. Students hold varied assignments, so weight on each element must vary with the man. An appendix traces testing in the first BIC (CS). Scripts for many guest lectures were lacking. Short tests were often built as the lecturer talked. A closing note warns that a security score from a set test does not measure security sense.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100070018-9:
Staff report dated 27 June 1953 from the Chief, Management Training Division, on the opening phase of the Human Resources Program in the Far East Division. Four groups of supervisors met between 25 April and 2 June, in four group meetings each plus a half-hour talk with every member. Follow-up meetings were planned about every eight weeks, starting after 1 September.

The program aimed to lift the quality of Agency supervision from unit chief to Director by fixing attention on human relations. Discussion brought out a clash between how the covert side was organized and accepted rules of sound management. Three deep problem areas are named: the role of a chief of mission in the field, senior staffs acting as line rather than staff, and where division command duty truly sits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030060-9:
Task Force memorandum dated 15 April 1951. Its subject is post differentials. It went forward for review and action. A post differential is extra pay. The rate is ten, fifteen, twenty, or twenty-five percent. It is figured on base salary. It serves staff at harsh foreign stations. Living at such a station is a hardship. The payment aids hiring for those posts. Unlike allowances, it is taxable pay.

Two sets of rules cause the core trouble. Foreign Service rules both apply here. Standardized Post Differential Regulations apply as well. The two sets differ in substance and wording. The paper traces how the rules grew. A State Department serial came first. Executive Order 10,000 followed it. A Director's approval ran from 19 September 1948. The paper urges one clear course. One set should be dropped. The other should be adapted to Agency needs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030079-9:
Regulation extract on the powers of the Personnel Director. One power covers posts the Secretary of State has not classified. For such posts, the Director may set foreign allowances and differentials. An assistant director must recommend the step first. The Comptroller must agree as well. Rates must follow State Department standards. The Director must review them each year.

Other powers cover single hard cases. The Director rules on fitness for post differential pay. Special or blanket rules may be set for some staff. A hardship salary differential may enter a contract. Cover needs or work needs must cause the hardship. The Director also appoints staff agents. Staff agents hold nearly all Agency staff employee rights. Consultants and experts may be named too. A roster of consultants must be kept.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020080-9:
Basic Training Program description, in three phases. The program forms a whole by itself. Each phase is a prerequisite for the next. Phase one covers induction and orientation. Later phases build toward field readiness. One phase runs three weeks in length. Top Secret clearance is required for it. Class size runs from five to twenty.

Phase three treats headquarters structure in depth. Major parts and their functions are covered. Placement of Agency staff abroad is treated. Project procedure gets its own heading. Security and control problems are covered too. Reporting of information is also taught. Lectures are mixed with group discussion. Speakers bring field and headquarters experience. A shorter two-week course follows in the text. It serves the headquarters area. Its final week runs outside that area. Basic program completion is required first.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100040006-9:
Tab stating Office of Training functions and activities. The office has two main parts. One part is the Office of Training (Special). The other is the Office of Training (General). Training (Special) serves the Clandestine Services. It teaches the activities charged to those services. Staff learn planning and conduct of such work. Administration of the work is taught too.

Agent personnel train for set assignments there. The office studies clandestine training needs first. It runs programs, staffs, and facilities at home. Help goes to overseas training on request. Student evaluations aid assignment choices. Liaison runs inside and outside the Agency. A plans and programs staff looks ahead. It learns current and future training needs. New objectives and programs are prepared by it. Experienced staff are drawn on for teaching. Current operations supply teaching material there.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100060013-9:
Agenda and record for group meeting number two. Administration directorate training liaison officers attended. The meeting sat on Friday 10 July 1953. It began at 10:30 in the morning. The room was 117 Central Building. Supervisory training headed the agenda list. Specialized training by the offices came next.

Training policies of the offices followed on the agenda. Short courses after duty hours were listed. Budget follow-up and old business came later. The record shows a request from all offices. Supervisory training beyond the Human Resources Program was wanted. The partners and background of management training were sought. Talks with General Cabell had covered the subject. Training policy was stated in reply. Only work assigned to the training office would be done. Later items survey office-run courses. Finance and personnel courses are named. Logistics briefings for staff grades GS-13 and up appear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000200020046-9:
Announcement of a Near East area course. The Foreign Service Institute of the State Department offered it. The course ran five months, from October to February. It formed part of language-and-area training. Foreign Service Officers were the main students. They had volunteered for Arabic, Persian, and Turkish. The course continued their intensive language study in part.

Other government staff could also attend the course. Sessions ran half-time each work day. Three afternoon hours were set aside daily. Two hours went to a speaker's presentation. One hour went to group discussion afterward. The last month differed from the rest. Problem papers and research papers filled that month. Students presented and discussed their own work. Language study filled the mornings for officers. Charles A. Ferguson at the Institute took questions. An attached description lists weekly topics.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000010088-9:
Assumptions and tentative understandings for contractor personnel. A forward base of operations is the setting. What such employees are owed is the subject. The government would provide room and board. That cover applies to each person on the mission. Exchange privileges would be open to them. Theater law and rules would govern that access. Money conversion would be free of charge.

Employees should keep overseas pay requests small. Most pay should not be drawn at the base. Word on the chosen base would come later. Climate and commodity cost facts would be supplied. Recreation choices and their costs would be listed. Pay handling rules take up the rest. The contractor makes the employment agreement. A schedule lists each name and amount. Only the original payroll is signed by employees. An Agency disbursing officer certifies all copies. He certifies that each person got the sum shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000170135-9:
Memorandum dated 26 June 1956 on pending requisitions. It went to the Agency Project Comptroller. The Director of Project Materiel sent it. Three categories of requisitions are listed. Category A covers items ordered before 1 May 1956. Those items were received after that date. Category B covers items still not delivered. Category C covers orders from May and June.

Each category lists requisition numbers in long rows. Amounts stand beside many of the numbers. Allotment account numbers head each group of rows. Category A totals 2,576 dollars and nineteen cents. One later group totals 8,376 dollars and seventy-six cents. A single item there reads 7,610 dollars even. Other groups total only a few hundred dollars. The memo answers a request for status. No narrative beyond the lists is offered. The tables run over three pages in all.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000180017-9:
Agency letter contract number TR-500 with a university. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology is the contractor. Its address was 77 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge 39. An order is placed for work in Exhibit A. The exhibit is made part of the contract. On acceptance, the university must proceed at once. Materials must be procured without delay. Work must go forward with all diligence.

Air Force Procurement Instructions supply the clauses. They enter by reference with full force. Limitation of cost is among the clauses named. Allowable cost and payment are covered too. Inspection, records, and subcontracts appear in the list. Small business use and termination are named as well. Excusable delays and disputes clauses follow. A definitive contract was to be negotiated later. It would carry a detailed delivery schedule. Prices and terms would be agreed by both parties. All clauses then required by law would enter it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100080002-9:
Project paper titled Project I, on microfilming documents. All incoming intelligence documents are its subject. The CIA Library stands at the paper's center. It is called the Agency's documentation center. New intelligence documents reach the Agency there. The Library indexes those reports for the Agency. It distributes them to appropriate CIA offices. Requesters use it for reference and circulation daily.

Requests vary by the person making them. Subject information and specific documents are both sought. Bibliographic service and research help are sought too. No guide to agency documentation resources exists yet. That gap is stressed in the paper text. No checklist of facilities is available either. No basic reference tool covers intelligence materials. CIA researchers have nowhere to turn for such help. Microfilming every incoming document answers that weakness. Bibliographic control like unclassified work is the aim.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100009-9:
Report on the combined OPC and OSO control office. Its Top Secret area office is the subject. An Organization and Methods examiner wrote it. Survey dates ran from 7 to 11 April 1952. Compliance with Agency regulations was the review aim. Uniform operating methods across CIA were the goal. A merger frames the whole report text.

The two area offices merged on 3 April 1952. Separate control systems still ran through 11 April. A joint system had been proposed meanwhile. That system was approved, the examiner was advised. It would take effect on 14 April 1952. Findings rest on that system going into effect. Title and duty changes came with the merger. Security problems in one office are called acute. Documents must come back when a person leaves for the field. Staff circulate through offices and training meanwhile. Listing all items issued to them is hard.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200080001-9:
Survey report dated 30 April 1953 on personnel procurement. The Personnel Procurement Division is the subject throughout. Purpose and scope open the report. Processes and procedures of procurement were surveyed. Immediate improvements were the first goal sought. Further action for the mission was the second. Internal and external relationships got special attention.

Problems from a proposed move were considered as well. Background explains why procurement stays hard here. Many area and program specialists are required. Secrecy surrounds the Agency's purpose and functions. Operations are cloaked by that same secrecy. Administrative burdens add to the difficulty later. Entry on duty figures appear in the body. Only forty-two had entered under one combined program. No definite plans existed to meet that quota. Statistics cover the first nine months of a fiscal year. Sources, results, and costs of recruitment are compared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150003-9:
Appendix II paper by Alden H. Emery on literature searching. Scientific aids for searching are its subject. The American Chemical Society interest began in 1946. A Committee on Punched Cards was appointed then. Roger Adams chaired that committee for the Society. Potentialities of mechanical aids were its charge. Successful uses by persons and institutions were found.

Each use covered a small part of chemistry only. Doubt remained about covering the whole field. Chemists and chemical engineers form that whole interest. Significant accomplishments justified serious consideration anyway. The Board of Directors was favorably inclined. Funds for the purpose were not available then. Adams was authorized to pursue the matter regardless. Coding ideas fill the later pages. Punched patterns can designate meaningful symbols directly. Animal, vertebrate, and mammal combine as codes. Dog and cat extend that symbol chain. Names as ordinarily spelled are not used.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150012-9:
Part seven of the Agency indexing study argues against standard subject headings and classing. Old systems make a poor basis for machine searching. Any prior heading set could run on new machines. That path was open but turned down on thought. Broad generic terms would become reference points. Insect and weapon are the examples used. Analysis often yields specific terms instead.

Mosquito and torpedo illustrate those specific terms. Such terms suit machine searches far better. They avoid burdening the indexer with factoring. A semantic factoring technique was developed instead. Standard classing carries its own drawbacks too. It sorts contents into groups for storage. That grouping logic fits machine search poorly. Building new indexing methods needs much trial work. Prior work still saved time and effort here. Classing systems and heading lists were mined. Textbook indexes were used in the same way. The Intelligence Subject Classification received close attention.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200200034-9:
Agency Personnel Office statement dated 9 January 1953 on functions. Staff split under the current table is its subject. Regular staff testing leads the function list. Skills and aptitudes of applicants are tested. Fit of background for employment is judged. Employees are tested for staff actions too. Promotion and reassignment decisions use those tests.

Training needs of clerk staff are judged thereby. Special testing work follows in the statement. Sets of psychological tests run daily there. Clerk and professional staff take those sets. An estimated two thousand tests come monthly. About 275 applicants take them each month. About 125 employees take them monthly too. Test giving takes fifty hours per week. Scoring and computing take sixty-five hours weekly. Reports and permanent records take twenty-five hours. Preparation for testing takes fifteen hours more. Reliability studies appear later in the statement. Trial studies on promising new tests follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000100030007-9:
Minutes of an OTR staff meeting on housekeeping matters. Use of telephones for outside calls leads the items. A deputy's meeting announcement prompted the discussion. About 175,000 dial 9 calls were made in one month. Employees were urged to reduce those calls. Personal calls were the particular target there. No public telephone facilities exist in the buildings.

Desk calls were preferred for personal business anyway. The Incentive Awards Committee had supplied that information. Losing Agency time hunting coin boxes was worse. A placement officer assignment is announced next. Both immediate predecessors had joined OTR itself. Promotion Panel actions are discussed after that announcement. Many actions had to return to supervisors repeatedly. Professional Panel referrals drew that pattern most. Catalog listing drafts get a schedule later. All projected courses must be listed by chiefs. Even dream stage courses belong on the list. The deadline moved from October to 15 September.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100020002-9:
Copy of a CIA redraft of a foreign information paper. Draft number fifteen lies under this 1949 text. Overt psychological warfare planning goes with the program. Foreign information in peace is a lasting instrument. Such warfare in crisis or war is equally lasting. Both must aim at all times at national aims. Department and agency work forms the core elements.

That work is the core nucleus for warfare. Continuity between peace and war plans is sought. Strengthening and coordination of work is required. The Secretary of State bears set charge here. Policy shaping for the national program is his. Swaying foreign views favorably is the purpose. All department and agency work falls inside it. Wartime planning appears in the later paragraphs. Advice covers readying for national crisis. The initial stages of war are included there. Plans coordinate at all times with joint war plans. Its director is appointed by the Secretary.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100050009-9:
National Security Council directive text on covert work. The Council takes note of Communist covert activity first. The USSR, satellite states, and Communist groups are named. Their aim is to harm United States aims. Free world powers are targeted along with it. Open foreign work must therefore be added to. Covert work is the addition settled here.

The Central Intelligence Agency already holds related charges. Espionage and counterespionage abroad are its existing work. Creating a new agency was deemed unwanted. Charge for covert work goes to CIA instead. Linking with espionage work is required alongside. The Director of Central Intelligence holds overall control. Purposes of covert work follow in an ordered list. Wartime planning duties appear in the later text. Plans must be drawn with Joint Chiefs assistance. Fit with approved military war plans is the test.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100120010-9:
Memo on duty for obtaining receipt reports. Materials sent and services done are its subject. Much trouble had occurred in the Comptroller's office. The Fiscal Division met that trouble in practice. Proof of hand-over was hard to obtain there. Contracts with Armed Services elements covered the items. Receipt reports were missing in many cases. Proof of performance was missing as well.

Payment of vouchers suffered undue delay thereby. Reimbursement claims from the Armed Services waited unpaid. Sent items and services fall into groups. Purchase of real property heads that grouping. Construction of plant forms the second group. Mixed services form the third group named. Shipments from ports of sailing form a fourth. Hand-over to Agency depots forms a fifth. Hand-over ticket details are set out later on. Allotment codes apply to each hand-over shown. Joined receipt reports move in two sets.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100120100-9: Short Agency memo on buying of supplies and services. An added list of contact points goes with it. Services are charged to the unit concerned. Faults in service are sent up directly for fixing. Urgent services can be got quickly by telephone. A form confirms the request later where needed. The list names motor pool vehicle upkeep. Official car and chauffeur service is listed too. Contacts sit at the North buildings and Rosslyn. Required forms include a copying form. A request for home travel order is also named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100170015-9:
Letter dated 26 September 1951 reviewing the counsel office. Twenty Exchange Place heads the letter paper. Three days were spent with the Agency's General Counsel. Eric Hager accompanied the writer on that visit. Sufficient personnel and sources were consulted regardless. A clear picture of the office emerged. Its relation to other Agency departments was mapped.

The better part of three days went to Houston. His staff members were interviewed at length. Operating department members were talked with briefly. The general nature of their legal problems was sought. The Agency Loyalty Board was investigated closely. Its composition, procedure, and problems received that attention. Other discharge methods were discussed alongside it. Statutory termination authority forms one such method. Administrative discharge forms the second method discussed. Official procedures of two boards were read fully. A typical loyalty case file was read. Recommendations close the letter's later pages. All Agency lawyers should sit in the office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050060-9:
House bill H.R. 8925 of the 81st Congress, brought in by Mr. Murray of Tennessee on 22 June 1950, would set a hiring path for the competitive civil service. It went to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. The short title in the text is the Federal Personnel Recruitment Act of 1950. Open contest and merit in the choice of staff are its stated aims.

Opening clauses define department broadly across the federal government and the District of Columbia. The bill then builds rules for tests, lists of those who pass, and appointments under the Civil Service Act. Read beside the Senate twin in the same file, it shows the full text Congress weighed, clause by clause, in the summer of 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060168-9:
Addressed to the Comptroller General of the United States, a letter presents the cases of two employees brought back to civilian posts after Navy service. Both held permanent classified civil service standing. Their return rested on the Selective Training and Service Act of 1940. When they took military leave, both worked for the Office of Strategic Services.

That office was wound up on 1 October 1945 under Executive Order 9621, its people and funds split between the State and War Departments. The men's unit passed to the Strategic Services Unit, which took them back. The question put to the Comptroller General concerns a possible right to within-grade salary rises, counting grades held before leave against the posts they now filled.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400090002-9:
Issued for the Department of State and the unified Foreign Service, a directive sets out a course to improve staff systems and staff management. It grows from the findings of the Secretary's Advisory Committee on Personnel. The plan works mainly through changes managers can make on their own authority. Its authors note plainly that it does not yet go as far as the committee urged.

Chief aims include winning, growing, and keeping a seasoned career service able to shift shape as needs change. The directive also wants ways to add staff fast when work suddenly grows. Sections that follow take up hiring, training, grading, and movement between home and overseas posts. The text captures a reform drive inside the foreign affairs agencies just after the war years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400090020-9:
Classification of foreign posts is the legal question in a memorandum dated 19 December 1952 from the Office of the General Counsel. Two earlier papers frame the issue, one from the Personnel Director in September and one from a Near East and Africa division chief in August. At stake is payment of allowances for an unclassified post. The lowest rates for a classified post in the same country were being used as the measure.

Counsel sees no legal bar to stretching that practice past the first six months set in the standard allowance rules. Even so, the opinion urges that unclassified posts be graded at the earliest fair moment once staff are assigned. Executive Order 10130 and the rules on grants of allowances sit behind the reasoning.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400160004-9:
Executive Order 9805 prints the rules for paying travel and transport costs when federal staff move between official stations for good. Issued under Public Law 600 of the 79th Congress, it covers officers and employees across the government. Costs in view include the worker's own travel, the move of the immediate family, and shipment of household goods and personal effects. Opening sections fix what words like employee and department mean inside the rules.

Later parts set when costs may be paid from public funds and what limits apply to weight, distance, and time. The order forms the base rulebook that Agency travel papers of the period keep citing. Its text here is marked as the best copy available, and the scan carries the full set of numbered sections.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400170003-9:
Dated 11 December 1950, a legal memorandum gathers the laws that would spring into force on a presidential proclamation of national emergency. A first group covers powers where the joint resolution of 25 July 1947 had ended the old state of war and past emergencies. Entry by entry, it quotes the trigger words of each act. A 1925 act, for one, guards government use of a Hoboken railroad in war or other national emergency.

Other entries deal with taking control of airfields at Tucson and near Yuma for military ends in an emergency. The survey runs through dozens of such sleeping clauses across the statute book. Its use is plain: lawyers wanted to know, before any proclamation, exactly which powers would wake the moment one was signed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180002-9:
What About Allowances, a January 1952 booklet from the Allowance Branch of the Department of State's Division of Foreign Service Personnel, answers common questions on extra pay abroad. A contents page lists post allowance, quarters allowance, and temporary lodging first. Post differential, separation allowance, travel per diem, and representation allowance follow in their own sections. Transfer allowance and emergency storage payment close the list.

The body runs in question-and-answer form, starting with what payments beyond base salary Foreign Service staff may draw. A second early answer limits staff of other agencies, as a rule, to quarters and post allowances. Each section then works through who qualifies and on what terms. The booklet served as a plain guide for staff posted overseas and the clerks who paid them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180011-9:
Moving a group of overt staff, whose names are redacted, draws a General Counsel memorandum dated 19 December 1952 for a division chief. A cable of 2 December 1952 from a senior representative raised the case. Counsel is asked for the safest legal way to shift these people to known or future overseas posts. Their credit for overseas service toward statutory home leave must not be put at risk, while the Agency's working needs are served.

Staff who have finished two years of unbroken service abroad, counsel notes, can move in the normal way with home leave travel. Harder cases are then tested through a run of supposed examples. Each example stands for a pattern likely to arise, so the advice covers the group without naming anyone.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400190001-9:
Court of Claims case Number 49874, Herman P. Hevenor against the United States, was decided on 4 December 1951. The court set out special findings of fact on facts agreed by both sides. Hevenor served as Principal Budget Examiner in the Bureau of the Budget, stationed in Washington. On 29 October 1941 he was ordered to visit a number of island possessions of the United States. The trip served inquiries into defence projects there.

His travel order Number 42-138, dated the same day, is quoted in the findings. Counsel for both sides are named at the head of the text, with the Assistant Attorney General acting for the government. The case turns on what a travelling official could claim for such a wartime inspection tour. Its findings run long and detailed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500020080-9:
One employee's travel on compassionate leave is ruled not payable in a legal opinion whose surviving text opens mid-argument. The worker had travelled to and from the continental United States in January of that year. Counsel holds the cost cannot count as a refundable expense under the authority cited. Though the payment grew out of an office error, that kind of slip is not what the authority was meant to cover, and a ruling at 31 Comp. Gen. 191 is invoked.

Unvouchered funds, counsel adds, were not granted to lift money burdens caused by misread rules. No legal duty to pay existed, and the gain from the trip was purely personal to the worker. The request cable itself, noting the return was sought for private reasons, is used as proof. Names are redacted throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500020099-9:
Public Law 201 of the 82nd Congress, printed as Chapter 554 from S. 622, raises the basic pay rates of federal officers and employees. It rewrites parts of the Classification Act of 1949, starting with the pay schedule for the General Schedule. Grade by grade, the new yearly rates are printed in full, from GS-2 upward through the senior grades. Early rates cluster near twenty-five hundred dollars a year.

Later sections adjust other classes of staff and settle points left by the rise. The act, cited at 65 Stat. 612, set the pay tables under which Agency staff were graded in the early 1950s. Its long tables make the record a reference text rather than an argument. Anyone checking a salary of the period starts from these printed figures.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500030034-9:
Weight limits for shipping household goods sit at the head of a draft bill that would amend a string of older expense laws. Section 1 of the Administrative Expenses Act of 1946 is the first target. New caps are written in by weight and by packing: seven thousand pounds uncrated, or eight thousand seven hundred fifty pounds crated, for moves inside the continental United States. Moves to, within, or from the territories allow ten thousand pounds uncrated or fourteen thousand crated.

Other clauses would repeal parts of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, the Foreign Service Act of 1946, and the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949. A 1954 defence appropriation clause and a 1940 act are also on the list. The bill tidies the money rules behind every government move.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050014-9:
On 29 July 1949 Mr. Johnston of South Carolina, by request, brought in S. 2351 to gather the laws on compensation from dual employments. The bill went to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service after two readings. Its opening bar says that, unless law clearly allows it, no one paid from one United States office may take pay from a second. Combined sums actually received are the measure of the bar.

Later text works through the exceptions and the classes of post covered, from elected office to jobs in government companies. The District of Columbia is named along with the federal branches. The bill is an early Senate draft of a reform that returned in later prints in this same file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500070049-9:
Hiring consultants prompts a guidance paper of 4 September 1948 from the Chief of the Budget and Finance Branch, acting as Fiscal Inspector. Questions had arisen on appointments, pay limits, overtime, holiday pay, leave, and travel costs. Transcripts of appointment papers and attendance data for six fiscal consultants are attached for study. All six show an excepted appointment under Schedule A authority, with the title Consultant and per diem pay.

Those appointments sat outside the open testing rules of the Civil Service Commission. Whether that exemption was sound is one of the first doubts raised. The paper then sets out proper steps and firm policy for each pay question. It is a pay desk manual drawn from real cases the branch had handled.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500080002-9:
H.R. 18 of the 82nd Congress, brought in by Mr. Brooks on 3 January 1951, would authorise a death gratuity across the armed services. It went to the Committee on Armed Services. Covered services run from Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps to the Coast Guard, the Coast and Geodetic Survey, and the Public Health Service. Reserve parts of those services are included as well.

Payment would fall due at once on the death of a covered person in active or training service. Deaths from the person's own wilful misconduct are carved out. The bill then fixes sums, the order of those who may receive, and the handling of claims. For Agency staff with service ties, such a gratuity scheme framed the baseline of what a death in service paid.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090001-9:
Public Law 873 of the 81st Congress, Chapter 1123 from H.R. 7824, carries the Performance Rating Act of 1950 in full. The act provides for running performance-rating plans for certain federal officers and employees. Its first sections fix what the word department covers. Executive departments, independent bodies, government companies, the courts' administrative office, and the Library of Congress are all named. The District of Columbia government is included too.

A list of those left out follows: the Tennessee Valley Authority, the Post Office field service, and named medical staff among them. Later sections set how plans are approved, how ratings are given, and how a worker may contest one. The act replaced older efficiency ratings across most of the federal service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090010-9:
Proposed element patterns for efficiency ratings go out in a Central Intelligence Agency memorandum of March 1949. All rating and reviewing officials receive it. Attached lists give the elements that matter most in most Agency jobs. The lists serve as a general guide. They are meant to bring sameness to how ratings are prepared across offices. The patterns are stated not to be binding.

A rating official who finds a pattern weak for a job may drop or add elements. The revised pattern must fit the duties of that post. Jobs missing from the list are handled by borrowing from a like job. The memorandum also fixes what a rating should show. It should show how well, how much, and in what manner a person works. The measure is a fair standard set and accepted by the supervisor.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500100036-9:
Basic acts, rules, and regulations governing employment in the federal competitive civil service fill a thick Civil Service Commission pamphlet. Pages 3 through 75 are reprinted from the Federal Personnel Manual and are current as of 26 December 1950. The pamphlet holds section 1753 of the Revised Statutes and the Civil Service Act of 1883. Reorganization Plan Number 5 of 1949 and the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944 follow.

A foreword lists what the pamphlet leaves out: the Classification Act of 1949, the Hatch Act, and the Civil Service Retirement Act among them. Retention preference, leave, and pay rules are also handled elsewhere. The volume is the hiring rulebook in one binding, the base text an Agency personnel office reached for daily.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500120007-9:
Instructions for Agency Form 34-42 guide the clerks who kept time and attendance for the payroll. The form joins a time and attendance report with a pay roll change slip in one sheet. It takes the place of Standard Form 1130. Designated clerks, rather than each office at large, carry the duty of filling it in. Delivery is by hand to the Payroll Branch, Room 1710 in Quarters Eye, by 1600 on the Monday after each pay period.

Every one of items 1 through 10 must be completed in a uniform, accurate way before delivery. Name style, ordering of the forms, and care of the carbon copies are all prescribed. A second copy of the same instruction set, this one is the cleaner print of the two in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140005-9:
Recent changes in the federal civil service retirement system are explained in Civil Service Commission Pamphlet 30 of March 1948. The changes rest on the Langer-Chavez-Stevenson Act of 28 February 1948. The pamphlet aims to answer, in plain terms, the questions federal staff would ask about the new rules. It grows out of a talk given on 4 March 1948 by Warren B. Irons, chief of the Retirement Division, to personnel officials in Washington.

About a million and a half government workers belonged to the retirement system when it was written. New annuity rates, service credit, and the choices open at separation fill the pages. Personnel offices across the government, the Agency's among them, used such pamphlets to advise staff in person.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700120023-9:
Marked as a final copy sent onward in March 1950, an untitled agreement sets out a career agent's terms for 1950. The United States, through the Central Intelligence Agency, hires an unnamed employee for overseas intelligence operations. He must provide himself with an appropriate cover for the work. In this copy he serves under the Central Intelligence Agency itself, rather than under a named office. He accepts the cover duty as part of the bargain.

Article I makes him furnish a cover occupation suited to his professional background and attainments. Conduct in the cover role is prescribed next. The articles that follow deal with direction from headquarters, compensation, and secrecy. Rough draft markings on the copy show the form still being settled in the spring of 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800220157-9:
Air carrier certificate orders under CAR 42 and CAR 45, revised in September, list carriers cleared to operate large aircraft of 12,500 pounds or more certificated take-off weight. Each entry gives the carrier's business address, operations base, and maintenance base. A registration or certificate number, an authorisation code, and the aircraft type follow in columns. Aero Finance Corp. of Hialeah, Florida, flying a DC-3 from Miami International, heads the visible list.

Aerovias Sud Americana of St. Petersburg appears with a C-46 on cargo work. Burbank and Seattle carriers flying C-46 and DC-3 types follow in name order. The table is a Civil Aeronautics reference sheet, kept because the Agency dealt with charter and contract carriers of exactly this kind.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020075-9:
A letter dated 4 September 1948 answers Mr. Eberstadt, chairman of the Committee on National Security Organization of the Hoover Commission. A question had been raised on Friday about guarding defence information and the laws, passed or proposed, that protect it. The writer gives his views at Eberstadt's request. Attention centres on a proposed amendment to the Espionage Act, prepared in the Bureau of the Budget but not yet sent forward.

That proposal, the letter stresses, is not sponsored by CIA, and the Agency was not consulted in drafting it. The views offered are therefore free comment, not an official backing or objection. The writer adds that his post as Director of Central Intelligence shapes his outlook. The letter shows the Agency keeping a careful distance from a secrets bill it had not written.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020101-9:
A chapter headed Your Continuing Obligations speaks to staff leaving the wartime intelligence service about keeping its secrets for life. Two ways of making the point are weighed at the start. One stresses the good reasons: silence guards both the worker and the work of the agency he served. The other stresses fear, noting that a recent Supreme Court reading has put teeth in the Espionage Act.

Those teeth, the chapter warns, will bite the plainly careless as well as the disloyal, where pride or gain loosens a tongue. The oath taken on joining is recalled: no disclosure by word or conduct of anything learned through service with the Office of Strategic Services. Secrecy, the oath ran, was forever. The chapter is an exit lecture in print.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040028-9:
S. 3842, brought in by Mr. McClellan on 28 June 1950, would amend section 109 of the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. It went to the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments. The rewritten subsection sets up a General Supply Fund in the Treasury as a special fund. Into it pass the assets, including any surplus, of the older general supply fund created by an act of 27 February 1929.

Those assets transfer to the new fund under the amendment's terms. Later clauses adjust how the fund is used for buying stores for the agencies. A supply fund sounds dry, yet it decides whether a government storehouse can buy ahead and bill agencies later. The bill keeps the 1949 act's money machinery in repair.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000060008-9:
A second copy of Salary Table Number 26, dated 31 May 1946, carries the same executive branch rates effective 1 July 1946. The text matches the other copy line for line: forty-hour week, two-week period figures by rate, and the Pay Acts of 1945 and 1946 as the base. Hourly and daily unit rates are shown. Tax deductions follow the Revenue Act of 1945.

Duplicate sets of pay tables were common in working files, since each payroll office needed its own. Part 3, on what payrolls and vouchers must show for proper examination and audit, closes the front matter. The tables that follow run rate by rate in dense columns. Keeping both copies let a reader check one against the other where a figure looked doubtful.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100050080-9:
Defamation risk in republishing monitored broadcasts is studied in a legal paper whose names are largely redacted. The question is whether CIA, or the monitoring body, could face liability if libellous matter went out again in the course of reproducing foreign broadcasts. Suits against the United States for tort claims run under the Federal Tort Claims Act of 1946. That act expressly shuts out claims arising from libel or slander.

So the study turns to a sharper point: personal liability of the Director or of staff under him. Before judging that risk, the paper builds a full study of defamation law, starting with definitions. Broadcast monitoring put foreign words into American print daily. A station's insult, repeated by a government bulletin, raised exactly the trap this paper maps.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200020082-9:
Combining Type I with Type II insurance is urged in a sales sheet for an employees' protective plan. A worked example drives the pitch: a member aged thirty-two takes three units of each type. Type I units at fifteen hundred ninety-six dollars each give forty-seven hundred eighty-eight dollars of cover. Type II units add thirty-three hundred fifty-seven, for a total of eighty-one hundred forty-five dollars in force until the sixty-sixth birthday.

Death by accident would pay double that total to the beneficiary, and death by common carrier accident triple. After age seventy, death from natural causes still pays a stated sum. A table of issue amounts by entry age follows, with dismemberment benefits in the newer offer. The sheet is plan marketing aimed at staff weighing family cover.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030072-9:
Appendix B, marked secret, sets out foreign economic intelligence requirements tied to national security. Its first part states what such intelligence is for. It must give a factual, objective account of economic conditions abroad as they touch United States interests. It must also read economic factors for likely future developments of concern. A third use is weighing, on economic evidence, whether courses of action open to the United States can work and what they would bring.

A great many agencies feed this work, the paper notes, each with its own needs. Later parts sort requirements by region, industry, and topic, from raw materials to transport and finance. The appendix served the planned economic intelligence committee as its demand list: what the government needed to know about foreign economies, in order.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030108-9:
Censorship of publications entering the United States is researched in a General Counsel paper dated 22 June 1949, sent to a chief in a foreign branch for the attention of Mr. Robert I. Thiele. Enclosures sent on 15 April 1949 had forwarded a request for word on how such control and censorship work here. The answer was wanted as a guide for shaping law and policy in the requester's own country.

Counsel examined the views of authorities on the topic and the laws and rules now in force. Printed material that could be gathered without an endless search is forwarded with the paper. Gathering waited on the latest postal regulations, shortly due out. A short background note precedes the rules themselves, to help a foreign reader follow the American scheme.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00039a000100050026-9:
An outline of possible topics for a Foreign Language Lecture Program invites additions and changes before the program was set to begin in October. The outline is held by the Central Intelligence Agency and released through CREST. The list is presented only as a starting point, with country names left as blanks such as Italy or France, so lectures could be fitted to a given language and place.

Headings cover economics, literature, and politics, with later sections on labor and other fields. Economics topics include the Point Four program, Soviet use of trade, tariff policy, and the Schuman Plan. Literature topics range from best-selling novels and the city novel to Sartre and French drama, while politics topics take up colonialism, balance of power, totalitarian society, and party systems.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300003-9:
Senate report number 2006, dated 29 July 1954, from the Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs, supports H.R. 8634, a bill to amend section 22 of the Organic Act of Guam. The committee reports the bill without change and urges that it pass, after a hearing by its territorial subcommittee and letters from citizens of Guam and other interested persons.

The aim is to make clear that the jury system should not be imposed on the people of Guam without their consent, shown by action of their elected legislature. Support is noted from the Governor of Guam, the judge of the District Court of Guam, and the Judicial Council of Guam. The Department of the Interior also supports it, with no objection from the Department of Justice. Background pages trace Guam from Spanish rule to United States control in 1898 and the doubt raised by federal court rules.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200160008-9:
Printed bill H.R. 9709, Union Calendar number 721, report number 2001, was introduced in the House on 28 June 1954 by Mr. Reed of New York and sent to the Committee on Ways and Means. Its title is to extend and improve the unemployment compensation program, and the text is given in numbered sections with line numbers.

An early change, effective for services after 31 December 1954, amends section 1607(a) of the Internal Revenue Code by replacing eight or more with four or more, widening the firms covered. A further section amends section 1602(a) on contribution rates, allowing a shorter experience period for a person or group not yet under state law long enough for a three year count. Later sections deal with assignment of federal service and wages to a state and payments to state agencies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200160017-9:
Public Law 767 of the 83rd Congress, chapter 1212, second session, is the enacted form of H.R. 9709, an act to extend and improve the unemployment compensation program. The printed act gives the full statutory text, with each change tied to a section of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 or the Social Security Act.

One change, effective for services after 31 December 1955, amends section 3306(a) by replacing eight or more with four or more. Another adds a rule on contribution rates, allowing a shorter experience period, but not less than one year, for a person or group not yet under state law for three years. A further section repeals section 6152(a)(3), and section 4 adds Title XV, Unemployment Compensation for Federal Employees, to the Social Security Act.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020002-9:
Tab A, titled Legislation Which Affects CIA, surveys bills of the 83rd Congress that touched the Agency. The only bill introduced for the Agency alone was S. 1110, with H.R. 4224, authorising appointment of a Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, sent to Congress 25 February 1953, passed by both houses, and signed 4 April 1953 as Public Law 15.

General bills with provisions affecting the Agency follow. One, S. 2665, carried fringe benefits for federal employees. At Agency request it also carried an exemption from the Performance Rating Act of 1950 and repeal of section 9 of the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949. It became Public Law 763. Later items include registration of persons with knowledge of foreign espionage services, with discretion for the Attorney General and the Director in drafts sent up at Agency request.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160034-9:
Notice of Pending Legislation, dated 2 January as the day is printed in a garbled heading, circulates S.J. Res. 21 for comment from the Director of Security on whether it is of interest to Agency activities. The comment returned states the Agency view in one short paragraph.

From the standpoint of the Agency, it is important that the provisions of section 8 be retained throughout the bill's processing. The Office of the General Counsel is asked to follow the measure to insure a basis for exempting the Agency where security considerations demand. The attached resolution, 84th Congress, first session, was introduced in the Senate on 18 January 1955 by Mr. Humphrey for himself and Mr. Stennis, to establish a Commission on Government Security, with power to appoint staff without regard to civil service laws.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160043-9:
Public Law 304 of the 84th Congress, chapter 664, first session, is the enacted form of H.J. Res. 157, a joint resolution to establish a Commission on Government Security. The printed law gives the full text as resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives in Congress assembled.

Section 1 declares it vital that there be adequate protection of national security, including safeguarding national defense secrets and defense installations, against espionage, sabotage, disloyalty, subversive activities, and unauthorized disclosures. Policy is stated as a sound government program. It covers security investigation, evaluation, and adjudication of employees, and security requirements for persons privately employed on work needing access to defense secrets. It also calls for vigorous enforcement of realistic security laws and careful administration that protects national security and preserves basic American rights. Later sections establish the Commission, cover its staff, and authorise sums to be appropriated for its expenses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100230009-9:
Sectional analysis of a bill to facilitate the procurement of doctors and dentists for the Armed Forces, by grants and scholarships for medical and dental education, explains the bill section by section. Section 1 is described as authorising the service Secretaries to establish annual scholarships to help meet Armed Forces needs.

Section 2 sets up separate Medical Services Scholarship Groups for the Army, Navy, and Air Force under the Department of Defense. It lists basic qualifications for enrollment, and allows termination of membership under rules of the Secretary of Defense. Section 3 gives members an allowance not to exceed 133 dollars per month at a school of medicine or dentistry. It also states that members gain no military or veteran benefits by membership alone. Later analysis covers service duties after training, one year of active duty for each year of training, with a three year minimum in stated cases.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020001-9:
Printed joint resolution S.J. Res. 96 was introduced in the Senate on 30 June 1953 by Mr. Hickenlooper, for himself and seven other senators, and sent to the Committee on Foreign Relations, in the 83rd Congress, first session. Its title is to strengthen the foreign relations of the United States by establishing a Commission on International Telecommunications.

Recitals state that the overseas information program carried on through telecommunications is of growing importance in support of foreign policy. They quote the President's State of the Union message of 2 February 1953 on making international information activities more effective. They also cite a Senate special subcommittee report of 15 June 1953 on linking Atlantic nations and much of the non-Communist world in television networks. Later sections authorise staff under the Classification Act of 1949, help from agencies on a reimbursable basis, and experts at up to seventy five dollars per day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020047-9:
Letter on Central Intelligence Agency letterhead, Office of the Director, is addressed to Senator Alexander Wiley, Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Relations. It replies to his request of 3 July 1953 for comments on S.J. Resolution 96. The letter is short, occupying two pages in the file, and gives the Agency's view in general terms.

International telecommunications are called a powerful instrument of national policy. Their technical and engineering side must be closely fitted to the overall needs of national security and tied to overall policy, planning, and guidance. Studies for the National Security Council are cited, as are the March 1951 report of the President's Communications Policy Board and a recent report on international information activities. New techniques said to be capable of sending television across oceans should be weighed against urgent security needs, the small number of sets abroad, and differing transmission standards.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200080005-9:
State Department circular instruction CA-2532, dated 15 October 1954, marked for official use only, is the second circular instruction on the proposed trip of the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy. Posts addressed run from Athens, Baghdad, and Bangkok to Tokyo, Tehran, and Wellington, with American consuls at Auckland, Hong Kong, Melbourne, Sydney, and Calcutta informed.

The committee had revised the schedule sent by CA-2021 of 23 September 1954, and the new schedule, approved by Chairman Cole and Vice Chairman Hickenlooper, is attached. The itinerary no longer includes Okinawa, Singapore, and Rangoon. Japan is deleted, and Saigon is also deleted but still a possibility. Tehran replaces Baghdad, and Hong Kong and Athens are added. Later guidance covers dress, asking that the whole official party be included in official functions, and hotel reservations for members travelling on standard government per diem.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690029-9:
Analysis of the Proposed Overseas Allowances Act of 1954 works through an earlier draft of the bill, section by section. Section 111 defines the areas covered, and differs from the later draft. The definition of Territories and possessions excludes the Canal Zone and the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. The foreign plan replaces the territorial plan in the Trust Territory.

Section 121 continues presidential rule making on allowances and differentials. Section 122 extends eligibility for foreign post differentials and territorial cost of living allowances to employees whose basic pay is fixed administratively. Present authority covers only staff whose salaries are set by statute. A note on the education allowance says the bill would be the first permanent provision aiding civilian staff of all agencies in foreign areas in educating their minor children. It was attempted in H.R. 9364 of 1950 and in S. 1985.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200040001-9:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated April 1955, comments on S. 1542, the Notaries Public Expense Act of 1955. The bill proposes to authorize an allowance for civilian officers and employees of the Government who are notaries public.

The memorandum finds the bill of direct interest to Agency personnel activities and recommends the Agency support S. 1542 if an opportunity arises. Attached are the notice of pending legislation form and a Senate report on the bill: Mr. Johnston of South Carolina, from the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, reported it favorably with amendments on 24 March 1955 and recommended passage as amended. The report text in the file restates the bill's purpose, an allowance for government staff who serve as notaries public in their work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200130001-9:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated 1 July 1955, comments on H.R. 6547, a bill providing for a simplified performance rating system for federal employees. Because the bill would set up a new performance evaluation system for all government agencies, the memorandum finds it would conflict with the Agency's policy. That policy judges employee suitability through its Fitness Report procedures.

An effort is therefore requested to seek an Agency exception to the bill's provisions if it gains favorable consideration in Congress, and the office asks to be told of further developments. A second comment in the file takes a narrower line: the Agency is exempt from the Performance Rating Act of 1950, so no Agency action or position is necessary. The Agency still tries to adhere closely to Civil Service regulations, procedures, and policies. The notice form and bill print are attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200310001-9:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel, dated 7 April 1955 and marked copy, is headed Proposed Legislation Affecting Military Personnel. Three bills are referenced: H.R. 2436, to provide hospitalization and medical care for dependents of members of the uniformed services; H.R. 4720, to provide incentives for members of the uniformed services by increasing certain pays and allowances, the Career Incentive Act of 1955; and S. 936, its Senate companion.

The proposals are of interest to individuals detailed to the Agency while in an active military status, the memorandum finds. They are not of direct interest to Agency personnel activities, and no further action by the Legislative Counsel's office is recommended. The long file holds the bill prints and notice forms. Career Incentive Act text in the file sets incentive pay at one hundred dollars a month for officers and fifty dollars for enlisted persons, with no such pay for aviation cadets.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100060003-9:
A CIA letter to the Bureau of the Budget's legislative reference staff is partly garbled in the scan. It comments on a proposed employees' personnel act. It asks for a specific exemption for the Agency. Many foreign nationals work for CIA, under varied arrangements. The letter warns of serious problems if the act applied in full. Reports, statistics, and local job standards in some areas would clash with security needs.

The wording sought would guard the Director's duty to protect intelligence sources and methods. It follows an exemption already in the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. The letter offers more detail on request. Later pages comment section by section. One section, on a residence rule, should be deleted rather than waived. Another point asks whether 'public interest' means that of the United States.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100210051-9:
A CIA legal memorandum comments on a new draft of section 606 of the Communications Act of 1934. It was written for the Director of Communications. Section 606 governs presidential power over communications in war or national emergency. The draft came from the Executive Office of the President in August 1955. Asked for comment, this office chose to rewrite the whole section instead.

The rewrite has clear aims. It states plainly when the President may act, and it defines that situation. It extends his reach to radio and wire traffic in the Panama Canal Zone. It lets him delegate the powers. It also lets him set aside some compulsory parts of the Act in an emergency. The office says its version changes the order and clarity, not the substance. It adds one exact test: action only when another country's conduct endangers national security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100230013-9:
A CIA legal opinion of 16 July 1955 answers a spending question. It went to the Deputy Director (Support). Could Agency funds buy air conditioners for four windowless rooms? The rooms were built for storage. Overcrowding had turned them into offices. No spare equipment on hand could ventilate them.

The opinion answers no, on ordinary authority. Under the statute cited, only the General Services Administration may buy such equipment, with its own funds. The General Accounting Office would take exception to CIA vouchers for it. The Director's special authority under section 10(b) of Public Law 110 is no help either. That authority serves only the Agency's special and unique functions. The rooms might stay unusable in summer. Still, no ground was found to use that authority here.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100250011-9: A CIA legal memorandum gives the General Counsel's opinion on GEHA's overhead costs. It went to the Acting Deputy Director (Support). GEHA is the Agency's insurance association. The scan is partly garbled, and one original page is marked missing. The opinion weighs what share of Agency overhead GEHA should bear. That overhead pays for the support the Agency gives the insurance program. It concludes that the Agency will go on giving GEHA office and secretarial support.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030005-9:
A CIA memorandum to the Director summarises a bill prepared to amend the CIA Act of 1949, for submission to the next session of Congress. The bill has eighteen sections and aims to broaden Agency authority where work had been hampered by a lack of legal power. The summary gives the reason and effect of each section in turn.

Early sections add procurement authority drawn from the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947 and let the Agency commit research and development funds for up to five years instead of one. Another deletes 'its territories and possessions' from section 5, so staff stationed there receive the same benefits as staff in foreign areas, ending an inequity the memo stresses. Later sections cover storage of effects and payment of medical costs tied to a post's conditions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030078-9:
A CIA memorandum sends branch chiefs a list of laws for the 1952 fiscal year. The Chief of the Fiscal Division wrote it. The branches covered are Accounting, Claims, Travel, and Payroll. The list is partial, not full. Each entry cites the law or regulation to consult. Most civil service and pay material is left out.

Entries are grouped under Services, Personnel, and Fiscal. The grouping follows the function with the main interest. Readers are told to review all three groups anyway. One rule caps typewriter prices at 90 percent of the lowest net cash price. Another sets a $2,200 cost limit for passenger vehicles, under a 1951 act. A third frees diesel fuel sold for state or local government use from tax. Because Public Law 110 governs CIA, the list is to be read with that Act in mind.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030096-9:
A CIA memorandum of 7 April 1948 explains the proposed Agency bill. The General Counsel wrote it for the chairman of the House committee studying the bill. It gives the background first. In January the Agency told the committee a hard fact. The Central Intelligence Group could not operate in the coming fiscal year. Rules on the use of funds blocked it. Some came from the Agency's own needs. Others came from the Comptroller General's reading of the law.

The memo then defends the bill's boldest features. Section 6(a) lets the Agency move funds to and from other departments. Transferred money could be spent without the limits of the first appropriation. The memo calls this without precedent, yet necessary. Section 6(f) shields the size of the Agency from disclosure. It also shields its officers' functions. Section 7(a)(1) would act as permanent appropriation language. No specific yearly appropriation was proposed, for security reasons.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030104-9:
A draft bill of 16 February 1948 would provide for the administration of the Central Intelligence Agency. It rests on the National Security Act of 1947. Its table of contents lists eleven sections. That is more than the later February drafts. Besides definitions, a seal, procurement, training, and travel, it adds two extra topics. One is investigation of personnel. The other is death benefits.

The personnel section sets a strict bar. No one may be assigned to departmental duty before an FBI check. The Bureau must report on character, associations, and loyalty. The Director may waive the rule only in an emergency. The travel section covers expenses, leave, and cars. It also covers hospital care. An officer who falls ill at a post with no suitable hospital may be sent to the nearest one. The general authorities exempt the Agency from publishing personnel data.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030113-9:
A draft statutory section is headed 'General Authority'. Parts of the scan are badly garbled. The section sets out powers the Central Intelligence Agency would hold. Legible parts let the Agency move funds to and from other departments and agencies. The Bureau of the Budget is tied to those approvals. The transfers would ignore laws that limit moves between appropriations.

Other legible parts cover pay for outside staff. The Agency may reimburse other departments for staff assigned or detailed to it.
