Added pay from the Director's and Deputy Director's differential would come from Agency funds. A reference to Public Law 724 of the 79th Congress appears, as the scan renders it. It applies named benefit sections to staff stationed outside the continental United States. Because the OCR is so degraded, only these broad powers can be read with confidence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030122-9:
A statutory text headed 'General Authority' prints section 6 of a draft CIA act. The section appears twice, and the second copy is cleaner. It lists what the Agency may do. First comes procurement. The Agency may buy services, supplies, and equipment without regard to section 3709 of the Revised Statutes. The Director must certify that the action serves the common defence and security. Or someone must show that advertising is not reasonably practicable. Partial and advance payments are allowed.

Next come transfers of funds. The Agency may send funds to, and receive funds from, other departments and agencies. The transfers ignore laws limiting moves between appropriations. Transferred sums may be spent under this Act alone. The Agency may also apply the benefit sections of Public Law 704 of the 79th Congress to staff at permanent posts abroad. It may repay departments for staff assigned to it, and exchange funds freely.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220003-9:
An appendix sets out the statutory basis of Executive Order 10450. The Order is dated 27 April 1953. It extends the Act of 26 August 1950 to all departments and agencies. The appendix lists the authorities the Order cites. They include R.S. 1753, the Civil Service Act of 1883, and section 9A of the Act of 2 August 1939.

Each authority is then explained. Section 9A made membership in a group seeking violent overthrow a ground for removing civilian staff. It was repealed by the Act of 9 August 1955. R.S. 1753 lets the President set rules for admission to the civil service. The Civil Service Act sections cover the Commission's duties. One bars removal without pay except for cause that promotes efficiency, with reasons in writing. The 1950 Act, by contrast, lets named agency heads suspend staff without pay in their absolute discretion. Termination may follow when the head finds it needed for national security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220049-9:
Two CIA memoranda of July 1953 work out the steps needed under Executive Order 10450. The Order is dated 27 April 1953. The first memo, of 23 July, reviews an outline sent by the Chief of the Security Division. The outline came from a CIA regulation of 27 May 1953. That regulation began as a Justice Department draft under paragraph 13 of the Order. Its substance came from the Internal Security Act of 1950.

The second memo, of 31 July, reports a talk on the proposed changes. They would go into a revised outline, with no resubmission to this office. The reviewer proposes detailed edits to single steps. One change concerns the word 'notice' in a step. Another aligns a step with section 5(b)(2) of the regulation. The memo also notes where the CIA regulation departs from the basic statute, seeming to limit the types of derogatory information that count as a security risk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300240155-9:
A CIA legal memo settles questions on congressional privilege and immunity. It begins with a proposal of 30 September 1947. The Executive for Inspection and Security suggested cautionary notices on secret material released to Congress. Two wordings are quoted. One limits the document to the recipient's use. The other cites the Espionage Act, at 50 U.S.C. 31 and 32.

The conclusions are firm. A Member of Congress may say anything on the floor or in committee. The statement may be reprinted in the Congressional Record. It is absolutely privileged, even if it includes secret CIA material. Warning words do not change that. Use of such material outside Congress, in press or speeches, is not privileged. It could draw prosecution under the espionage laws. Still, the memo judges prosecution of a Member very unlikely. It recommends the Espionage Act wording as the better notice.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300270017-9:
A CIA file holds an adjuster's letter and a damage statement for a third household shipment. The letter is dated 2 October 1951. R. R. Runkles, an adjuster for insurance companies, wrote it. He had investigated the crating in claim PO/PCD-1037. He found it done in accordance with the Agency's requirements. He suggested the claim be filed against the carrier.

The owner's statement is blunt. The effects arrived battered and shattered. Fragile items were thrown loosely into boxes with no packing. A Toastmaster toaster was smashed, and a 16mm movie projector broken into pieces. Two children's tricycles were thrown onto two new mahogany lamp tables, which came out in splinters. A mahogany desk came from an undamaged crate in some thirty-five pieces. A dining table lost all four legs. Records were stacked without protection, and dozens broke. Nails were even driven through encyclopedias, and a mattress was ripped.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100010023-9:
A CIA compilation lists accomplishments and objectives for Agency offices. Each office reports in turn. The Cable Secretariat revised cable forms to end the use of preprinted paper. It also revised the Agency regulation setting basic cable policy. Its aim is to cut cable traffic by diverting messages to pouch channels. The Office of the Auditor-in-Chief prepared regulations on audit scope at headquarters and overseas.

The Medical Office cut its stock list from about 5,000 items to about 2,500. It standardized items under generic rather than trade names. A stock rotation plan now guards drugs with expiration dates. Medical kits for field operations were standardized. The Security Office placed badge records on electric accounting machines. It prepared headquarters and field manuals of investigative standards. Objectives include management surveys and better manpower distribution.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100010041-9:
An annual management report of the CIA Security Office is dated 17 August 1954. It went to the Chief, Management Staff. The office's problems are stated plainly. Budget limits restrict the personnel available. Chances to advance are too few, above all in lower clerical posts. Name checks with other federal agencies process slowly. In that area the office is at the mercy of other agencies' staff.

For fiscal 1955 the office chose faster processing of investigative cases for emphasis. It will establish a guard training program. Security processing of new employees will be simplified. The Night Security Office will move and run on a more operational basis. The photographic and laminating rooms will be redesigned and consolidated. Up to twenty employees will be organized with special police powers from GSA. A procedures manual for the Physical Security Branch is planned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030030-9:
A House subcommittee paper explains the functional approach to manpower utilization. The subcommittee covers manpower utilization and departmental personnel management. It sits under the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. Its chairman is James C. Davis of Georgia. The paper expands Recommendation C of the subcommittee's report on manpower management, House Report No. 1740, 84th Congress.

Functions are defined as the major systems or processes by which an organization meets its objectives. A functional approach surveys one function across a whole agency. The paper contrasts this with surveys by organization, program, or object class. Each approach stresses something different: authority lines, objectives, purchases, or processes. A combined approach, the paper argues, gives the fullest picture. A functional survey follows one function from beginning to end. It crosses every bureau and division involved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030076-9:
A CIA memorandum of November 1955 reviews manpower in the Office of Communications. It went to the Deputy Director (Support). The office studied the effects of a ten percent cut in its present ceiling. Its ceiling divides between regular and special activities. Regular work covers headquarters staff, U.S. field sites, signal centers, and overseas stations. The figures themselves are redacted.

The regular-activities ceiling was already cut by more than six percent on 31 July 1955. Compensated and voluntary overtime is now needed to meet the workload. A further ten percent cut is possible only if a substantial part of the workload ends. The office lists activities where positions could come from. Reductions in the Middle East and Southeast Asia are considered. Training staffs could be cut, at the price of fewer courses. Signal center coverage could drop from 24 hours to 16, 12, or 8.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040020-9:
A CIA memo of 23 November 1955 reports manpower use in the Contact Division. It went to the Deputy Assistant Director for Operations. The division's functions are listed, though the function text itself is redacted. Several carry common-concern aspects. No real order of priority can be set among them. The support function, the memo argues, should not rank lower on practical grounds. All are treated as equally important.

Personnel figures rest on duty strength as of 31 October 1955. Division work is so interwoven that counts by function are rough estimates. They rest on professional time spent, with clerical support assumed to split the same way. Later pages weigh cuts. Ending one machine-recording method would sacrifice nine years of source records. Reducing headquarters support would end staff positions that aid collection through source studies and analysis.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100350004-9:
A CIA report of 26 July 1957 covers participation in Operation Alert 1957. The writer served on the Executive Committee of the Emergency Economic Warfare organization. That body was set up under the Secretary of Commerce. Its tools were export controls, preclusive buying, blacklisting, and financial controls. On 15 July the organization passed to its wartime status. Its Executive Committee began simulated action at the Relocation Center.

The report gives the exercise highlights from the intelligence point of view. Planning and execution of the simulated problem showed substantial gaps. Much more work is needed to build an effective system. Pre-planning was vital. Coordination with allies was also stressed. One unanswered cable asked whether CIA support existed for the preclusive buying program. Blacklisting drew its own lessons. Officers named include Edward P. Rains and Clarence R. Nichols.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410016-9:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 May 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. Eight USSR foreign trade charts are complete for April. Nuclear research organization charts are also complete. Entries cover synthetic and shale oil, sulfur consumption, and the Bezymyannaya volcano in Kamchatka. Organization charts cover Soviet institutes tied to bilateral agreements and nuclear research.

Rumania entries track growth under five-year plans. Bulgaria's party and government chart appears in third revision. Latin America entries close the list. Oilfields and refineries are charted for Argentina, Chile, Bolivia, and Cuba. An Indonesia petroleum sheet is in first revision. South Vietnam hospitals and Afghanistan's agricultural, mineral, and industrial resources are also listed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490009-9:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 243 of 30 April 1957. The chairman raised use of the NIS Standard Instructions. Analysts, he said, are not following them. In many cases they have not even read them. Members were asked to fix this before the revised instructions issue later this year. Page proofs are expected before the fiscal year ends.

The chairman then described a proposed NIS Reference Guide. It would serve users below the strategic planning and policy levels. It should rest on the Standard Instructions but present only what users need. Its tasks are spelled out. It should acquaint readers with the fundamentals of the NIS program. It should explain practical points, such as why one country's NIS is never produced all at once. Contributor statements for Section 22 and Supplement II were also approved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100140028-9:
Dated December 6, 1950, a memorandum from the Technical Publishers Group goes to the Department of Defense Task Force on Publishing, Printing, and Distribution of Training and Educational Literature. It asks that every armed service office producing training literature be reminded of official policy on the use and republication of copyrighted material. Offices should also be cautioned against breaking that policy.

The memo quotes the Armed Services Procurement Regulations, Section IX, Part 2. Those rules state that the departments respect a copyright owner's property right. The memo then sets out how permission should be sought. The publisher must hold the original copyright. He must receive a statement of the proposed use, including how many copies will be printed at first. The statement must also say whether those copies will be sold, and if so, how and at what price. The memorandum survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100190023-9:
Training Bulletin Number 12, issued by the Office of Training on November 23, 1953, circulates remarks by Lyman B. Kirkpatrick, the Inspector General, to Agency personnel. Kirkpatrick spoke at the Twelfth Agency Orientation Course on November 6, 1953. The bulletin, signed by Director of Training Matthew Baird, asks that the text be given the widest circulation its classification allows.

Attached material includes Kirkpatrick's remarks and his answers to questions from the course, offered for the information and guidance of all concerned. The file also carries the remarks of Charles P. Cabell at the Eleventh Orientation Course on August 4, 1953. Together the speeches give new staff a senior-level view of the Agency, its work, and its standards in its early years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100120012-9:
A staff paper lists the functions then assigned to a logistics support element serving the Agency's SE Division. The office's own name was removed in review. The duties cover liaison on logistical matters with the Logistics Division and the Procurement Office. They also cover the preparation of requisitions for equipment and supplies. Those supplies serve the division, both abroad and in the United States.

The element also kept records of logistical matters and supplies, including cable and dispatch files. It arranged shipment of equipment to overseas installations. It handled requisitions for official and quasi-personal motor vehicles. It kept the division's vehicle records and inventory. At headquarters it supplied furniture, telephone upkeep, and repair work. A second section sets out proposed functions. It adds review of the logistical side of division programs and projects. That review would run in coordination with the Office of Logistics and other offices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100140002-9:
A short office memorandum dated January 24, 1957, reports the third annual Agency briefing of the Foreign Service Inspection Corps of the Department of State. The Chief Instructor of the War Planning Course writes to the Chief of the Operations School. The briefing itself was held on January 22, 1957, from 0900 to 1230 hours, in the Director's conference room in the Administration Building.

Nineteen members of the Inspection Corps attended, along with three members of the Office of the Undersecretary of State. The session followed its attached schedule with one exception: the Chief, PPC/DD/P, back from temporary duty, gave the talk on the organization of CIA. The writer also credits a colleague who stayed through the meeting and helped it run smoothly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200010005-9:
Agenda planning for an Agency Senior Administrative Officers Conference lays out the support and personnel questions senior administrators were to take up together. Early sessions treat the present system for support planning. They stress how specific support requirements are determined. They also stress the role of the Chief of Administration in meeting them. That role forms a basis for planning the support services.

Other sessions cover the budget. They cover its relation to other planning exercises, and allotment and obligation controls. They cover the value of realistic obligation data in using a budget as a management tool. A personnel block follows. It takes up motivation, legislation, suggestion awards, and other incentives. A job satisfaction section covers use of employees' skills. It also covers communication up and down, counseling, and supervision. The handling of unsuitable staff is included. Parts of the scan are garbled.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200010014-9:
A report to the Director of Training describes an Operational Management Seminar given to supervisors of the Agency's FE Division in 1956. The course grew out of presentations made the previous June, and the division's training officer put in a formal request for it on October 3. The report judges the offering well received and, with qualifications noted, worth repeating.

Participant comments quoted in the report are warm. One officer says the course was stimulating and made him look at his job afresh; another reports a lasting effect on job performance and a wider view of management problems. A third says he has already put several things learned into practice. The report adds that the course could be adapted for other audiences to good effect.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200020004-9:
An essay on the training problems of the Central Intelligence Agency starts from a structural handicap. Unlike the armed forces, the Agency cannot draw on the product of academies like West Point or Annapolis for trained manpower. It must instead select from the graduates of private universities those who specialized in the physical, natural, and social sciences and who show high motivation and potential.

Such recruits, the paper says, bring only a foundation. Professional competence has to be built on it through formal and on-the-job training. Outside help is limited: some universities run cross-cultural area programs, but not framed around national security problems, and not in numbers near the Agency's needs. University treatment of international Communism, in philosophy and economics courses, is weighed in the same way.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100005-9:
The June report of the Committee on Language Development, dated July 29, 1957, summarizes a meeting held on June 17. The agenda ran over five items. They were the language development policy document and the results of Form 444c submittals. They were the status of proficiency tests and the DD/P reaction to the Erwin Report. The state of the Agency's off-duty language training courses came last. Policy decisions from the meeting are recorded first.

The report then lists the voluntary courses that carry the program's reach. New off-duty classes started on June 10 and June 24. They covered German, Italian, Spanish, and French. Most were held after hours, with 55 students in all. Eleven further off-duty courses continued from May. They included French and German classes at the entry level.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100014-9:
Qualification instructions dated February 4, 1957, set the schedule of awards under the Agency's Language Development Program. Development awards may be granted in the amounts shown, under a regulation of the same date and the further provisions of this notice. Both achievement awards, for reaching a level, and maintenance awards, for holding it, are fixed by the schedule according to the type and level of proficiency.

The criteria for judging proficiency are those in Form 444c, the Language Data Record, and they match the criteria used in scoring the official proficiency tests. An applicant's self-evaluation is compared with his test scores in a process that balances strengths and weaknesses before the type and level of proficiency, and so the award, are set.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200120003-9:
Statistical tables record how much the Office of Training traded teaching with the rest of the government in 1955. One set counts OTR instructors, school by school. It counts those who took part in the training programs of other agencies. The agencies include the Army, Navy, and Air Force. They include the United States Information Agency and the State Department. They include the International Cooperation Administration and the National War College.

Companion tables run the traffic the other way. Guest instructors from other agencies taught in OTR programs. A separate table tracks use of CIA training by outsiders. Its entries include eighteen Foreign Service inspectors and ten National War College graduates. A final set carries the exchange into the first quarter of 1956. The tables are raw counts, with no narrative attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030002-9:
Weekly Activities Report number 42, dated October 23, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Language and Area School. It is built around the school's efforts to sell itself inside the Agency. The chief reports giving the school's story at a staff meeting. He had a tight, fully packed thirty minutes. He covered all of the school's activities and the ways it could serve the logistics side of the house. The same presentation was given again that week to another audience.

The Qualifications Review Panel sat that day on four candidates. Three were OSI candidates for German. One was a Western Hemisphere candidate for Portuguese. The report also describes area training sessions. They were built around talks by speakers of contrasting cultural backgrounds. One speaker was William Crockett of the State Department. He spoke on life as seen by American officials posted abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030011-9:
Weekly Activities Report number 33, dated August 21, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Language and Area School. It opens with a planning problem in a single language. The school was trying to tie together a set of differing requirements for Indonesian. The requirements were partly changing. The aim was to offer the best quality training at the least cost to the Agency. Within a few days it hoped to have the facts in hand. It would then have a plan of courses for about eight people.

Routine consultation on training needs fills the next item. Attached reports add the week's detail from other parts of the school. One comes from the Deputy Chief for Plans, Research and Administration, dated August 20. It records twenty-nine people reporting to take proficiency tests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030020-9:
Weekly Activities Report number 24, dated June 18, 1958, comes from the Acting Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. It is largely a wrapper for three attached reports. Those reports come from the school's three components. The principal item of interest, the chief writes, was planning. The subject was a Language and Area School summer program for junior officer trainees.

On Monday, staff from several offices met to trade views. They came from the school, the Assessment and Evaluation Staff, the training directorate, and the JOT staff. Responsibilities were sketched out at that meeting. One officer would work on finding the most suitable person to direct the course. Another would gather material for it. The attached component reports carry the week's detail. One comes from the Deputy Chief for Area Training.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050037-9:
Trainees abroad come first in Weekly Activity Report number 6 of the Registrar's office. The report covers February 5 to 11, 1958. Deposits were made to bank accounts toward return trips. They included two Agency junior officer trainees finishing the Russian Language Program in June. Those trainees would come back to Washington in July. They would travel ahead of the heavy summer tourist season.

The bigger job is records. Initial processing of more than 25,000 individual training record cards was to be finished by February 17. The matching phase would follow at once. It was complicated by name changes from marriage or agent status. The report also notes attrition in the processing crew itself. Four of the original eight trained hands had been reassigned elsewhere. They were borrowed from the Office of Personnel.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400060023-9:
Weekly Activity Report number 9 of the Agency's Instructional Services Branch covers February 26 to March 4, 1958. Five film projects are reported in a line or two each. The Secret Writing Film held to its estimated completion date of April 1 under its contractor. The Logistics Film was due on April 15, subject to any changes required by a second interlock screening set for March 5.

For the Intelligence Process Film, a treatment of the matrix film was being written, folding in suggestions made on the pattern. The Security Film's second draft treatment was absorbing psychological material supplied by the Assessment and Evaluation Staff. A supervision film rounds out the slate. The report is a snapshot of a small film shop juggling several productions at once.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400090002-9:
Weekly Activity Report number 50 of the Agency's Junior Officer Training Program covers December 10 to 16, 1958. In the Intelligence Techniques Course, the long projects were being assigned: each trainee stated his order of preference among twelve subjects. Some chose ground where they already had strong academic training and area familiarity. Others deliberately chose new areas about which they knew little, and the science and English majors among them scattered their choices widely.

Student judgment of the American Heritage Course was mixed at the edges. A few trainees regretted that some of the men who briefed them held high places in government despite modest ability. The report stresses that this was no consensus, applied to only a few speakers, and sat alongside the highest regard for many who addressed them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400080014-9:
A memorandum dated June 17, 1952, goes to the Deputy Director (Administration). It warns of serious gaps in the powers handed to the Assistant Director (Personnel). Those powers govern running the Personnel Office. The writer lists the papers from which the powers flow. Each grants only part of the whole. They include a directive of the Director dated December 1, 1950. They include the Agency's rules and the Confidential Funds Regulations. They include a grant of powers by the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council. The Director concurred in that grant.

The file carries the Council's grant itself, dated December 1, 1950. It rests on a Council resolution approved September 26, 1947. It also rests on Section 102 of Public Law 253 of the 80th Congress, approved July 26, 1947. That statute is the one under which the Agency's work was first carried on.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400110001-9:
A memorandum dated October 10, 1952, from the Agency's Director of Training circulates the Office of Training's table of organization as approved on September 17, 1952. Official copies had just become available. The general portion is sent to the Deputy Director of Training for retention, with individual copies of each staff and division portion for the chiefs concerned. The information, chiefs are warned, is for their own use and is not to be shown to others except on a need-to-know basis in assignment discussions.

The Personnel Section was already at work on the preliminary reslotting of people against the new table. Attached position notes sketch the staff the office wanted, including the officer who would develop the Human Resources Program and supervisory training running from assistant director level down to the first-line supervisor.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100060002-9:
A survey annex on the Agency's Office of Training opens with a blunt judgment. Its Administrative Services Branch is poorly organized and confused. Part of the trouble is traced to an earlier merger. Overt and covert administration inside the office had been merged. The merger was still slow to settle. Position records and the people actually doing the work do not match. Budget and fiscal work had been handled by shifting hands on an ad hoc basis. A Budget Officer was lately appointed to end the confusion by specializing.

The annex doubts the cure fits. There is not enough work for a full-time Budget Officer and a clerk-stenographer. The Comptroller's Office exercises little technical supervision over the work. Payroll mechanics fill the rest of the annex. They include the separate handling of contract agent salaries. They include staff in field slots paid from unvouchered funds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100090027-9:
An interim report on the Printing Services Division of the Office of Logistics takes stock after a takeover. In January 1957 the Agency assumed operating control of a plant. It was the GPO-State Service Plant, now the Administration Building Plant. The report deals mainly with the new plant. It makes side references to the division's other plants. It organizes its evidence by management factor, in tabs. The tabs cover intelligence printing, physical plant, personnel, finance, materials, workload, and equipment.

Two personnel problems stand out. Since the merger the division has had no time to build a reserve. It needs trained people for peak workload periods. Some overtime will therefore be necessary for an indefinite time. The salaries of former GPO staff need adjustment too. Their job titles and hourly pay scale must be converted into the civil service GS system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220004-9:
A staff paper on the Technical Review and Policy Staff of the Agency's Logistics Office explains a merger. The new staff combines the Technical Review Staff's inspection and review functions with those of the Special Staff, and adds the printing advisory function, transferred from the General Services Office. The Special Staff had once been justified by a heavy load of projects handled under the Chief of Logistics' immediate direction, as a four-member staff.

That load, the paper's justification shows in man-months, has shrunk, and the combined staff can absorb it. The functions carried forward include developing and controlling the procedures that govern the office's regulatory issuances, improving existing logistics procedures, and putting new and revised ones into effect across the office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200010006-9:
A Department of State handbook dated March 1956 teaches one skill. Titled Preparation of Outstanding Performance Ratings, it shows how to build the rarest rating. Its contents run in order. They cover how an outstanding rating is initiated and the criteria it must meet. They cover how the justification is prepared and the time limit for submission. They cover the performance awards that follow. A summary closes the argument, and examples do the teaching.

The exhibits give model texts. They give outstanding ratings for a clerk-typist at GS-3 and a secretary at GS-7. They give them for a foreign affairs officer at GS-11 and an international economist at GS-15. A fictitious disapproved rating shows failure. One model praises an employee who managed the flow of office work. Matters needing a higher level were cared for in the supervisor's absence. The copy survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200040003-9:
A memorandum to the Deputy Director (Support) poses a custody question. Which element of the Agency should hold the file record of Form 37-6? That form is the Personnel Information Card, known as the locator record. The present custodian is the Telephone Section, under the Office of Logistics. The record holds employees' home addresses and telephone numbers. It is distinct from the telephone information file, a flexoline index kept beside it.

The Agency's watch regulation bears on the answer. Telephone operators supply the locator service the watch officer depends on. If custody moves, the memorandum argues, the function should go to one element. That element must be able to enforce the regulations and render the service efficiently. It must ensure positive identification of Agency employees. One office had already agreed, verbally, to accept the service from another source.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200050011-9:
A memorandum to the Agency Comptroller from his deputy, filed as an annex in 1952, urges the establishment of a Technical Accounting Staff. It is imperative, the deputy writes, to build a staff of high-level accountants. They are needed for the large amount of staff work in the Comptroller's office. That work includes the accounting and fiscal procedural studies, developments, and installations, and the instructions that go with them. The present structure makes no adequate provision for it.

The cost of doing without shows in the principals' own days. Too much of the Comptroller's time, and his deputy's, goes to framing answers. The questions are the accounting, audit, and financial problems that arrive daily and demand policy decisions after hours of work. A task force of two key Finance Division men, borrowed for a covert accounting project, is offered as proof of the strain.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200110005-9:
Recommended duty assignments for senior CIA administrative posts are set out in a staff paper, followed by a Management Officer memo dated 24 March 1950 on a survey of the Publications Division. The assignments cover advice on organization, budget, personnel, training, and services, plus liaison with other Agency parts on set administrative policy. Named roles include a training officer, a security officer, an evacuations officer, and a budget officer.

The paper also assigns work within the Administrative Staff itself. Its chief would act in the senior chief's absence, supervise staff work direct, and sign staff studies on logistics and outside research backed by the office. Further items deal with review and approval of papers before signature. The record shows how support duties were split at a time when the Agency's offices were still taking shape.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200110014-9:
A Management Staff study examines the regional divisions of the Office of Reports and Estimates, the CIA office then charged with reports work. Its findings tie the divisions' competence to five needs. They are a set production plan, a sound requirements system, and clearer support duties between Agency parts. Better collection support and internal realignment of functions, staffing, and procedure complete the list. Analysts also needed orientation and guidance, the study says.

The remedy urged is joint work by the office itself, the Coordination, Operations, and Policy Staff, and the Management Staff. Tabs back each point with detail. One section deals with the Map Division, urging clearer ties with the Office of Scientific Intelligence so support could be given without wasteful overlap. It also urges better briefing of other Agency units on map services.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200130003-9:
Regulation SI 1-151, dated 19 November 1956, states the mission and functions of the Office of Scientific Intelligence. The scan is partly garbled, but the structure is clear. Senior deputies serve the Assistant Director for Scientific Intelligence in two broad fields, collection and production, and act for him in his absence. Each deputy's duties are listed, with notes on working with the other deputy where fitting.

The collection deputy advises on scientific and technical collection, collection priorities, overseas collection work, and new collection methods, and speaks for the office with other offices and agencies. The production deputy covers research and production on the same terms. Review duties include judging proposals to use outside facilities to speed scientific work. The regulation gives a compact charter for the office's top staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200170009-9:
Annex A explains a set of analysis sheets drawn from a survey of CIA personnel files. Sheets 1 to 12 sum up the main contents of personnel folders. Columns run from left to right in falling echelon order, and marks show the highest echelon keeping a record, with numbers for duplicate and further copies. Material in subject files, such as a pending file of forms, is counted too, in a second color.

Sheets 13 to 15 cover staffing records, pseudonym cross-reference files, training records, skills locators, and career plans. The official table of organization list, made monthly by the Personnel Office, is described, as is an in-casual list for staff awaiting assignment. Security rules for the pseudonym file are spelled out: true names and false names sit in separate cabinets, linked by a key number.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030031-9:
Allen W. Dulles, Director of Central Intelligence, closed a National Strategy Seminar for Reserve Officers at the National War College with remarks on the evening of 24 July 1959. He notes that the seminar had covered Soviet strategy and tactics, the Communist threat, the military balance of East and West, and the face of war in the nuclear age. His opening warning is against extremes in judging Soviet power.

Some experts, he says, magnify every Soviet gain and become prophets of gloom, while others discount real Soviet work, above all in outer space, on thin evidence. Later he asks where peoples behind the Iron Curtain had a free choice, naming Czechoslovakia in 1948 and Hungary in 1956. The speech sets out his middle view of Soviet strength and of open competition with the West.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300030068-9:
Congressional Record Appendix pages headed 1 September carry a wide mix of inserted material. The item named in the catalog title reports Senator Richard L. Neuberger of Oregon on the strong House passage of the federal employees health bill and his views in favor of a strong advisory council. That item sits among many other appendix pieces placed in the Record that day by different members.

One long piece attacks improper lobbying methods while defending lobbying itself as public participation in government. It faults Time and Life magazines for their approach to public debate. Farther on, the pages turn to farm news, including corn picking and drying in Iowa and storage loans for a large crop. Readers should treat the set as a bundle of separate Record items, not as one continuous speech or report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300190025-9:
Senate Congressional Record pages from 1959 gather statements tied to the Secretary of State and the Committee on Foreign Relations, mixed with other Record matter. One early passage gives a career sketch of a Bureau of the Budget official named Jones. It traces his service from a state statistical board in 1939 through wartime duty with the Combined Chiefs of Staff and the Munitions Assignments Board. Promotions to colonel by May 1945 complete the sketch. Later pages turn to the United Nations.

The General Assembly is described as a forum where free world needs find a voice; it cannot legislate change, the passage says, but it can induce change. Other inserted matter ranges widely, as Record pages do, including praise for New York City as a convention site. The set should be read as separate printed items sharing a file, not as one speech.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300200005-9:
A second, shorter set of briefing notes for the House Foreign Affairs Committee covers the same Soviet ground as a companion outline, in rougher OCR. It also updates a 22 October briefing tied to the Taiwan Straits. Abroad, conflict lines with the West had tightened and easing tensions had faded as a Soviet theme. At home, the aim was to steady and consolidate, with more rigor in policy and belief but no return to a police state.

Khrushchev stands firmly in control, though succession maneuvering may be under way, with Suslov, Kirichenko, and Kozlov to watch. A harder foreign policy tone is shown by Berlin, the Middle East, and support of China at Quemoy. Middle East and Asian pages discuss new governments, mostly neutralist and leaning left, and a Soviet Bloc move into economic aid shaped to exploit local pressures at least cost.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100090011-9:
A second copy of a background paper on the iron and steel industry covers the same ground as its companion file. The ferrous field is defined broadly, taking in the mining and preparation of raw and alloying materials as well as iron and steel output. Iron ore, manganese ore, metallurgical coke, and limestone head the raw material list, and alloy metals from chromium to vanadium are named.

Facility types are tabulated by product, from open pit and shaft mines through crushing, washing, and enriching plants to smelters, blast furnaces, and refineries. Coke making in by-product and beehive ovens is also covered. Investment discussion near the end compares plan periods, putting heavy industry near ninety percent of industrial investment and noting a shift toward electric power over engineering and metals work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180002-9:
Committee papers on East-West exchanges open in mid-discussion of machine translation, weighing what each side might gain from an exchange in that field. Soviet gain was expected to be small, since Soviet workers could not yet program well for digital computers and used them little for translation. American gain would lie mainly in handling non-alphabetic languages. Soviet work in the field, the paper says, aimed in part at flooding less developed areas with Soviet texts.

Knowledge of the Soviet program came from technical literature, talks with Soviets in the United States, and observation in the USSR. A slow start was planned, and the program director would first try a one-sided visit to the USSR to spur an exchange. Other passages discuss using a plain subject as an entry to plants of real interest, a view the committee shared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180020-9:
A status report on exchanges for the Intelligence Advisory Committee's Ad Hoc Committee runs to many pages and is rough in the scan, with discussion set for a 1958 afternoon meeting. One early passage weighs proposed conference visits, noting that some gatherings take place in open areas in the United States and could replace more contentious ones. A proposal credited to a Mr. Brook would not, the report warns, limit Soviet attendance if other Americans brought forward worthwhile plans.

Later discussion turns on gains and losses in specific fields. On powder metallurgy methods, the judgment given is that the intelligence gain to the United States from an exchange outweighs any Soviet gain. Other passages cite open material inside the Agency and the Air Technical Intelligence Center confirming Soviet interest in a field under debate. The report is a working paper, mixing status notes with committee argument.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180039-9:
Paper IAC-D-103/6, dated 11 February 1958, carries the Third Semi-Annual Report of the Intelligence Advisory Committee's Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges. A cover note says the report would go on the agenda of an early committee meeting for noting. The committee itself was set up on 28 February 1956 to gain the most intelligence value from East-West delegation exchanges, with paper IAC-D-103 as its guide.

Membership matches the earlier pattern: State, Army, Navy, Air Force, the Joint Staff, CIA, and the Atomic Energy Commission. The information agency attended regularly, and CIA provided chairman and secretariat. A mid-report case weighs a medical exchange. An American party brought back vaccine samples, medical literature, and much information on Soviet medical research. The Soviet party likely gained from visiting American institutes. The net gain, the report judges, probably fell to the United States.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200070012-9:
Comments on Svalbard review the status and strategic weight of the Arctic archipelago, though the scan is garbled in many lines. Under the treaty settlement, Svalbard is a possession of Norway, and no military installations of any kind are allowed on the islands. Foreign nationals may gain concessions for coal and other resources under Norwegian rules. The USSR was actively using that right, while British concession holders were not working theirs.

Near the end of the Second World War, the comments recall, Moscow demanded Bear Island outright. It also demanded a joint rule over the archipelago in place of the treaty terms. Norway rejected the proposals and the matter was not raised again. Strategic value flows from position. A later passage warns of danger tied to Soviet coal workings on the islands, with detail referred to another paper in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200100009-9:
A CIA paper from January 1958 suggests how material from National Intelligence Survey 26, on the USSR, could be adapted to Parts I, II, and III under the Chapter IX outline. Section 90 heads the scheme, covering the development and extent of mapping, charting, and related work. Sub-headings list topographic mapping, specialized physical mapping, terrain evaluation mapping, aeronautical charting, hydrographic and oceanographic charting, and other mapping fields.

A grid then assigns coverage by part. Part I takes all or most of the USSR, including central government organizations and countrywide charting. Part II takes the European USSR and Part III the Asiatic USSR, with smaller areas such as Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, and Karafuto placed by area covered. Responsibility columns follow in a dense table. The paper is a planning aid for fitting one large survey into a standard chapter shape.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200220015-9:
Problems of the Territorial Sea survives in a scan so garbled that most lines cannot be read with confidence. Legible fragments match a weekly summary preview of the International Conference on the Law of the Sea at Geneva, opening 24 February, with representatives of many countries attending. The width of the territorial sea, and the coastal state's full sovereignty within it, can be made out as the central problem the conference would try to settle. Beyond that, detail in this copy should not be relied on.

The readable frame shows states holding divergent claims over their adjacent seas. The conference was convened to define points of maritime law by agreement. Because the OCR here is largely illegible, the description rests only on the fragments that remain readable in the file itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00423a000100060006-9:
A Management Staff project assignment control form records a study of cable distribution in the IO Division. The form sorts the project under the Organization and Methods Staff side, with boxes for functions, procedures, staffing, and research study. The project description is narrow. It is a limited study of how cables were distributed in the division, presenting facts without conclusions or recommendations. The study was for use by a senior plans official in deciding the division's request for added copies.

Estimated effort is entered in man days for analyst and clerical time. A note on the reverse side adds context from a related review of cable copy needs in the SR Division, where a temporary increase had been allowed pending a study. If the IO study were delayed, the note suggests, a similar temporary relief measure might be worth considering for that division as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060005-9:
Weekly Activity Report No. 22 from the Chief, Overseas, Operations School, dated 3 June 1959, opens by reporting no significant items. Under other items, plans and personnel come first. Staff met in what the report jokingly calls solemn conclave to plan the coming months. They expected a named officer to join Overseas Training by 1 August, and allowed two-week vacations for each member of the small team.

The board also reviewed a Survey of Training Materials Currently Needed in the training office, dated 30 July of the year before, with comments. Only a few listed items had been finished in the past year, and most would appear again in a survey made that day, the report judges. Later notes touch on printing guides bought more cheaply by the hundred and an English index to an Army English-Chinese dictionary of terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060041-9:
Weekly Activity Report No. 16 from the Chief, Overseas, Operations School, dated 22 April 1959, reports no significant items. Its first item is a frustrated scheduling tale. After repeated efforts to arrange a visit by a doctor to the Director of Training, the chief asked the Director's office direct for an appointment. The Medical Office had packed the doctor's final week so tightly that no meeting time could be found.

The writer is plainly disappointed. He notes the doctor at least knows the training office tried to arrange for him and his wife to meet staff he would work with over the coming eighteen months. A second item opens the desert survival materials matter, with a call to an Air Force lieutenant colonel in the Subsidiary Plans Division. Later pages find wide diversity among divisions and field stations in training on a system, and a staff member drafting guidance for separate dispatches.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100010016-9:
Senate bill S. 3460, with Report No. 2032, would govern salaries and personnel practices for teachers, certain school officers, and other staff of Department of Defense dependents schools in foreign countries. Mr. Johnston of South Carolina introduced the bill on 12 March 1958, by request, and reported it with amendments on 29 July 1958. It was referred to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, and amended text is printed in italics.

The bill starts by amending the Classification Act of 1949 to add a new class. It covers United States citizens employed in schools run by the Defense Department outside the United States, its territories, and possessions. Later sections build a leave system for those staff. Leave earned under the act may not be cashed out, and staff who move to a post under a different leave system carry set rules with them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100030014-9:
A course schedule for an Intelligence Production Course in February lays out a first week in a time grid, though parts of the grid are garbled in the scan. The week opens with introduction and assigned reading of a national estimate, plus readings on atomic energy. A reading list is handed out. A briefing on the Office of Current Intelligence follows, and much of the week is given to conferences, research, and study. Students choose a country for a course project during the first week, and individual conferences on summary items recur.

A briefing on peaceful uses of atomic energy leads into basic facets of such a program. A film titled Our Friend the Atom follows, with tools of peaceful uses research and controlled thermonuclear power. Later weeks cover use of specialists and consultants, an analyst's in-box, and use of libraries and librarians.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100040022-9:
A transcript headed Mr. Dulles records remarks to a training audience, in rough OCR, in which the speaker sets out his ambition for the Agency. He says he looks forward to these gatherings each year, jokes about the lighting, and states his great aim plainly: to help build up a career service. The Agency, he argues, should be built from within, by people with training and experience, not by amateurs brought in from outside.

Training is the means, through the Office of Training and its curriculum, studies, and exercises, which he says he reviews each year. This year, he judges, the program has reached a degree of competence beyond what it ought to be. Farther on he turns to a book he calls The Ugly American. He says he has read four or five chapters and did not like it much, and hopes the author is not in the room.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00463a000100070001-9:
A memorandum to the Deputy Director for Support reports on wartime preparation by the training office for the fiscal year ending 30 June 1958. It answers a June 1957 call for an annual report on the subject. Training tied to wartime preparation grew during the year. A special three-day program in covert evasion and escape was run at a named site for nineteen selected military personnel, its location removed in this copy.

A one-week program in clandestine operations served seven officers from selected Defense Department offices and Headquarters Marine Corps. The office also ran the annual Project USEFUL, with thirty-two senior Armed Forces officers attending, a course meant to inform officers in key overseas posts. Later pages note that stockpiling of supplies and equipment for an expanded wartime training load had not begun at the present site. Headquarters vital materials, meanwhile, were being sent to the Agency repository.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100190033-9:
Paper IAC-D-74/5, dated 5 August 1957, carries the Fifth Annual Progress Report of the Scientific Estimates Committee for fiscal year 1957. Authority and organization match the committee's standing frame. It was set up on 14 August 1952 by directive, with members from the CIA, the Joint Staff, State, Army, Navy, Air Force, and the Atomic Energy Commission. Ad hoc subcommittees were formed for single subjects as needed. Accomplishments fill the body.

One item reports a study of gaps in biological warfare reporting, with recommendations for action, which the parent committee noted and approved as amended in May 1957. Another reports a coordinated, all-source program of electronic studies bearing on the working capability of Sino-Soviet Bloc air defense radars. The first community product of its kind was drawn from that program. The report follows the same yearly pattern as its neighbors in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030002-9:
A draft memorandum to the United States Intelligence Board proposes a limited codeword control mechanism, put forward by the CIA. A codeword, a footnote explains, is a word given a classified meaning by proper authority to protect security. The proposal seeks an orderly way to clear and assign chosen codewords across the intelligence community, so that one word does not carry several definitions at joint level and cause confusion.

The problem is called small, but the gain in coordination could be large for little effort, mainly by redirecting current staff work inside member agencies. The mechanism would cover only codewords whose use could cause joint confusion if definitions clashed. Agencies would not need advance community clearance for codewords used only inside their own work. An attachment begins revised material at the point where the sample text ends.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200050028-9:
A report on the achievements of the Intelligence Advisory Committee during 1953-54 looks beyond the estimates process that took most of the committee's time. Many actions, it says, had been taken or were under way to improve collection and production of intelligence across the whole community. Leadership in coordinating and carrying out many of these actions came from the CIA, matching its statutory duties, above all through the subcommittees that guide work in key fields. Significant subcommittee work is then sampled.

For the Scientific Estimates Committee, the report credits the first community-wide estimate of Soviet electronic warfare capabilities. It also credits a survey of gaps in reporting on Soviet Bloc weather activities, and coordination of twenty-seven survey sections. The scientific committee also produced its first annual report in the period. Other committees' gains are listed in the same survey style across the report's many pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200080007-9:
A background paper dated 9 March 1957 sets out the Kashmir situation. Politically and militarily, it says, the position had more or less settled on 1 January 1949. A United Nations directed cease-fire then took effect, and Indian and Pakistani troops were split by a cease-fire line running irregularly through the western part of the state. Both sides have since kept regular and irregular forces in the parts they hold. Force figures follow.

India is credited with three infantry divisions and many service troops in Indian-held Kashmir. Pakistan is credited with about two thousand regular army personnel and twenty battalions, totaling twenty thousand men, of state troops in Azad Kashmir. Order keeping is described as easy for India among a docile population, and harder for Pakistan among tribal inhabitants. A later judgment holds that Pakistani action to break India's hold would wait until United Nations resources were plainly exhausted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300030001-9:
Paper IAC-D-119/2, dated 11 July 1958, transmits a report on the inspection problems in a possible United States-Soviet agreement banning production and deployment of long-range ballistic missiles. A cover note encloses Mr. Dulles' letter sending the report to Mr. Farley of the State Department. The report had been discussed at the Intelligence Advisory Committee meeting on 8 July, and a revised foreword and page were enclosed for substitution.

Those pages were redrafted to take in the committee discussion and remarks by a general named in the note. One change is flagged in detail: a former paragraph was converted into a footnote and is now called an assumption rather than a fact or estimate. The report itself divides its discussion by time, separating points little changed by delay from points that matter most at once or grow with delay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300030010-9:
Paper IAC-D-116/2, dated 24 February 1958, is a Top Secret file whose title and names are partly removed by sanitization. Its subject, as the catalog title gives it, is a proposal on how estimates of Soviet military capabilities tied to the defense of North America should be considered. A signature record and cover sheet heads the file, with registry fields for copy number, pages, and attachments, and the standard warning on handling Top Secret matter.

Letter pages inside argue that the sides had held an extremely full exchange of all relevant information. Differences remained mainly in one field, the letter says. They rested on the hardest issues of judgment: above all, how far the coming of long-range missiles would change the Soviet need for long-range bombing strength. On that issue, the position taken by the United States side is then set out, with the opposing names removed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300050009-9:
Paper IAC-D-103, dated 28 February 1956, is a special report on the intelligence aspects of exchanging delegations with the USSR and the European satellites. It was submitted by the Director of Central Intelligence with the concurrence of the Intelligence Advisory Committee. Concurring officials are listed from State, Army, Navy, Air Force, the Joint Staff, and the Atomic Energy Commission, and a CIA dissemination notice heads this copy.

The report's case turns on access. Exchange visits, by their nature, lead to itineraries covering areas and installations not otherwise open to American observers. Beyond the delegation's own field, facility visits can give more detailed observation by better qualified observers than other routes allow. The paper founded the exchanges work that a standing committee then carried on, reporting half-yearly on the intelligence yield of each exchange and advising the State Department on proposals.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300090014-9:
Minutes numbered IAC-M-354 record an Intelligence Advisory Committee meeting at a quarter to eleven on 29 July 1958 in the committee room of the CIA Administration Building. Deputy Director General Charles P. Cabell presided. Members present are listed for State, Army, Navy, Air Force, the Joint Staff, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, several of them acting for their principals.

Business recorded includes approval, as amended, of estimate NIE 20-58 on the outlook for Western Europe, with no member objecting to its release to the information agency. Estimate SNIE 71-58 on France and North Africa was also approved as amended and agreed for release the same way. A further item, SNIE 100-6-58, concerns implications of certain United States earth satellite matters. One earlier item deals with finding experts in the field of a study then under way.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100040164-9:

cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100120011-9:

The team was specifically tasked to obtain information on C-130 range and on the possibility of extending or supplementing its fuel system.

At Sewart, the host was a troop carrier wing whose aircraft type is garbled in the scan; the wing had built up enough experience to offer data of considerable value. A material list later in the report names items obtained at Sewart, including kits and technical orders, several entries partly redacted.

Questionnaire notice from 1958 concerns overseas duty and the planning data behind a possible retirement program. Extra retirement credit for overseas service was under study, but past service records were scattered. The Agency needed the kind of service, the country, the dates by month, and the government component for each period of duty.

Payroll insert questionnaire cards were chosen for vouchered employees, who would fill in their own cards for statistical use. Staff paid from confidential funds got cards through their components, and staff agent cases were handled on an Eyes Only basis. Where security barred sending a card to the field, that fact was to be noted and the card returned to Personnel.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100130008-9:
Numbered advice for an Agency Logistics Section opens with the Book and Periodical Procurement Log. The paper would drop the log as a needless control. A monthly IBM listing from OCR, it argues, already shows charges for goods in hand. The same listing gives cost figures for goods still on order. That is enough to hold down costs and stop staff from owing more than the fund allows. Copies of requisitions on file would still answer questions on the status of an order.

More items cut other paper controls in the same way. Dispatch abstracts would be kept only for items sent to another office. The Reproduction Log would no longer post a cost centre for each job order. Staff would also stop keeping copies of requisitions begun by other units. Each change is paired with a short note on the staff time it saves.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00901a000100080012-9:
Memo for the Director of Central Intelligence, dated 18 August 1954, takes up area and language training. It rests on an Office of Training staff study of 28 June 1954, attached as Tab A. The memo asks what program would give the Agency enough trained staff for its needs abroad. The DD/P operator is the central case used to test the argument.

Three kinds of knowledge are set out in the study. They are professional skill, knowledge of the foreign area, and language ability. Staff who work on a foreign area should take an area course of at least sixty-four hours. The course could be given at the Agency or at a university. Past training of like quality would count toward the rule. Living in the area, by itself, would not.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100070004-9:
Annex II for the Agency Records Center gathers basic facts on the centre's standing, in four tabs. Tab A traces its past phases. Tab B lists what was done in fiscal year 1953. Tab C gives a master plan of aims and methods. Tab D sets the office program for fiscal year 1954. The annex is marked Secret in the scan.

The history reaches back to March 1946. In that month the idea took shape in the Central Registry of the Executive Office. In OSS days, by contrast, each part of the service kept its own central registry. Tab B notes sharp rises in distribution work late in fiscal year 1953. Extra distribution of finished intelligence reports rose steeply in that span. First distribution of regulations rose 233 percent in one quarter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010043-9:
Agency resubmission dated 7 November 1955, sent through the Chief, Services Division and the Chief, Trade Branch, restates requirements on East German trade organisation and methods, reference RD C-700. First target is the Chamber for Foreign Trade. Collectors are asked for an organisation chart showing line and staff links, key people in each post, the duties of each subdivision, and its ties to other government bodies.

Further items probe how the Chamber worked in practice. Questions cover membership rules, Soviet control machinery and whether it ran past administrative matters, and use of the Chamber in trade talks. One item asks whether the Chamber negotiated with a recent Iranian trade delegation in East Germany and what barter or other deals followed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100010124-9:
Economic needs dated 1955, for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List for 1 June to 30 September 1955, cover the Far East. Railroad data are wanted urgently. Items ask what share of locomotive and car parks was laid up in reserve or for repair. They ask car numbers by type and size, with 50-ton gondolas as one case. They ask the volume of freight traffic, in total and by goods type.

Other items seek car loadings per day. They seek the mean time from one loading to the next. They seek use of track and car capacity, and traffic on named lines. Timber and cement are added to the goods list in these pages. Southeast Asia items cover Soviet sway, military stockpiling in the south, and truck park growth. They also cover the nature and volume of trade with Communist China.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020060-9:
Submission of November 1956 gives economic requirements for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List for 1 December 1956 through 31 March 1957. Amendments are keyed to an St/I office notice of 13 October 1956. One change fixes the expected timing of a coordinating committee meeting to December or February, and another corrects the trend in Austrian East-West trade, noted as upward in 1953 and through 1956.

Country sections follow the same retain, revise, and add pattern. Netherlands items are largely retained. A new item on Bolivia asks for the level and character of Bolivian trade with the USSR and other Bloc countries. Argentina items are kept in part, with set paragraphs and items named by number.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020231-9:
Submission dated February 1956 puts forward keeps, rewrites, and adds for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List. The list runs from 1 March to 30 June 1956. It covers the Near East and Africa, and it cites Guide No. 164. Ethiopia and Eritrea open the list. One item is widened to cover offers by any Bloc countries. The offers may be loans, technical aid, or plants built in the country. Most Egypt items are kept, with the wording revised.

One revised Egypt item covers the regime's growth and factory projects. It covers the Egyptian bodies set up to plan and run those projects. It covers the lead people in them, and their views toward Bloc aid. A Sudan item is rewritten to track Bloc interest in a new way. The tracks are swapped delegations, lasting Bloc offices, and trade agreements with values and terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100050003-9:
Reading panel requirements for the Agency's S/COM, the communications unit, supersede an earlier set dated 20 July 1956. S/COM produced economic estimates and reports on postal and telecommunications services. To do that work it needed data on how much postal and telecommunications plant a country had in service, under construction, and planned, and where that plant stood.

Capacity, use, and unused capacity held for war, emergencies, or systems such as the military, railroads, and air services are all in scope, as are the users of the facilities. Shortages, defects, and delays matter too, along with prices, income, spending, investment, labour, and trade in communications equipment. System lists run from air defence and broadcasting to clandestine, diplomatic, and guided missile links.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100050030-9:
Memo dated 3 July 1958 revises needs for the reading panels of the Agency's Construction Branch. The branch mission is stated first. The branch makes all-source reports on the building of fixed sites in the Sino-Soviet Bloc. It reports on the making of building supplies there as well. Civil defence work in the Bloc falls in the same scope. The branch works with other parts of the government and has a share in National Intelligence Estimates.

The fullest part of this copy is its data list for building supplies. For each supply, panels were to note the place and make-up of plants that produce it, and the output and reach of single plants. Unit costs and prices were to be noted as well. Yearly output figures, in total and by plant, close the list. Import and export figures were to be kept where they appear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100070010-9:
Submission dated 2 December, in the late 1950s by context, gives items for the Agency's Periodic Requirements List. The list runs from 1 September to 31 December 1958. Albania gains an item. It asks for any further grants of credit to that country. It asks for facts on the true level of Albanian trade. Bulgaria gains an item on a reported Soviet credit. Two years before, Bulgaria had said it would receive a credit from the USSR in 1958. Details are wanted on that credit, most of all how it ties to a Soviet growth credit of 19 May 1956.

Trade items for Albania and Bulgaria ask for import and export figures broken down by kind, not totals alone. An East Germany item cites a 10 July agreement with the USSR. The agreement covers joint growth of the East German chemical industry. The item asks what prices the USSR paid for East German uranium.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100160010-9:
Tab A paper outlines a planned outside research study on Eastern Europe. It sets out what the chapters would give the Office of Research and Reports. The study would supply set-out facts from unclassified sources. It would add many references to source material. Some of that material might not have reached Agency analysts. The first four chapters were already done, for a DD/P request. So the new work would cover Chapters V through X only.

Chapter I covers the goods and the people of Eastern Europe. It covers prewar uneven growth in the region. It covers population and factory jobs, and the weight of each industry there. It covers farming as well, with land shares and output per acre. Later chapters feed named ORR projects. They include work on growth of the services sector of the Soviet economy, and on Soviet foreign trade totals and structure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180009-9:
Memorandum in the Agency's files from the Defense member of the Executive Committee, for a meeting on Tuesday, 1 October 1957, proposes action on embargo of copper wire. Extended negotiations and current bilateral talks on the subject were assumed likely to end without result. Defense urged the committee to settle a follow-up course at once, since pending British and Soviet trade agreement talks would bring the prior commitment policy into play.

Defense proposed that the United States delegation put a proposal in COCOM, soon after 1 October, to raise copper wire to embargo status. Bilateral talks with other copper wire exporters would run alongside to offset friction. An attached paper notes Bloc copper imports in 1956 estimated between 110,000 and 120,000 tons, of which 85,000 tons was bare wire.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180036-9:
Minutes ED/EC M-247 in the Agency's files, issued 1 July 1957, record the meeting at 2:00 p.m. on Thursday, 27 June 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. Notes cover EDAC D-136 of 26 June, International List II China quotas for 1957, a redacted June 24 item, and a Foreign Affairs Committee hearing. The single numbered item is the NSC and CFEP assignment to review economic defense policy, under EDAC D-135 of 27 June.

On the hearing, time ran short and the admiral presenting the United States case had no chance to speak, though the written statement was accepted for the record. On the policy review, Commerce and Defense members were charged with preparing check lists of recent events and other points their agencies wanted covered in the new review.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180063-9:
Minutes ED/EC M-277 record a meeting at 11:00 a.m. on 21 October 1957. The meeting sat in Room 913 of the District National Building. The minutes were issued on 23 October 1957. Mr. Hale chaired a table of MDAC, Commerce, ICA, State, Treasury, Defense, and an Agency member. A note covers the embargo of copper wire. The numbered item is the criteria issue raised in the Ad Hoc Subcommittee report, ED/EC D-126/1.

On copper wire, the chairman had news at last. A response was expected to United States efforts to place the item under embargo. State added that the matter would likely be taken up with the Secretary of State on 22 October. On criteria, the subcommittee had proposed a change to criterion (a). The words designed specially or would be cut from it. The subcommittee judged those words of little weight. The Bloc would never import the items in question.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180072-9:
Minutes EDAC M-65 in the Agency's files, issued 1 November 1957, record a full Economic Defense Advisory Committee meeting at 2:30 p.m. on Monday, 28 October 1957, in Room 819 of the District National Building. Admiral DeLany chaired, with Mr. Hale as Executive Committee chairman, and members from Commerce, Defense, ICA, ODM, State, and Treasury. Agenda items in the scan are partly redacted, but one named item is an appeal from Working Group I on furnishing technical data on generators to Poland, item 1266.

Debate on the Poland item runs through the minutes. One side held that NSC statements gave guidance enough and that common sense could be applied case by case. State argued that United States policy was to promote Poland's reorientation to the West, and that objecting in such cases would work against that policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180117-9:
White House report in the Agency's files, dated 25 October 1957, gives the President's findings under the Battle Act. The findings rest on section 103(b) of the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act of 1951. They cover the quarter ending 30 September 1957. The report goes to Congress, as the Act requires. New findings made on 23 August 1957 are listed by country and amount. Italy stands at 578,656 dollars. France stands at 51,392 dollars. The United Kingdom stands at 6,504 dollars. The total is 636,552 dollars.

The President states that he has reviewed these findings. He has reviewed the findings made earlier as well. He has concluded that no further comments are needed. An addendum then sets out trade with the Soviet Bloc by country. It covers the countries for which findings had been made since the Act passed in 1951. The span runs through August 1957. Shares of world trade are shown in percentages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180126-9:
Statement of United States Economic Defense Policy, in the Agency's files as Annex A, opens with general policy. Its ground is the lasting threat to free world security from the Sino-Soviet Bloc. That threat is said to warrant economic defense measures by the United States and the free world. The measures would slow growth of the Bloc's war potential and reduce its unity. At the same time, the program must not raise the chance of war. It should keep open paths toward a sounder basis for peace.

Trade between the free world and the Bloc should be touched only where a clear advantage to the free world follows. The paper also treats contacts. Personal, cultural, and trade contacts with the European Soviet Bloc may carry real gains. Later pages give rival wordings for the aims, one backed by Commerce, Defense, and OEM.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180162-9:
Second copy in the Agency file of the ES-DRAFT general policy paper of 23 January 1957 carries the same opening points. The threat to free world security from the Sino-Soviet Bloc calls for measures to slow the Bloc's war potential and loosen its unity. The program is set out as one part of the free world's alliance system, spanning military and political ties and depending on joint effort and shared sacrifice.

This copy shows the later numbered points more clearly. One point seeks to keep, and as needed extend, two-way arrangements with other free world countries. The aim is support for controls agreed by many nations. The next point keeps United States export controls toward the European Soviet Bloc. They cover items agreed by many nations. They cover other goods, gear, methods, and services the United States can control on its own.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200080045-9:
Comment sheet by the Agency's S/TR branch takes up the ACE Intelligence, USAF input to NIE 13-58. The estimate covers Communist China. The comments work through the transport sections page by page. On railroads, they call the draft a real forward step. A study of the data shows the announced working figures to be of the right size. The draft drops counter-figures in favour of a general caution. That may let an estimate pass at last with no dissenting footnote on the subject.

Highway items correct two points in the draft. Imports did not furnish all highway gear needs in 1956 or 1957. Home output may have reached about 1,654 units in 1956 and 2,000 in 1957. Native transport moved 36 percent of highway ton-kilometres in 1956. It moved 79 percent of tons originated that year. An aviation passage is faulted on one point. It treats air freight as the sole function of civil aviation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200100006-9:
Study in the Agency's files covers Sino-Soviet economic relations from 1950 to 1957. It credits Soviet support with making China's rapid factory and military build-up possible. Since 1950 the USSR had extended loans to China of about 1,325 million dollars in total. The parts are named in the study: loans for economic growth. They are special loans tied to the return of four joint stock companies to Chinese ownership, and military loans. China was estimated to have repaid about 490 million dollars of the credits received.

The two countries were each other's chief trading partner at the time. In 1950 the Soviet Union accounted for 26 percent of China's trade. That trade came to about 320 million dollars. Tables in the study track Soviet project aid by agreement. They count plants built or renovated with Soviet gear and technical help. Sums are converted at the official rate of four roubles to the dollar.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200100033-9:
Memo dated 3 September 1956, through the Agency's Services Division and Trade Branch, lists gaps in facts on Bloc aid programs in Egypt. The programs span economic and military aid.
