Background states Egypt had been a chief target of the Bloc economic offensive since 1955. Bloc offers to buy Egyptian cotton surpluses came while Egypt had trouble selling in the West. Egypt's call for arms led to a Soviet and Egyptian arms agreement in September 1955. Soviet readiness to take cotton in payment for arms helped that deal along.

The Bloc had by then given Egypt about 250 million dollars in economic credits. That was enough to fund about half the foreign exchange costs of Egypt's five year factory program. Questions in the memo seek what was missing: oil exploration work, senior Soviet advisers at the Ministry of Industry, and the cost and payment terms for technicians in Egypt.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200110005-9:
Subject Code S/CM, revised 2 January 1958, is a filing scheme for one Agency branch's papers. Section A covers CEMA and Bloc coordination. It breaks into organisation, work, joint plans, and the control system. It covers standardisation, specialisation, joint undertakings, and joint defence. Money, trade, and other ties between Bloc states follow, and social problems and personalities close the section. Section B covers a Soviet high commission, with a control commission, joint stock companies, and reparations under it.

Section D covers central government structure and setup, opening with the Council of Ministers, its structure, decrees, personalities, work, and speeches. It then runs through fields of state work: state control and finance, state security, labour and labour reserves, home affairs, defence, and foreign economic ties outside the Bloc. Resettlement, goods reserves, statistics, planning, technical growth, and science follow. Later sections reach procurement, allocations, spread of goods, medical care, and religion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120013-9:
Agency Current Support Memorandum maps the bodies that built for the Ministry of Defense in the USSR. Its subject is the setup of military construction there. It is marked as holding code word material. A central directorate for airfield construction, TsUKAS, heads the account. With it sat the Chief Directorate of Special Construction, GUSS. The two were responsible for building and upkeep of all types of airfields for the ministry.

Under TsUKAS sat departments of Capital Airfield Construction, OKAS. One such department sat in each military district. Each held jurisdiction over the field units in its district. Before its merger with TsUKAS, GUSS had handled building of set projects. Those projects were essential to all parts of the Ministry of Defense. The paper gives analysts a chart of who owned which building task in the Soviet military system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130030-9:
Routing memo dated 26 April 1957 requests information on USSR inland waterways for the Agency. It was sent to a list of branch chiefs in ORR and the Services Division. The covering note in the scan is badly garbled. Its purpose still matches the title and the attached tables. Analysts were asking field and office holders for waterway facts the office lacked. The ask fits the office's other needs work that spring.

Attached data tables list Soviet rivers one by one. They give the length of each river's navigable stretches. They give the normal navigable season at set points. Seasons are given as opening and closing months. They are given as average season lengths in days. One river entry shows seasons of about 124 to 176 days at different points. Another shows an average of about 160 days. The tables gave planners the working window for river movement in each district.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130058-9:
Agency memo dated 2 August 1956, through the Chief, S/TF, suggests changes in the first draft of the Eighth Battle Act Report. Early items are small and exact. One inserts the words imports from before the USSR on page 1-2. One deletes a sentence beginning Communist China on page 1-3. China is already inside the Sino-Soviet Bloc named in the sentence before it. One deletes two sentences on Eastern European trade with the Free World. Those sentences do not characterise trade with Western Europe.

Figure corrections follow in the memo. Finland's increase should read 131 rather than 135 million. Two page figures on page 1-9 should be reversed. A phrase, to the vanishing point, is cut as overstating a decline. Later comments take up Bloc credits to the Free World. They take up a chapter said to lack a summary or conclusions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140084-9:
Agency paper dated 16 April 1958 reports on trading in Soviet ruble bank notes on Western money markets. There is little evidence, it opens, to suggest any formal trading in Soviet ruble notes on Western markets. The ruble, a non-convertible paper currency shielded from foreign influences by government fiat, had since 1945 remained unquoted and generally unwanted on exchanges. Notes appearing in Vienna and Swiss money markets, filled in by East-West tourist and delegation exchanges, ran to a trickle, possibly less than 100,000 rubles a month.

Buyers were few even at 0.025 United States dollars, a discount of 75 percent from the official non-commercial rate. The discernible market was the diplomatic community in Moscow, for whom cheap rubles eased a high cost of living, plus a smaller tail of tourists and curiosity seekers. A small, active black market inside the USSR is also noted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200200078-9:
Monthly report list for the Agency's Services Division, January 1958, tables the reports the division sent in that month. They are tabled by project number and title, with the analyst or contributing branches named for each. Entries include an OCI Handbook on Poland from S/TR, S/TF, and S/COM. They include an ORE evaluation of reporting for 1 July to 30 September 1957 from all branches. A Bloc Trade item and guided missile intelligence collection support from S/COM, S/CST, and S/TR close the entries.

Other January titles include a Review of Sino-Soviet Bloc Foreign Economic Activities, a Sino-Soviet Economic Relations paper, a Soviet Shelter Program study, and Trends in Economic Management in the German Democratic Republic. They include a contribution to NIE 54-58 on the outlook for Ceylon, and Coal Consumption by the Chinese Communist Railroads. Branch notes at the back record committee and liaison work in progress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000100020017-9:
Memo dated 20 April 1950, to the Acting Executive, takes up an ORE proposal. The proposal would transfer L/OCD functions to the ORE Requirements Staff. Two references of 10 April 1950 frame the memo. One is an AD/ORE memorandum on requirements, and one a joint AD/OCD and AD/OSO memorandum on an Office of Overt Collection. Standing instructions gave OCD final coordination of intelligence requirements. OCD judged which government facilities could best meet each requirement, and assigned collection missions.

The memo works through the proposal paragraph by paragraph. It concurs in one statement only in part. The statement holds that production offices should be the sole originators of requirements. OSO and OPC also place requirements, the memo notes. They must be ranked with the two production offices when an overall Agency priority is set. Priority and deadline setting for ORE requests is also addressed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200050059-9:
Untitled Top Secret table in the Agency's files lists Soviet installations by city, in alphabetical order through the letters shown. Columns give city name, installation, coordinates, category, and a basic encyclopedia number, with interest marked primary or secondary. Entries visible include Engels, Feodosiya, Glazov, Gomel and Pribytki, Gorkiy, marked as a complex at 56-20N 044-00E, Gorokhovka, Grodno, Iokanga, Irkutsk, and Kapustin Yar at two coordinate pairs.

Later pages run on through Kharkov, Kirovograd, Kishinev, Kiyev, Klaipeda, Klimovo, Krasnoyarsk, Kuybyshev, Kyshtym, Leninakan, and Leningrad, with cross references such as see Moscow and Khimki, and see Sverdlovsk and Koltsovo. One Gorkiy entry is classed as an aircraft plant. The table is a targeting reference: a place-by-place index of installations of interest, fixed by coordinates so each can be found again.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400070046-9:
Memorandum dated 13 January 1956, to the Special Assistant to the Director for Planning and Coordination, reports an examination of Agency responsibilities for implementation of the Killian Report. The writer was asked to learn the status of each item and prepare action so the Agency would not later show up in default of its obligations. Findings from many inquiries are set out item by item, with papers attached for signature to make each component's responsibility clear on the record.

An NSC action of 4 August 1955 had placed set duties on the Agency. On peripheral war, the study of techniques and weapons technology ran through the Weapons Systems Evaluation Group and an Agency contract, and assurance is recorded that work was on schedule. Specific Recommendation C.5 is quoted in the later pages: the need to find ways to increase the number of hard facts behind estimates, for better strategic warning and less surprise.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000500030030-9:
A short memorandum dated 9 October 1957 sets out a program for Aquatone coverage of the USSR. Recent Aquatone flights, a Soviet missile test firing, and the launch of an earth satellite frame the case. Those events, the memo argues, show how far Soviet work on guided missiles had come. It urges a broad photographic program aimed at known targets tied to missiles and the long range air force.

Two attachments support the plan. One lists the principal targets, and the other ranks them by how feasible coverage would be. The memo also argues for systematic search along the way to known targets. Flights had already found Tyura Tam, not precisely located before, and a large radar type array near Krasnovodsk. It notes that Aquatone had so far covered fourteen percent of Soviet territory with usable photography.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600030002-9:
An informal review of the Collection and Liaison Division fills the file, written after a request from the division's parent office. A new division chief was expected, and the reviewer took the moment to suggest other changes. The focus falls on the division as a whole, its branches, and above all its Requirements Branch. The findings rest on quick impressions, the reviewer admits, not on a full study of facts.

Early praise goes to the pipelines the division built. Its first hard task, making contacts and channels through which intelligence could flow, had largely been achieved. The new risk was volume: too much paper arriving for users to absorb. Later pages weigh outside research work, ties with a sister division, and staffing. One proposal asks for an added slot in the Requirements Branch to handle one agency's outside research needs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600130010-9:
A roster of military reserve officers in the current intelligence office fills the file, laid out as a coded table. Columns record grade, rank, branch or arm, and reserve status for each officer. A final column gives a call-up ruling: deferred, releasable, or not the office's call to make. Names are withheld in the released copy, so the table reads as rows of codes. 

Role notes appear beside many rows. Most name analyst posts: air, ground, and naval analysts, grouped under a component code. A few rows name a military war room post instead. Read as a wartime planning tool, the roster shows how the office sorted its reserve officers ahead of time. Each man was graded, classed by arm, and marked for whether he would be held or released if called up.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600130047-9:
Annex D to the global war plan covers scientific and technical intelligence. Dated December 1955, it rests on the main plan's premises. In general war, the Office of Scientific Intelligence would keep its peacetime missions. Effort would shift toward tasks tied most closely to the Agency's war effort.

Five wartime missions head the list. They cover research and production, coordination of scientific work, guidance and support to collection, and new uses of science in intelligence work. Office running costs, training, security, relocation, and call-up form the fifth. Under production, goals and yearly programs would be rewritten. Foreign science and its use in hostile war power would draw far more study. Contributions to national estimates and current publications would grow on the same lines. Collection guidance follows the same shift.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700050036-9:
A further run of coordination office projects fills the file, each stated as a problem with a status note. First comes psychological warfare support. Talks with all agencies touched have produced a rough split of the kinds of support needed. Three tasks remain: test whether that split is sound and complete, assign each kind to a provider, and fix who coordinates what. 

Civil defence support follows. Talks have been held with Mr Babbitt of the Federal Civil Defense Administration and other agencies. A recommendation for the Director is being drafted. Outside research comes next: how far should Agency and member agency contract studies be joined up? Later entries include a survey of committee links, due with advice in early May. One closing item seeks final terms for CIA to speak for civilian agencies when captured people, papers, and materiel are exploited.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070179-9:
Minutes record a meeting held on 8 November 1950 in the Director's conference room at CIA. James Reber chaired. Around the table sat staff from Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, Interior, and the Treasury. The Library of Congress, Tariff Commission, Federal Reserve, and Smithsonian also sent people. An NSC staff member sat in as well.

Economic intelligence requirements drove the talks. The Security Council had told CIA to do two things. First, find out what economic intelligence support each government agency truly needs. Second, judge how well current sources meet those needs. Talk also turned to wartime gaps. Members asked whether present coverage would serve special agencies set up in a full-scale war. The record keeps the attendance list and the main lines of debate, not full speeches.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700100030-9:
A survey form, called a pre-conference barometer questionnaire, lists questions for use in five countries. They are Great Britain, France, Italy, West Germany, and Austria. Early items ask what problem matters most at home. A card then grades how people feel about named countries, from very good to very bad.

Later items probe the Cold War mood. People say what strikes them as worst about the United States, and best about Soviet Russia. They judge whether world war will come in three or four years, and whether the danger in Europe has grown. Blame for the East-West clash is asked outright. So is whether their country should back West, East, or neither. Closing items test when peace should yield: if home independence faced attack by an outside army, should people fight, or stay at peace? Compromise gets the same test.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470015-9:
Minutes of the twelfth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 13 October 1955. The group met on 6 October. First, the September minutes were corrected. A magnesium working group would stick to weighing intelligence data. Technical facts would come from a separate interagency task group. Another line now tied cost research to a CG meeting, not a foreign ministers' meeting.

Next came suspected rerouting of American ferrotitanium and ferrovanadium through Western Europe to the Soviet bloc. Commerce would dig out fuller detail. CIA would write a report on such diversions. The case paper was also cut from secret to confidential. Members agreed to set up a working group on collection requirements. Later talk weighed scope: should effort chase new list items, or stick to goods already held on the international lists? The defence member backed the narrower course for now.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470024-9:
Minutes of the third meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 15 December 1954. The group met on 9 December. Talk picked up an old thread: how action agencies draw facts from the military intelligence arms. The defence member reported that all three services held needs from Commerce and State. A State reader also scans and picks incoming material inside G-2, the air office, and naval intelligence.

No service, though, held reading needs from the mutual defence office. G-2 had issued a collection guide. Like guides from the air and naval arms, tuned to economic defence needs, were now being urged. One member flagged a routing flaw: most word on secret arms shipments reached him through two channels, yet some CIA material never reached his desk. The chairman voiced concern and called for the cause to be found.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490004-9:
A report on CIA's part in a 1955 fact sheet program is laid out as tables. Columns name each fact sheet, its code, and who gave the material. Early rows cover trade patterns. One sheet tracks Soviet and satellite buying of chosen consumer goods from the free world in 1952 to 1954. Its twin tracks their sales of chosen goods the other way.

Gold and rubber fill the next rows. Soviet gold shipments of 1953 to 1954 get a sheet. Rubber shipments to the bloc run back to 1948. Ceylon's rubber trade with Communist China has its own entry. Bloc oil exports and copper follow. Closing rows widen out: trade with the whole bloc across 1948 and 1952 to 1954, split by country and by chief goods. One sheet weighs Soviet trade growth worldwide. Office codes mark which arms wrote, checked, or reviewed each sheet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510092-9:
Notes dated 30 November 1955 plan intelligence backing for a joint American program against bloc economic penetration. The term is defined with care. It means gifts of capital goods on soft terms, long credit or barter, to poorer free world lands. Military kit can ride in such deals. Trade missions, fairs, expert visits, and trade tricks count as well.

The bloc's aim, the notes argue, is chiefly sway, not trade. Such deals win political and economic footholds, or pry open doors for spying and subversion. Washington is moving fast toward a program to block this push. Backing it well will take wide data, steady analysis, and close liaison between intelligence and action desks. The notes then ask who owns what: which agencies and committees hold the skills, and where the gaps sit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050029-9:
A second copy of the seventeenth meeting minutes of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee fills the file. The meeting ran on 11 October 1956, and the minutes are dated 31 October. Business matches the first copy. Commerce asked the group to rethink killing a subcommittee on trade in freed goods. State raised no bar, and the subcommittee was restored.

A gold sales paper then won approval, and its case closed. Ship deliveries to the bloc fill the next item, with forecasts out to 1958. In this copy one point reads more fully: CIA said 1958 figures were not yet in hand. A shipbuilding intelligence conference was also due to open on 17 October, and hopes rode on it. A last item covers the propellants seminar of June. Its official summary would go out once written, the working group lead reported. The chairman's hope for fresh facts from the conference is noted before the record moves on.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050038-9:
A letter dated 3 August 1956 sends a draft seminar record out for checking. It goes to a solid propellant expert at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory in Silver Spring, Maryland. Two copies ride along. They hold his talks, and those of four colleagues, from a June propellants seminar in Washington. The seminar was run by a working group on propellants and fuel additives.

The writer is frank about flaws. The recording failed at points, and some speech could not be made out. Staff checked what they could against the expert's own survey on solid propellants. Where talks strayed from that survey, they wrote down what they heard, even when it sounded wrong. Such words might jog memory, they reasoned. Boron gets a special plea: given his stake in boron as a propellant part, he should check those sections with extra care.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050056-9:
A progress report for May 1956, dated 1 June, logs work on a string of numbered projects. Copper leads. Staff are building a joined estimate of total 1955 copper shipments from the free world to the Sino-Soviet bloc. Talks ran all month among two branches, and a working group on copper shipments met.

Oil gear follows. A bid tied to a maker of such kit went to an export policy meeting, which advised the Secretary to refuse it. A bauxite study lags: no draft will reach reviewers till mid or late June. On boron, a requirements memo has cleared inside CIA with no fresh facts found. Around 21 May fresh collection needs went out on the bloc boron picture. A magnesium project waits in the wings. Later lines track planning for a propellants seminar, with liaison kept up among all offices and outside groups involved since a 3 May session.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300040007-9:
A thick legislative file builds a bill on foreign gifts and decorations. At its head sits a memo for the Director. Counsel took part in every talk of a study group drawn from many departments. That group was set up to face the constitutional snag on gifts. Its agreed draft, the memo states, suits the Agency as it stands. The Director is asked to back telling the Cabinet Secretary so.

Lawrence Houston signs as General Counsel, with the deputy director for support concurring. A letter of 17 February 1959 to Phillip Hughes at the Bureau of the Budget moves the draft along. Deep in the file, older practice is mined for light. In many lands beyond Christian Europe, the file notes, swapping presents with foreign agents was fixed custom. Refusing a gift could itself give offence. That history frames why a flat ban chafes in real diplomacy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300110009-9:
A study weighs how to place retired senior military officers inside CIA. Flag rank men are applying in a steady flow, the study opens. Law sets the frame: Public Law 53 of the 82nd Congress caps such hires at fifteen. The cap skips men retired for service or combat wounds. A 1956 bill sought to lift the cap to thirty-five. 

The task is thus to find where such men's service helps most. Legal roots follow. The 1951 act amended the CIA Act of 1949. It let the Agency hire and pay up to fifteen officers or warrant officers of the armed services while they serve it. It also freed them from the old bar on holding two federal offices at once. Later pages sort the terms of such hires: retirement and life insurance cover, and a pay cap for men taken on as consultants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300110027-9:
A memo dated 25 March 1955 sorts out when military service counts toward a civil service pension. It answers a query on one clause of the certificate of membership in the retirement system. Workers were unsure which spans of service count toward an annuity, and which do not.

Part of the fault lies in the form itself. It must give plain guidance in tight space, in layman's words, so fine points blur. The base law is the act appended to the memo as its second attachment. Under it, men drawing plain military retired pay get no second credit for the same years. Service after 31 December 1956 does count for social security, under a later act appended in turn. Some classes drawing military retired pay do keep pension credit, though. The first named rests on Title III of Public Law 610 of the 80th Congress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150014-9:
A memo to the Director builds a plan for staff savings at Headquarters. Two guesses frame it. Waste and overlap may exist in the present setup. And work may be reshaped to save posts without harm to core tasks. 

Ground rules follow. A Headquarters cut is required if it can be made safely. Growth in the field, by contrast, will be allowed on the merits of each bid. The Agency, it notes, has no true selection-out scheme yet, bar lone cases. Three paths to savings are weighed. First, weed out staff who are poorly used. That path also sweeps up overlap and doubled work, within units and between them. The plan then binds savings to real posts: units must tie each gain to named slots that can be declared surplus.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300200036-9:
Two memos from the fall of 1954 open a plan to print counsel's rulings. The first, dated 20 October, comes from the Office of General Counsel itself. It goes to the personnel chief, the comptroller, the security chief, and two staff heads. A set of proposals on printing the office's opinions rides with it. Each man is asked to concur, or to pin his doubts to a fresh sheet by his name.

Talks among all hands will come first, the memo says. Filed doubts will set the list of points for those talks. A due date is set: Friday, 5 November 1954. The reply from the clandestine side, dated 9 November, is warm. Its units want a steady flow of the rulings, it says. A John Warner of counsel's staff had heard the same wish at a chiefs' meet. Its chief offers a man for the talks on shape and scope.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050014-9:
A pair of 1958 memos backs a bid to give the code chief his own security rights. Houston writes first, on 18 April, to the current intelligence office. General Erskine's plan, he holds, fits the shape of the intelligence world as it stands. It takes no power from the Director. With the code board and the top board set to merge, it would put NSA level with its peers on security.

A man in General Truscott's office backs the view. Houston adds a side shot of his own. He is much against a Defense plan to give its own counsel charge of probes and direct steps in security cases. The next memo takes the same line on a twin ask: free the NSA chief from parts of Defense's guard rules. His hold on secret traffic work, it argues, should match his security hold.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050023-9:
A memo weighs a leak that had hit print and the air. A known columnist, Drew Pearson, had put a batch of facts out in the open. The file's own scan is badly garbled, and much of its fine print cannot be read with trust. 

Men met in Mr Warner's room in March 1957 to judge one point: were those facts in truth stamped secret when Pearson aired them? The test turns on harm to the state's defense if the facts are loose. Two staff views split. One held the facts could not, on that test, be counted secret at all. Counsel's men were left to settle the state of the stock at the hour of the leak. Deep pages turn from the one batch to a wider fear: the mass of like facts that work on it will drag out in its wake.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400060004-9:
A memo dated 20 October 1959 moves a draft order on atomic facts toward the top. With it ride three texts: the draft order; a draft letter for the Director to the Budget Bureau; and a back note for the Director that sets out the tale so far.

A word with the Director is sought too. Once the pack goes up, a slip will ask that Scoville and John Warner, or men they name, brief the boss by mouth. The draft letter, to Budget chief Maurice Stans, states the ask in law. The order would let CIA pass Restricted Data under joint deals made in sections 144a, b, or c of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. Just the data found fit to pass under each deal would move. A fresh clause, section 144d, gives the ground. It was put in the act by a law of 2 July 1959.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400130015-9:
A file on crash claims pairs a ruling on fault with a plea on work load. The ruling is a note for the record by John Warner, dated 7 November 1957. The point had been thrashed out with the Justice Department in past talks, he writes.

The line drawn then still stands, Warner holds. Mere slack care is not enough to make a man pay. The fault must rise to set purpose or gross slackness. The next text, dated 25 October 1955, goes to the transport chief. Counsel's shop drowns in plain claim mail, it says. Forms go out to men who claim on the state. Word on how a claim stands is sent, chased, and sent again. None of that work holds a point of law, the memo stresses. Counsel seeks a cleaner split of the chores.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400140005-9:
A memo dated 20 May 1958 sends a car-crash pay study to the support chief. The Board of Survey had met on 8 and 16 May to work it through. A field post's own plan sits at its heart, quoted whole. The aim was one rule for Agency cars on a world-wide base, in work use and in leave use alike.

The post's rule has two rungs. Gross fault: the driver pays in full. Plain slack care: the driver pays the true loss, capped at one hundred dollars. A fall-back is added in case law bars the mix. For work use, charge gross fault alone. For leave use, keep the plain-fault rule, capped near the cost of crash cover. The post calls that fair, and fit for the Agency's needs. The board's legal adviser was asked to lay out the law under those rungs. His views ride as a clip.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100020023-9:
A six-month report from the Office of Training takes stock of the school house. Class counts fell a shade in the half year. The dip is laid to the slow spell of the summer months. 

The raw counts run as follows. Two hundred fourteen classes ran inside, across sixty-eight courses. Mean class load stood at five hundred twenty-three a week. Six hundred fifty-six staff won leave to train at sites run by the state or by firms. Night and off-hour tongue classes held a mean of two hundred seventy-nine a week, in one hundred forty-six classes across seventeen tongues. Set tests in print went to near fifteen hundred staff in thirty-five tongues. Spoken tests ran to eight hundred twenty-two, in nineteen tongues. Cash prizes, some eighty-two thousand in all, went to about seven hundred staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100050002-9:
A bound report tells the tale of the 1959 War Planners Conference. Its front note sets the aim. The meet gave desk men at the core and men from the field one room. There, views on war plans, for world war and for small wars, could be swapped in the open. 

The weight of the meet sat in small group work. Teams took set snags in the plans and sought fixes or paths to fixes. The point was touch: men who mail each other all year could test each other's minds face to face. This was no brush-up course, the note stresses. Each group had its list of snags up front, drawn from the core and from field chiefs. The book is built in four parts: front note, talks, group work with a sum, and last words.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080063-9:
A program for training staff to perform well overseas is set out in a 9 June 1959 memorandum from the Chief of the Language and Area School to the Director of Training. The opening pages argue that Agency work rests on dealing with people abroad. Staff must understand foreign beliefs, motives, and habits if they are to judge what people overseas are doing and why.

The proposal builds toward a formal course on overseas effectiveness, offered four times a year in two-week full-time sessions. An attached outline, marked Annex A, gives the planned course content in detail. The memo also notes limits in present training capacity, even though many staff across the Agency were seen as needing this kind of preparation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100120004-9:
Responsibility for arranging Agency briefings for very important visitors is examined in a memorandum to the Director of Training. The visitors in question are newly designated ambassadors and senior military commanders. Transferring part of that duty from one office to the central briefing officer raised workload questions that the memo sets out to weigh.

Regulations, the memo finds, set no single point of contact and draw few clear lines for briefing outsiders on Agency work. Separate rules assign military attaché briefings to one office and administrative support for briefing and debriefing to another. Practical detail follows on briefing rooms, timing, transport, and escort needs, showing how much hidden labour sits behind a single visit from a senior guest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200050007-9:
Goods embargoed to China under the China Committee's system are set out in the International China Embargo List, document CH/260 (54). An index maps the list by category and number range. Metal-working machinery comes first, followed by chemical and petroleum gear, electrical equipment, transport, electronics, metals, chemicals, rubber, and miscellaneous goods.

The list itself is the China Special List revised as at 30 November 1953, replacing document CH/170. It holds every item the committee had agreed for embargo to China and North Korea, beyond the goods already covered by International Lists I, II, and III. A source column ties each definition to the document that recorded agreement on it, giving enforcement officials a traceable record for every line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200070014-9:
Control of non-communist trade with Communist China and North Korea is surveyed country by country in a long report marked secret security information. A contents page lays out the structure. Multilateral controls come first, through the Coordinating Committee and its China Committee and through the United Nations, then bilateral controls, then the controls each nation applied on its own.

Annexes carry the embargo detail, including a conflation of security listings, the China Special List, and the United Nations resolution of 18 May 1951 on measures against aggression in Korea. Country sections run from the United States, Britain, France, and Japan to Hong Kong, Macao, and many smaller trading states. The text notes, for example, British embargo of machine tools, ball bearings, generators, and steel mill gear for Communist China.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200080004-9:
Income and spending of the Coordinating Committee's secretariat for 1959 are reported by the chairman of its Budget Sub-Committee on 25 March 1960. Three statements are attached. One gives total expenditure, one gives cash income and expenditure, and one shows the pattern of contributions in kind and cash as it stood in December 1959.

The tables show most support arriving in kind rather than cash. Countries supplied people and services directly: Italy provided the chairman, Britain an executive assistant, the United States nine secretariat members, and France interpreting help. Cash covered a smaller share, for cleaning, telephone, and repairs. Looking ahead, the report warns that a change of premises may raise rent and service costs, while staff changes could save money.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100020089-9:
Work of the Map Library Division for February 1959 is summed up in a monthly report. Staff forwarded 21,109 map sheets to requesters in answer to 1,431 map requests, and sent out 851 publications against 157 requests for geographic publications. More requests arrived that month than in any previous February, the report notes.

Demand rose for maps of the North Atlantic, Germany, Berlin, and Africa, a pattern the report links to current events in those places. Staff answered 1,113 place-name questions and handled hundreds of other information requests, while 29 State Department members did research in the library. A separate stream of work served requests for ATMP charts and texts, and the reference branch weighed reorganising its staff workload by region.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100020098-9:
Views on the Office of Personnel, asked for during an Inspector General survey, are given in a 12 February 1959 memorandum from the Chief of Geographic Research. The first question put to him concerned the merits of a CIA Career Staff. His answer works through what such a staff is for before judging whether setting one apart helps the Agency.

A career staff meant only to mark out a favoured group is questioned as poor management practice. Building the wanted qualities across the whole Agency would serve better, he argues, with employment itself treated as the mark of standing. Later pages develop the idea of the Agency as an elite service, staffed by dedicated people working anonymously with high morale, and call it a long-term effort in education and public relations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100280054-9:
A trip in October 1958 is laid out hour by hour in an itinerary. Names and places are almost all blacked out in the copy released. Entries that survive for Monday 20 October show a first briefing. They also show a talk on the use of area studies in planning for unconventional warfare.

A need was also noted for ranked lists of towns. The towns are in the Soviet Union and its satellites. Lists of facts wanted on urban areas were also needed. The heavy blacking out hides the traveller, the hosts, and the sites. The record thus shows the shape of the visit, not who took part in it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200260019-9:
Workload stayed high for the Cartography Division in May 1959, its monthly report records. The division accepted one hundred sixty-six new jobs and completed one hundred twenty-six, yet jobs on the books rose to five hundred seventy by the start of June. The pressure came from efforts to meet commitments for fiscal year 1959.

Receipts fell while completions rose, and survey map proofing began to taper as the year's scheduled production passed its peak. A joint procedure with the map library had cut rerun requests by printing more copies at first and storing surplus stock at a records centre. One new job stood out: two hemisphere maps in full colour for the Central Intelligence Bulletin, the first full-colour world job placed with the terrain section.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200040019-9:
Agency views on a carrier-based U-2 are summed up in a draft note for the record dated 31 July 1957. Talks among the Navy, the Air Force, and the Agency had bred some confusion. Each side's stance was not clear to the others. The note sets out the Agency stand at each stage of the talks, in order.

An Agency study early in 1957 had reached a clear view. Carrier flights would add little or no cover of the Soviet bloc. Land bases in Western Europe, Turkey, and Japan already gave that cover. A carrier type would be needed only if the project lost a land base. It would also be needed if staging rights could not be won elsewhere. One step was agreed: Lockheed would be asked to study the design of a carrier type, though the case for building one was weak.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200100030-9:
Financing of special projects for fiscal year 1959 is proposed in memorandum DPS-3074, dated 12 August 1958, to the Director of Central Intelligence. During the past year, tasks run under Project AQUATONE had multiplied. Some had been handled as informal subprojects with no separate funding or accounting, and others on an ad hoc basis with only their first sums approved.

The remedy offered is to treat the work as five separate projects, each with its own estimated operating budget for the year and formal approval. For security, the nature of each activity is kept out of this paper. A contingency passage looks ahead: feasibility studies then running could mature during the year into development and procurement of a major new intelligence collection system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200130055-9:
Approvals and financial controls for the Development Projects Division are explained in a 4 March 1959 memorandum, DPD-1469-59. Policy choices would be made by approving blocks of activity, called programs. Original programs, and amendments over ten thousand dollars, needed approval from the deputy director for plans or from the Director of Central Intelligence himself.

Four kinds of amendment are separated, since each raises different problems. The first firms up a program whose early estimates were rough on some cost items; contract authority at first covers only the firm items. Later guidance covers changes of scope settled by brief exchanges between the contracting officer and the contractor. Each contracting officer must keep a running estimate of the total funding each contract needs for the fiscal year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200200002-9:
Diplomatic notes between the United States and the Soviet Union over an alleged border violation in the Far East are gathered in this file. The State Department's reply acknowledges a Soviet note of 21 April 1958. It restates an aide-memoire of 31 March: a thorough investigation had found no United States military aircraft near the place named, either over or outside Soviet territory, at the time alleged.

Standing orders, the reply adds, bar naval and air force aircraft on routine weather and training flights over the Sea of Japan from approaching Soviet territory. Washington has nothing further to add. A translation of a Soviet aide-memoire follows, alleging that on 2 March 1958 an American military jet violated the Soviet border, and pressing its protest in strong terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200260141-9:
Program designations for navigation instruments are proposed by Baird Associates in a paper dated 23 November 1955. Five programs are defined in a ladder of ambition. Program I is a remote viewing sextant with manual control. Later programs add viewing of the sun's disc at high magnification, an automatic sun sextant with photographic observation, and large-aperture sextants meant to see stars in daytime.

The firm proposes starting Program I at once and funding a study of whether stars can be seen in daylight. That study's outcome would decide whether later work followed the sun-sextant line or the daytime-star line. Money is handled plainly: the original contract would be extended to 1 December 1955 with added funds, and a new contract from that date would cover Program I plus the extra studies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00101a000100120060-9:
Electronic intelligence collection requirements are taken up in a 16 March 1959 memorandum from Richard M. Bissell, Deputy Director for Plans, to the Chief of the Special Requirements Staff. Two staff memoranda of 12 March had made a good start on the problem, and Bissell concurs with their recommendation to review the requirements. He holds his signature on the draft, though, pending reaction to three changes of his own.

The review should run under plans directorate auspices, with the letter going out over his own signature. The committee machinery for overhead reconnaissance should carry the review. Before the letter is sent, other interested consumers should be sounded out informally on whether that route suits them. An attachment list and a notice of a missing page in the original file close the released copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100040029-9:
A draft agenda for an electronics session is dated 18 August 1958. The session deals with economic facts on electronics. It opens with the Soviet electronics gear industry. The theme is growth. Since the war, Soviet skill in science and technique has risen fast. Output has grown in size and range. The industry once held back arms programs. It is now judged able to match the West in big new steps.

A base for making goods now exists. It can turn big science gains into real output. What stays hard to judge is rival demand for scarce goods. Such demand may squeeze some arms programs. It may also narrow Soviet choices. Later sessions turn to phone and radio links. There the same industry's gains show far less. That gap frames the puzzle at the heart of the talks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100040038-9:
The task of the Electronic Equipment Branch is stated in a short paper. The branch sits in the Industrial Division of the Office of Research and Reports. It makes all-source economic studies of the electronics trades of the Sino-Soviet bloc. It also helps line up that work across the United States government. Its results feed into national estimates.

The field is drawn wide. It covers parts and sub-parts for electronics and fine power gear. It covers gear for radio links, radar, and steering. It covers special army devices. It also covers plant power machines, wire and cable, and batteries. The branch draws up needs for collection. It gives guidance on those needs and judges the results. It works with outside advisers and adviser panels where help is wanted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100040083-9:
Signs of fast growth in the East German semiconductor industry are reported from a highly qualified source with good placement, the paper stresses. East Germany may now be advanced enough in semiconductor production to matter for Soviet bloc output of electronic parts for specialised weapons. The report places East Germany well ahead of the other satellite countries in this field.

Capability is said to rest more on techniques gained from West Germany than from the Soviet Union, though germanium supplies are reported to come from the Soviet side. Production types include germanium high-frequency and power transistor types for military use, with development work reported finished on a series of silicon transistor types. Silicon devices, which run at higher temperatures than germanium, are used mainly for military applications such as guided missiles.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100050019-9:
General requirements for intelligence on a classified subject are laid out in a paper that pairs target lists with the sources who might supply the news. Named installations open the list, among them an aircraft plant numbered 54, a tractor plant, and a bearing plant, followed by sites for heavy machinery and agricultural machine production. Location, construction, and transport details are wanted for each.

Sources are then ranked by what they can report. Construction workers and railroad workers lead, with messengers and porters close behind, followed by anyone working near factories or rail sidings, power plant workers, telephone operators, and airfield construction workers. A closing section on construction activity asks for news of new or recent building, above all where rail-served, and any sign of military, railroad, or subway work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100050064-9:
Requirements for the Dnepropetrovsk Motor Vehicle Works, known as DAZ, are set out in a July requirements paper sent through the Industrial Division to the Guided Missile Branch. A major industrial site in the southwest urban area of Dnepropetrovsk, the plant holds several hangar-type factory buildings, two large cooling towers. One large chimney, all inside a high masonry wall that gives the exterior the look of a fortress.

Expansion is suspected, with new construction reported to include buildings about fifty feet tall. The paper also gives the site by air. It lies about six and a half nautical miles south-southwest of Voloshkoye airfield and one nautical mile east-southeast of the Dnepropetrovsk airfield. A single-track railroad on the plant's southeast edge curves southward to join the Nikolayev line.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120057-9:
Notes on Project 32.488 open with a house point. Pages four to six repeat what the paper's own word list already shows. Most of that matter should move to a back section. First, text and word list should be checked side by side. A meaning is also challenged. The point is not one plant only. It is all the works and gear under the trade sector's control.

How the money scope is drawn is queried next. Does a passage cover building paid from a firm's own funds? Or does it also cover social works run by trade but paid from the state budget? Wording on new capacity draws a further note. In 1958, as in 1953 to 1955, less capacity was set up than planned each year. Much of what was set up faced long test runs before it ran steadily.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100150054-9:
Clearer meanings for Soviet trade figures are sought in a paper dated 4 May 1959. Study of Soviet output figures had reached a point of block. Gaps in the meanings and scope of some classes held the work up. The facts wanted had not been picked out before. Yet Soviet officials had spoken openly of like faults in past years. They did so in learned and official settings.

The questions deal with classes for which the Soviets print figures. A rendering of the tables is attached. One table gives the shares of goods for making and goods for use. A sample question is then posed. What is the total ruble value of the turnover tax in one table? Or how would a stated share change if that tax were folded in?
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100020069-9:
Work of the Economic Research Area is summed up for the annual report to the President's Board of Consultants. The paper is dated 3 October 1953. Study of the economic side of Soviet arms technique kept first place. The office was the chief source on factors bearing on guided missiles and space craft. That work fed a recent national estimate.

Strong help also went to a special estimate on the Soviet long-range bomber force. The office fed estimates of Soviet nuclear attack strength and of air defence strength in 1962. The task backed the Net Evaluation Subcommittee of the National Security Council. It took in the timing and costing of the programs. It weighed their load on the Soviet economy. Special help went to judging the new Soviet bomber called 'Bounder.'
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040085-9: Enclosing letters from late November and December 1959, several on file in more than one copy, send out the Director's statement to the Joint Economic Committee of 13 November 1959. The statement is described as embodying the latest thinking on United States and Soviet economic growth and showing the close relationship between intelligence and policy. One writer thanks a host for an enjoyable campus visit and offers unclassified materials to help the reader's research. The scan is poor, and names are blacked out throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100040166-9:
First meetings of the Office of Research and Reports' Senior Economic Advisory Panel are recorded in a memorandum for the record dated 18 September 1959. The newly appointed panel of outside professors met in Washington from 9 to 11 September 1959. Briefings covered the United States intelligence community and the mission of the Economic Research Area within it.

The main work was a detailed examination of the office's contribution to National Intelligence Estimate 11-4-59, on Soviet capabilities and probable courses of action through 1964. Reviewing that paper let the panel sample the work of many components on a subject central to the area's mission. Findings were presented orally to senior staff. Discussion ranged over the Soviet manpower problem: one view held the Soviets keep much potential industrial labour tucked away in overstaffed activities such as security forces and school administration.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090026-9:
'The Nature of the Communist Threat' is addressed by General C. P. Cabell, Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, to the American Legion's national security meetings at Minneapolis on 21 August 1959. The threat of Communism is long-term and many-sided, he tells the Legion, and there must be no blinders in looking at its size. Its aim is stated flatly. The Communists want to rule the world and end free society.

The speech then works region by region through Communist tools. In Latin America, a Soviet spy officer is named. Vadim Kotchergin had travelled with a Soviet trade union team. His task was to guide Cuban Communists. He has since returned to Moscow. A chief Soviet tool in the region is also named. It is the Confederation of Workers of Latin America, based in Mexico. It acts as the regional link body of the World Federation of Trade Unions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090080-9:
The Soviet Challenge is the text of an address given at Yale University on February 3, 1958, kept in Agency files. Its theme is that the Soviet threat rests on science and technical skill. The speaker points to Soviet clandestine communications work as proof of that skill.

The address urges the free world to pool its scientific assets more fully. It grants that security rules must stay, but warns against letting them block joint work. It also weighs Soviet military output, made with less than half the industrial base of the United States. Low military pay and tight focus are offered as the reasons that output stays so high.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100006-9:
The Soviet Economic System Part I is a declassified Agency lecture text from an address at Maxwell Air Force Base on 25 January 1960. The speaker opens with a joke about giving two lectures on so broad a topic. He then sketches the Russian economy of 1903, the base year for many Soviet claims.

That sketch corrects two rival pictures of the old regime. Soviet accounts, he says, paint tsarist Russia as wholly backward, which the record does not support. Later parts explain how the Communist Party directs the economy through republics and regional councils. Party officials who run that machinery are named as the chief gainers from its restored control.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100040003-9:
Foreign Attitudes Toward Economic Defense is Staff Study No. 3 in the CFEP Drafting Group's Economic Defense Policy Review, in revised draft form from June 1955. Its contents list ten country studies. They run from the United Kingdom and Canada through France, Germany, and Italy to Greece and Turkey.

The Italy study shows the kind of detail the survey sought. Weak pay for enforcement staff is blamed for lax control work there. Monopolies and cartels, state and private, held a favored place. A small set of traders and firm heads is described as ready to deal in strategic exports for outsized illegal profit. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100120004-9:
An untitled policy paper in declassified Agency files asks what stance the United States should take when poorer nations accept Soviet Bloc trade and aid offers. It states that the same basic problem of Bloc entry exists in all poorer free world areas. Only the stress and degree change from place to place.

United States policy, the paper notes, sought joint selective controls on strategic exports, not a total embargo. It urges a flexible stance that leaves room to meet Soviet moves early. One tactic is named with care: aid recipients could hold up a Soviet offer to press Washington for better terms, and the paper warns against letting that game set United States policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100130003-9:
The Consultative Group; A Review of Major Accomplishments and Basic Problems is Staff Study No. 13 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 1, 1955, prepared by the Commerce Department. It looks back at the body that coordinated free world security export controls. Its first section traces the origin of United States and joint strategic export controls.

Open problems fill the later pages. Some goods left over from a list revision, such as metal rolling mills and ships, still lacked agreed treatment. That gap made it hard for the United States to defend embargoes on goods it judged highly strategic. Differing control levels toward the European Bloc and Communist China, sharpened by the Korean armistice, close the review. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100140002-9:
Comments on CFEP Staff Study #15 form a declassified Agency office memorandum on a draft of 6 June 1955. The study sought ways to make the CG, COCOM, and CHINCOM control bodies work better. The comment opens harshly: the draft offers thin conclusions with almost no supporting argument.

Credit is given where the draft starts well. It rightly notes that no shared philosophy backed the trade control system. It also catches the gap between an aggressive United States concept and the narrower stance of some allies. The comment's own remedy is a stated overall philosophy for controls. Such a creed would let partner governments explain the system's aims in plain terms at home.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020013-9:
Language Development Program is an Agency regulation in revised form, marked confidential in its release. Its contents run from policies and language requirements through testing, records, training, and awards. The program exists to build the foreign language skills the Agency's work demands.

Deputy Directors set the language requirements that form the program's goals. Tests of aptitude and skill are run, and personnel records track each result. Money awards reward staff who gain and hold useful language skill. The Director of Training holds wide duties under the scheme: naming awardable languages, running Achievement and Maintenance Awards, and issuing the material needed to carry the program out.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe — Volume 9 closes Richardson's novel in letters with the heroine's last arrangements and death. She repeats her request that Colonel Morden not seek to avenge her wrongs. Belford is asked to heal all breaches. A miniature of Miss Howe, kept at her bosom, is to go to Mr. Hickman after her decease.

Belford warns Mowbray to keep Lovelace from harming himself when the fatal news arrives. Lovelace's answering letter is filled with rage, curses, and swings of despair and hope. Three letters reach the house too late, addressed to the departed lady. They bring a general reconciliation on her own conditions, and her family's returning love.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-9:
The last Loeb volume of Dio Cassius holds books seventy-one through eighty in Byzantine epitome, with the set's index. Earnest Cary's translation closes the eighty-book history that Dio wrote around 230 CE. The story runs from Hadrian to Severus Alexander, close to the author's own lifetime.

Marcus Aurelius fights on the Danube, Commodus struts and falls, and the Severan house takes the throne. Dio served under these last emperors, so his tale turns into near-witness report. The history that began with Aeneas ends in his own senate years. No other Roman narrative covers so long a span in one voice.
easy-money-night-watches-part-9:
W. W. Jacobs lets his night-watchman spin another quay-side yarn in Easy Money, part nine of Night Watches. The watchman watches a young sailor walk off arm in arm with a girl and shakes his head. If a man marries he wishes he had not, he says, and if he does not, he wishes he had.

The tale turns to Sam Small's nephew, a country boy new to a London job and deep in love. His mother writes to Sam for advice, and Sam reads the letter aloud to Peter Russet and Ginger Dick about seven times. Peter recalls a girl a regiment could not have parted him from; another girl did. Ginger ends up on an omnibus beside a dressed-up beauty, sure this beats the sea. Jacobs writes the talk in thick quay dialect, and the laugh rides on old sailors matchmaking badly.
froude-history-england-vol-9:
The road to the Armada runs through the ninth volume of Froude's History, from 1856. The Babington plot aims at Elizabeth's life and Mary's release. Mary stands trial and dies at Fotheringhay, while Spain prepares its vast fleet for war.

Froude builds the tension chapter by chapter toward the coming storm. Readers feel the danger long before the sails appear in the Channel. Secret letters, Walsingham's spies, and Philip's slow armada drive the tale. The volume forms the penultimate act of his Tudor epic, a fuse burning toward the famous deliverance that his next book celebrates in full.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-9:
Thompson's minutes record the first plenary session of the Potsdam Conference, at 5 p.m. on July 17, 1945. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The three leaders met with Truman in the chair, a choice Stalin proposed and Churchill seconded.

Truman asked leave to propose agenda items, and Stalin agreed. Eden won the point that all members could add items of their own. Truman then read his proposal for a Council of Foreign Ministers. His second paper, on Germany, he handed in for study without reading it. Churchill asked if the matters were not to be considered now, and Truman replied he was merely proposing agenda items. Churchill moved that the first item go to the foreign ministers. Stalin agreed, but questioned China's place in a council meant for European problems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-9:
Ginnie Mae meets its mission but faces a changing market, GAO concludes in report GAO-06-9, dated October 31, 2005. Ginnie Mae is a wholly owned government firm. It backs mortgage securities built from loans insured by federal housing programs.

Congress noted that Ginnie Mae's share of the mortgage security market had fallen sharply. GAO studied the state of that share and of guarantee volume. It weighed what a smaller share could mean. It also set out the hurdles Ginnie Mae faces and steps it has taken, or could take. The report gives housing finance readers a clear snapshot of a public backer under market pressure.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-9:
The Darfur crisis and aid efforts fill GAO-07-9, a report dated November 9, 2006. Conflict broke out in Darfur, Sudan, in 2003. Rebels, government troops, and the Janjaweed militia drove about 2 million people from their homes. Over 1.9 million others need aid to survive. The United States has given help since October 2003. It also backs the African Union Mission in Sudan. GAO reviewed the aid flow and the peace mission's work.

The United States provided nearly $1 billion in aid from fiscal years 2004 through 2006. Food aid made up over 68 percent of that total. Malnutrition and death rates fell between 2004 and 2005. Attacks on aid convoys and banditry block deliveries, though. Sudan's government restricts access to displaced communities. The African Union force struggles with funding and logistics. GAO urged a lessons-learned review of the mission. The State Department backed that call.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-9: This 2007 GAO report studies D.C.'s voucher plan, which lets poor kids use public money for private school. GAO found the program's books and daily running needed tighter rules and cleaner steps. The report lands in the middle of a hot school-choice fight — asking whether the program's promise to kids was matched by grown-up management.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-9:
Haunted houses of the mind fill the ninth volume of Archer's 1908 Ibsen. Rosmersholm traps its lovers in a manor where the past poisons every present hope. The Lady from the Sea gives us Ellida, torn between a safe husband and a mysterious sailor who claims her from the deep.

Guilt drives Rosmer and Rebecca toward the mill-race in a ending of quiet horror. Ellida's story moves the other way, toward freedom granted and freely chosen. These middle plays show Ibsen leaving social realism for symbol and mystery. Their strangeness rewards slow reading or a darkened stage. Few volumes in the set feel so unlike anything written before them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-abba-ha-l: Aaron Abba ha-Levi ben Johanan, a prominent rabbi, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He was born about the close of the sixteenth century and died in Lemberg on June 18, 1643. He presided over a rabbinical college in Lemberg. His decisions appear in the responsa of Abraham Rapoport, Joel Sarkes, and Meir Lublin. Lublin spoke especially highly of him, the entry notes. In one case Aaron is shown condemning rigorism, or excess strictness, in the Law.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-9:
Part Nine calls New Orleans the metropolis of the South. Chapter 41 finds the city's approaches familiar and unchanged. High river water lifts boats level with the levee rim. Travelers look down into upper windows of houses below.

Old brick salt-warehouses cluster at the city's upper end. War news once turned their cheap salt into metaphorical gold overnight. The proprietor woke to find prices risen to dizzy heights. Vast plank wharves remained as Twain remembered them. Plank wharves stretched vast and unchanged along the landing. Aladdin's lamp, Twain jokes, had touched those vulgar salt sacks.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-9:
John Chrysostom, the golden-mouthed preacher of Antioch and Constantinople, enters Schaff's Nicene Fathers in volume nine of the first series, from 1886. The volume holds his treatise On the Priesthood, his ascetic writings, and select homilies and letters. The Homilies on the Statues close it.

On the Priesthood, a dialogue with his friend Basil, weighs the terrors of leading souls and Chrysostom's own flight from ordination. The Statues homilies were preached as Antioch trembled after a riot tore down the emperor's images, awaiting his revenge. Chrysostom calmed the city week by week. The volume shows why his preaching is still read for its force and pastoral nerve.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-9:
Hilary of Poitiers and John of Damascus, four centuries apart, share volume nine of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890. Hilary was the West's champion against Arianism, exiled for the faith he defended. John, a monk near Jerusalem under Muslim rule, was the last of the Greek fathers. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Hilary's work on the Trinity brought Greek theology into Latin dress. John's Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith then sums up the whole Greek tradition in one ordered system. His defense of holy images, written from beyond the empire's reach, helped win icons their place. The volume bridges the first councils and the age of Byzantium.
skilled-assistance-ship-s-company-part-9:
Skilled Assistance comes from Ship's Company by W. W. Jacobs, and a night-watchman at Wapping tells the tale. He grouses about a woman who keeps asking whether the Silvia has come up. She has, he says, called four or five times in a week, and she scolds him as if he were paid to wait on her alone.

Her temper puts him in mind of Cap'n Pinner, who sailed the schooner Snipe between Wapping and Hull. Pinner had a small cottage near Hull, and his wife's father, a man of near seventy, lived with them there. The watchman's pub talk sets up a yarn about help given, and help that may not be all it seems.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-9:
The burial of Jesus opens volume nine of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations. Matthew's text tells how Joseph of Arimathea begged the body, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in his own new tomb, rolling a great stone to the door. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary kept watch across from the grave.

Next, an angel rolls back the stone at dawn and tells the women Christ is risen. Then comes the walk to Emmaus. Doré's dark tomb scenes give way to bright ones as the gallery nears its close.
the-head-of-the-family-sailor-s-knots-pa:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Head of the Family, a story in Sailors' Knots, dated 1909. Mr. Letts leaves his ship by joint agreement after working as cook on the schooner Curlew, a job he took after years on long voyages. The crew musters to see him off, and their harsh words from the quay at Dunchurch show how his cooking was judged.

Letts takes a room at a seamen's lodging-house and sits by the sea to plan what comes next. A middle-aged woman joins his bench, and he asks her, out of curiosity, how long she would boil a piece of beef. She tells him she lost a son at sea, and that he puts her in mind of the boy.
the-madness-of-mr-lister-captains-all-bo:
W. W. Jacobs's The Madness of Mr. Lister is the ninth book in his Captains All series of sea stories. Old Jem Lister of the Susannah is possessed of two devils, Jacobs says: the love of strong drink and avarice. The two meet in one habit, getting a drink without paying for it. When Lister pays, his avarice preaches him a teetotal lecture; when he reforms, his thirst sends him cadging at public-house doors, to his shipmates' shame.

His crew finally sends Bill Henshaw as spokesman, whose remarks leave little to be desired for violence and nothing unsaid for profanity. Their demand is simple: turn over a new leaf, and stand the men a round at the Goat and Compasses out of his hoarded sovereigns. Lister answers with a senile, venomous laugh and goes on deck to glower.
the-persecution-of-bob-pretty-odd-craft-:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Persecution of Bob Pretty as part of his Odd Craft tales. An old man on his bench outside the Cauliflower inn, beer at his elbow and a churchwarden pipe smoking, entertains two resting young men with talk of Claybury. Poaching, he says, is not what it used to be in these parts.

He points out Bob Pretty, the slyest, most artful man who ever lived in Claybury, who never did an honest day's work and never lacked the price of ale. Bob's worst time came after old Squire Brown died, when a rich Londoner named Rockett took the place and game preserving tightened. Jacobs's humor rests on the old man's voice.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-9:
Part 9 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XXXII, Coronation Day. The narrative steps backward a few hours to Westminster Abbey at four in the morning. Torch-lit galleries are already filling with people content to sit seven or eight hours for a sight they may not hope to see twice: the coronation of a king. London and Westminster have been astir since the warning guns boomed at three.

The packed galleries wait through the dragging hours. The great north transept stands empty for England's privileged ones. On the carpeted platform the throne rises on four steps. Inside its seat lies the stone of Scone, a rough flat rock on which generations of Scottish kings were crowned. Throne and footstool are covered with cloth of gold. At last daylight softens the torchlight, and at seven the first peeress enters in splendour.
the-substitute-deep-waters-part-9:
W. W. Jacobs tells this Deep Waters story through his night watchman. The man has just returned to the office fire from the wharf bell. It was the third that week from mischievous boys. The watchman complains: some people have boys, other people have the trouble of them. He launches into the worst boy he ever knew. The lad was a former office-boy there.

The lad was undersized. His face was the colour of bad pie-crust, his eyes like shoe-buttons. He stayed late pretending to work for a rise. One eye watched the ledger. The other eye watched the watchman. Once the boy found the watchman gone for half a pint. He raised a false alarm of drowning. A policeman, two carmen, and the crew of the Maid Marian turned out. The watchman never forgave the trick. Then a little steamer, the Eastern Monarch, enters the tale.
un-ga-res-9:
Peoples who could not yet rule themselves had no seat at the first General Assembly, and Resolution 9, passed on 9 February 1946, speaks for them. The text notes that whole peoples still lacked a full share of self-rule and had no voice in the hall. Chapters XI, XII, and XIII of the Charter treat their plight as a core concern for peace and the common good.

Under Chapter XI, states that rule such lands accept a sacred trust. The good of the people in those lands comes first. The ruling states must build self-rule and help free political life grow, step by step. Chapters XII and XIII add the trusteeship system, UN watch over lands placed under its care.
un-ga-res-a-69-9: Joint work with the League of Arab States fills Resolution A/69/9, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls past votes on the tie and the League's own pact, which charges its council with finding ways to work with world bodies for peace. It takes note of the Secretary-General's Agenda for Peace and its call for closer work with regional groups. A 2013 Security Council meeting on such joint work is welcomed.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 9 (I), adopted by the General Assembly on 9 February 1946, is the Assembly's first word on peoples who do not yet govern themselves. It states that the Charter's Chapter XI obligations toward Non-Self-Governing peoples were already in force and did not depend on any later agreement.

The Assembly welcomes the stated intention of states administering League of Nations mandates to negotiate trusteeship agreements. It notes one territory's move toward independence. It asks the Secretary-General to include in his annual report a summary of the political, economic, social, and educational information transmitted under Article 73e of the Charter. Coming months after the Charter took effect, the resolution put the Assembly on record that colonial obligations were immediate duties, not future promises.

Resolution 69/9 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, covers cooperation between the United Nations and the League of Arab States. It asks the two secretariats to deepen consultations and information exchange. The exchange spans political, economic, cultural, disarmament and peacebuilding work. It calls for the review of their 1989 cooperation agreement to be sped up. It schedules the twelfth sectoral meeting for Cairo in early 2015, on human rights. It schedules the thirteenth general meeting for 2016.
un-sc-res-9:
Access to the World Court for states outside its Statute was set by the Security Council on 15 October 1946. Article 35 of the Court's Statute lets the Council fix the conditions. A state that is not a party to the Statute may still come before the International Court of Justice. It must first deposit a declaration with the Court's Registrar.

By that declaration the state accepts the Court's jurisdiction under the Charter and the Statute and Rules of the Court. It promises to comply in good faith with the Court's decisions. It also accepts the duties of a United Nations member under Article 94 of the Charter. The declaration may cover one named dispute or disputes in general, present or future. A state may accept the Court's compulsory jurisdiction, though not against Statute parties without agreement. The Registrar keeps the originals and sends certified copies to all states concerned.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 9, adopted unanimously on 15 October 1946, opens the World Court's doors to countries outside its own statute. The International Court of Justice had just begun work, and some states were not parties to its statute. Under the UN Charter, the Council sets the conditions on which such states may appear before the court.

The resolution sets one main condition: the state must first deposit a declaration accepting the court's jurisdiction under the Charter, the statute, and the rules. It must promise to comply in good faith with the court's decisions and accept the duties members owe under Article 94 of the Charter. Declarations may cover one dispute or disputes generally, including compulsory jurisdiction.
